paragraphs: Constrained optimization asks for a good solution while requiring that specified conditions remain satisfied. This paper explores whether analog circuits can carry out that kind of computation adequately. The focus includes constraints that change over time, making correct handling of the conditions part of the circuit's ongoing operation.

The authors design the circuits using the differential multiplier method. This provides the stated mathematical route from the optimization problem to an analog implementation. The reported circuits satisfy time-varying constraints correctly, addressing the question of whether changing requirements can be accommodated within the proposed circuit approach.

The examples include a quadratic programming circuit and a constrained flip-flop. They give concrete forms to the broader proposal that analog circuitry can implement constrained optimization. The significance of the reported result lies in constraint handling as well as optimization: a circuit must respect the permitted conditions while doing its computational work. The paper presents its designs and examples as evidence that these two requirements can be brought together.
summary.tldr: Analog circuits designed with the differential multiplier method perform constrained optimization while correctly satisfying changing constraints.

title: Analog Circuits for Constrained Optimization

abstract: Because eye muscles never cocontract and do not deal with external loads, one can write an equation that relates motoneuron firing rate to eye position and velocity - a very uncommon situation in the CNS. The semicircular canals transduce head velocity in a linear manner by using a high background discharge rate, imparting linearity to the premotor circuits that generate eye movements. This has allowed deducing some of the signal processing involved, including a neural network that integrates. These ideas are often summarized by block diagrams. Unfortunately, they are of little value in describing the behavior of single neurons - a fmding supported by neural network models.

The semicircular canals transduce head velocity in a linear manner by using a high background discharge rate, imparting linearity to the premotor circuits that generate eye movements. Unfortunately, they are of little value in describing the behavior of single neurons - a fmding supported by neural network models.

paragraphs: This paper explains why eye movements offer an unusually tractable setting for relating neural activity to behavior. Under the account given, eye muscles do not cocontract or contend with external loads. These properties allow an equation connecting motoneuron firing rate with eye position and velocity, providing a direct link between neural signals and movement.

The semicircular canals encode head velocity approximately linearly using a high background firing rate. This helps impart linearity to the premotor circuitry that generates eye movements. Such relationships allow researchers to deduce signal-processing operations, including integration by a neural network, from the behavior of the overall system.

The paper also highlights a limit of representing these operations with block diagrams. A diagram can summarize the computation performed by a circuit while offering little guidance about the behavior of a particular neuron within it. Neural-network models support this distinction, emphasizing that a system-level processing description does not directly specify individual cellular responses.
summary.tldr: Eye-movement mechanics reveal circuit-level computations, but those computations do not readily explain individual neurons' responses.

title: Information Processing to Create Eye Movements

abstract: We have recently developed a theory of spatial representations in which the position of an object is not encoded in a particular frame of reference but, instead, involves neurons computing basis func(cid:173) tions of their sensory inputs. This type of representation is able to perform nonlinear sensorimotor transformations and is consis(cid:173) tent with the response properties of parietal neurons. We now ask whether the same theory could account for the behavior of human patients with parietal lesions. These lesions induce a deficit known as hemineglect that is characterized by a lack of reaction to stimuli located in the hemispace contralateral to the lesion. A simulated lesion in a basis function representation was found to replicate three of the most important aspects of hemineglect: i) The models failed to cross the leftmost lines in line cancellation experiments, ii) the deficit affected multiple frames of reference and, iii) it could be object centered. These results strongly support the basis function hypothesis for spatial representations and provide a computational theory of hemineglect at the single cell level.

paragraphs: Hemineglect involves failing to respond to stimuli on the side of space opposite a parietal brain lesion. This paper asks whether a theory originally developed to explain spatial representation can also explain this impairment. In that theory, neurons compute basis functions of sensory inputs, collectively representing position without committing to one particular reference frame.

Such a representation can support nonlinear transformations between sensory information and motor responses, and it is consistent with the response properties of parietal neurons. The authors test its consequences by introducing a simulated lesion. This lets them examine whether damage to the proposed representation produces recognizable patterns of spatial neglect.

The damaged model reproduces three reported features: missing the leftmost lines during line cancellation, deficits spanning multiple reference frames, and neglect organized relative to an object. These results support the basis-function hypothesis by connecting its neural representation to behavioral consequences of damage. The work thus offers a single-cell-level computational account linking ordinary spatial processing with several manifestations of hemineglect.
summary.tldr: Simulated damage to a basis-function model of spatial representation reproduces three major features of hemineglect.

title: A Model of Spatial Representations in Parietal Cortex Explains Hemineglect

abstract: A new boosting algorithm of Freund and Schapire is used to improve the performance of decision trees which are constructed using the information ratio criterion of Quinlan's C4.5 algorithm. This boosting algorithm iteratively constructs a series of decision trees, each decision tree being trained and pruned on examples that have been filtered by previously trained trees. Examples that have been incorrectly classified by the previous trees in the ensemble are resampled with higher probability to give a new probability distribution for the next tree in the ensemble to train on. Results from optical character recognition (OCR), and knowledge discovery and data mining problems show that in comparison to single trees, or to trees trained independently, or to trees trained on subsets of the feature space, the boosting ensemble is much better.

paragraphs: This paper applies Freund and Schapire's boosting algorithm to decision trees built using the information ratio criterion from C4.5. The central idea is to construct a sequence of trees in which earlier mistakes influence the training examples presented to later trees. Each tree is trained and pruned using examples filtered through the preceding ensemble.

Examples that previous trees classify incorrectly receive a higher chance of being resampled. This changes the training distribution for the next tree, directing more attention toward cases the ensemble has found difficult. The trees are therefore connected through their training process: the errors of existing members guide the construction of subsequent members.

The authors report results on optical character recognition and on knowledge discovery and data mining problems. The boosted ensemble performs substantially better than single trees, independently trained trees, and trees trained on subsets of the available features. These comparisons support the usefulness of sequentially adapting the training distribution, beyond simply collecting multiple trees into an ensemble.
summary.tldr: Boosting improves decision trees by training successive trees more often on examples that earlier trees misclassified.

title: Boosting Decision Trees

paragraphs: This paper describes an alphanumeric handwriting recognition module built around two neural networks. The first finds individual characters within a field containing letters and numbers; the second classifies those characters. Both operate on Gabor projections derived from the original pixel images, a representation reported to improve recognition and resistance to noise.

The system also includes substantial application-specific postprocessing, extending its purely numeric counterpart. It runs on specialized parallel hardware at 80 characters per second per board and was installed at the United Kingdom's Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency. The contribution therefore covers a complete deployed recognition system, including character finding, classification, postprocessing, and hardware execution.

Without rejecting inputs, the reported success rate exceeds 96% per character and reaches 85% per field. Rejecting approximately 20% of fields raises success on the accepted material to 99.8% per character and 99.5% per field. These figures show why both evaluation levels matter: an entire field can fail when an individual character is wrong. They also make the tradeoff between coverage and recognition accuracy explicit.
summary.tldr: Kodak's deployed handwriting system combines two neural networks, Gabor features, and postprocessing, reaching 99.5% field accuracy when roughly 20% of fields are rejected.

title: KODAK lMAGELINK™ OCR Alphanumeric Handprint Module

abstract: We have already shown that extracting long-term dependencies from se(cid:173) quential data is difficult, both for determimstic dynamical systems such as recurrent networks, and probabilistic models such as hidden Markov models (HMMs) or input/output hidden Markov models (IOHMMs). In practice, to avoid this problem, researchers have used domain specific a-priori knowledge to give meaning to the hidden or state variables rep(cid:173) resenting past context. In this paper, we propose to use a more general type of a-priori knowledge, namely that the temporal dependencIes are structured hierarchically. This implies that long-term dependencies are represented by variables with a long time scale. This principle is applied to a recurrent network which includes delays and multiple time scales. Ex(cid:173) periments confirm the advantages of such structures. A similar approach is proposed for HMMs and IOHMMs.

paragraphs: Learning from sequences requires preserving information that may become useful much later. The paper starts from the difficulty of extracting these long-term dependencies in recurrent networks and hidden Markov models. It notes that researchers have addressed the problem by giving hidden states meanings based on knowledge of a particular application.

The authors propose a more general structural assumption: temporal dependencies form a hierarchy. Under this assumption, information needed over long intervals should be represented by variables that evolve over long time scales. They apply the principle to a recurrent network with delays and multiple time scales, giving different parts of the model different temporal roles.

Experiments confirm advantages for these structures. The authors also propose extending the same organizing principle to hidden Markov models and input/output hidden Markov models. The contribution is a way to use prior knowledge about the organization of time without specifying the meaning of every hidden variable. Its usefulness rests on representing long-lived context through correspondingly slow internal variables.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical recurrent networks use delays and multiple time scales to make long-term sequence dependencies easier to represent.

title: Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Networks for Long-Term Dependencies

paragraphs: Belief propagation is exact on cycle-free probabilistic graphs, which historically discouraged its use when loops are present. This paper highlights a surprising counterexample from communication: highly successful error-correcting decoders can be understood as probability propagation in graphs with cycles. Practical success therefore extends beyond the usual exactness guarantee.

The communication setting encodes information into redundant transmitted bits, observes noisy channel outputs, and infers the original message. The probabilistic view expresses decoding through posterior beliefs about information bits. Message passing provides a common language for understanding how strong decoding algorithms combine local evidence and coding constraints.

The contribution is a conceptual bridge between graphical-model inference and error-correcting codes. It motivates studying loopy propagation as an effective approximate algorithm instead of rejecting it solely because exact tree-based analysis no longer applies. The observation does not make propagation exact on arbitrary cyclic graphs; it shows that useful inference can arise despite that limitation.
summary.tldr: Successful error-correcting decoders reveal that belief propagation can work remarkably well on cyclic graphs despite lacking general exactness.

title: A Revolution: Belief Propagation in Graphs with Cycles

abstract: An asynchronous PDM (Pulse-Density-Modulating) digital neural network system has been developed in our laboratory. It consists of one thousand neurons that are physically interconnected via one million 7-bit synapses. It can solve one thousand simultaneous nonlinear first-order differential equations in a fully parallel and continuous fashion. The performance of this system was measured by a winner-take-all network with one thousand neurons. Although the magnitude of the input and network parameters were identi(cid:173) cal for each competing neuron, one of them won in 6 milliseconds. This processing speed amounts to 360 billion connections per sec(cid:173) ond. A broad range of neural networks including spatiotemporal filtering, feedforward, and feedback networks can be run by loading appropriate network parameters from a host system.

paragraphs: This paper presents a physical neural network containing one thousand neurons and one million connections, each represented with seven bits. The system uses asynchronous pulse-density modulation: activity is conveyed through the density of pulses. Its hardware can evolve one thousand coupled nonlinear first-order differential equations continuously and in parallel, making the network dynamics themselves the computation.

The authors assess performance with a winner-take-all network containing all one thousand neurons. Such a network makes competing units settle on a single winner. Even though each competing neuron receives inputs and network parameters of identical magnitude, one neuron wins within six milliseconds. The authors report that this corresponds to a processing rate of 360 billion connections per second.

The hardware also supports different network configurations by loading parameters from a host system. These include feedforward networks, feedback networks, and networks for filtering information across space and time. The contribution therefore combines a demonstration of fast collective dynamics with a programmable physical platform for several kinds of neural computation.
summary.tldr: A programmable neural hardware system runs one thousand neurons through one million physical connections and demonstrates rapid winner-take-all dynamics.

title: A 1, 000-Neuron System with One Million 7-bit Physical Interconnections

abstract: We prove that the Canonical Distortion Measure (CDM) [2, 3] is the optimal distance measure to use for I nearest-neighbour (l-NN) classifi(cid:173) cation, and show that it reduces to squared Euclidean distance in feature space for function classes that can be expressed as linear combinations of a fixed set of features. PAC-like bounds are given on the sample(cid:173) complexity required to learn the CDM. An experiment is presented in which a neural network CDM was learnt for a Japanese OCR environ(cid:173) ment and then used to do I-NN classification.

PAC-like bounds are given on the sample(cid:173) complexity required to learn the CDM. An experiment is presented in which a neural network CDM was learnt for a Japanese OCR environ(cid:173) ment and then used to do I-NN classification.

paragraphs: A one-nearest-neighbor classifier bases its decision on the closest stored example, making the definition of distance central to its behavior. The paper studies the Canonical Distortion Measure as a principled choice of distance and proves its optimality for one-nearest-neighbor classification within the framework considered.

The authors also establish a connection to familiar feature-based distances. When the relevant function class consists of linear combinations of a fixed collection of features, the Canonical Distortion Measure becomes squared Euclidean distance in that feature space. This links the abstract measure to a concrete procedure: represent examples through the chosen features and compare their squared distances.

The paper provides PAC-like bounds on the number of samples required to learn the measure. It also presents an experiment in which a neural network learns a Canonical Distortion Measure for Japanese optical character recognition and then supplies the distance for nearest-neighbor classification. Together, the theory and application treat similarity as something grounded in the learning problem and potentially learned from examples.
summary.tldr: The Canonical Distortion Measure provides a theoretically grounded distance for nearest-neighbor classification and reduces to feature-space squared distance in a stated setting.

title: The Canonical Distortion Measure in Feature Space and 1-NN Classification

abstract: We consider online learning in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space. Our method is computationally efﬁcient and leads to simple algorithms. In particular we derive update equations for classiﬁcation, regression, and novelty detection. The inclusion of the -trick allows us to give a robust parameterization. Moreover, unlike in batch learning where the -trick only applies to the -insensitive loss function we are able to derive gen- eral trimmed-mean types of estimators such as for Huber’s robust loss.

paragraphs: The paper develops online learning in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a mathematical setting for kernel-based prediction. Online learning updates a model as observations are processed. The authors aim for a computationally efficient approach that produces simple algorithms while retaining the expressive framework supplied by kernels.

They derive update equations for classification, regression, and novelty detection. These cover assigning categories, predicting numerical values, and identifying observations that differ from the expected pattern. Presenting updates for all three tasks shows how a common online kernel framework can support several kinds of learning objective.

The paper also develops a robust parameterization and extends the construction to trimmed-mean types of estimators, including an estimator for Huber’s robust loss. The abstract contrasts this flexibility with a batch-learning construction restricted to an insensitive loss function. The significance is that the online formulation supports a broader range of robust estimation choices alongside its simple updates, making robustness part of the learning framework rather than a separate task.
summary.tldr: An efficient online kernel framework supplies updates for several prediction tasks and supports broader robust estimators.

title: Online Learning with Kernels

abstract: Label ranking is the task of inferring a total order over a predeﬁned set of labels for each given instance. We present a general framework for batch learning of label ranking functions from supervised data. We assume that each instance in the training data is associated with a list of preferences over the label-set, however we do not assume that this list is either com- plete or consistent. This enables us to accommodate a variety of ranking problems. In contrast to the general form of the supervision, our goal is to learn a ranking function that induces a total order over the entire set of labels. Special cases of our setting are multilabel categorization and hierarchical classiﬁcation. We present a general boosting-based learning algorithm for the label ranking problem and prove a lower bound on the progress of each boosting iteration. The applicability of our approach is demonstrated with a set of experiments on a large-scale text corpus.

paragraphs: Label ranking asks a model to order every label in a predefined set for each input. This paper develops a supervised batch-learning framework for that task. Training examples provide preferences among labels, but those preferences may omit comparisons or even contradict one another. The desired prediction is nevertheless a complete ordering of all labels.

This separation between flexible supervision and a fully ordered output lets the framework accommodate different kinds of ranking problems. The authors identify multilabel categorization and hierarchical classification as special cases. The approach therefore connects several prediction settings through the common problem of learning an overall label order from the preferences available in training.

The paper introduces a general boosting-based learning algorithm and proves a lower bound on the progress made in each boosting iteration. That result supplies theoretical information about the learning procedure’s advancement. Experiments on a large-scale text corpus demonstrate the approach’s applicability. Together, the contributions address both learning from imperfect preference information and producing complete rankings from it.
summary.tldr: A boosting-based framework learns complete label rankings from preference lists that may be incomplete or inconsistent.

title: Log-Linear Models for Label Ranking

abstract: Computer animated agents and robots bring a social dimension to hu- man computer interaction and force us to think in new ways about how computers could be used in daily life. Face to face communication is a real-time process operating at a time scale of less than a second. In this paper we present progress on a perceptual primitive to automatically detect frontal faces in the video stream and code them with respect to 7 dimensions in real time: neutral, anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, sur- prise. The face ﬁnder employs a cascade of feature detectors trained with boosting techniques [13, 2]. The expression recognizer employs a novel combination of Adaboost and SVM’s. The generalization performance to new subjects for a 7-way forced choice was 93.3% and 97% correct on two publicly available datasets. The outputs of the classiﬁer change smoothly as a function of time, providing a potentially valuable repre- sentation to code facial expression dynamics in a fully automatic and unobtrusive manner. The system was deployed and evaluated for mea- suring spontaneous facial expressions in the ﬁeld in an application for automatic assessment of human-robot interaction.

paragraphs: This paper develops a real-time visual component for evaluating human–robot interaction through facial expressions. The system detects frontal faces in video and classifies them across seven categories: neutral, anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise. Its motivation is the rapid timescale of face-to-face communication, where useful perception must keep up with ongoing interaction.

Face detection uses a cascade of feature detectors trained through boosting. Expression recognition combines AdaBoost with support vector machines. On two publicly available datasets, seven-way forced-choice recognition for new subjects achieves 93.3% and 97% accuracy. These figures describe that specific generalization task and evaluation format.

The classifier’s outputs vary smoothly over time, which the authors identify as potentially useful for automatically representing expression dynamics. The system was also deployed and evaluated in the field to measure spontaneous expressions during human–robot interaction. The work therefore combines real-time recognition, dataset evaluation, and an applied deployment, while presenting the value of its temporal output as a potential benefit.
summary.tldr: A real-time face-expression system combines boosting and SVMs, achieves high seven-way recognition accuracy on two datasets, and is evaluated in human–robot interaction.

title: Towards Social Robots: Automatic Evaluation of Human-Robot Interaction by Facial Expression Classification

abstract: We describe a nonparametric Bayesian approach to generalizing from few labeled examples, guided by a larger set of unlabeled objects and the assumption of a latent tree-structure to the domain. The tree (or a distribution over trees) may be inferred using the unlabeled data. A prior over concepts generated by a mutation process on the inferred tree(s) allows efﬁcient computation of the optimal Bayesian classiﬁcation func- tion from the labeled examples. We test our approach on eight real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when only a few objects have labels but many more are available without labels. Its central assumption is that the domain has an underlying tree structure. A nonparametric Bayesian approach uses that structure to connect the larger unlabeled collection with the smaller set of labeled examples.

The tree, or a distribution over possible trees, can be inferred from the unlabeled data. A mutation process on the inferred structure then generates a prior over concepts. This supplies a probabilistic account of how classifications relate across the tree, allowing the labels to inform predictions through the relationships inferred from all the objects.

Under this model, the optimal Bayesian classification function can be computed efficiently from the labeled examples. The authors test the approach on eight real-world datasets. The contribution is the full connection from unlabeled structure to a concept prior and then to classification, with the latent-tree assumption providing the organizing principle that makes those stages work together.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian classifier uses a tree inferred from unlabeled data and a mutation-based concept prior to learn from few labels.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning with Trees

abstract: We claim and present arguments to the effect that a large class of man- ifold learning algorithms that are essentially local and can be framed as kernel learning algorithms will suffer from the curse of dimensionality, at the dimension of the true underlying manifold. This observation sug- gests to explore non-local manifold learning algorithms which attempt to discover shared structure in the tangent planes at different positions. A criterion for such an algorithm is proposed and experiments estimating a tangent plane prediction function are presented, showing its advantages with respect to local manifold learning algorithms: it is able to general- ize very far from training data (on learning handwritten character image rotations), where a local non-parametric method fails.

The argument concerns methods that are essentially local and can be expressed as kernel learning. It motivates looking beyond separate neighborhood-based estimates of the data's structure.

The proposed direction is to learn structure shared by tangent planes at different locations. A tangent plane describes the local directions along which a manifold varies. Sharing information across these planes could let a model predict local geometry at locations distant from its training examples. The authors propose a learning criterion and experiment with a function that predicts tangent planes.

In experiments involving rotations of handwritten character images, the method generalizes far from training data where a local nonparametric method fails. This supports the value of shared, nonlocal structure in that setting. The evidence connects a specific generalization result to the paper's broader argument, without establishing that every local method fails or every nonlocal method succeeds.
summary.tldr: Learning shared structure across manifold tangent planes enables distant generalization in character-rotation experiments where a local method fails.

title: Non-Local Manifold Tangent Learning

abstract: Given a set of points and a set of prototypes representing them, how to create a graph of the prototypes whose topology accounts for that of the points? This problem had not yet been explored in the framework of statistical learning theory. In this work, we propose a generative model based on the Delaunay graph of the prototypes and the ExpectationMaximization algorithm to learn the parameters. This work is a first step towards the construction of a topological model of a set of points grounded on statistics.
originalAbstract: Given a set of points and a set of prototypes representing them, how to create a graph of the prototypes whose topology accounts for that of the points? paragraphs: A collection of prototype points can summarize a larger dataset, but the prototypes alone do not specify how they should be connected. This paper asks how to build a graph whose topology reflects the structure of the original points. The objective is to represent relationships through graph connections as well as through representative locations.

The authors propose a generative model based on the Delaunay graph of the prototypes. They use the expectation-maximization algorithm to learn the model's parameters. This places the graph representation within a statistical modeling framework, connecting the desired topology to a model of the observed point set.

The paper presents the approach as an initial step toward statistically grounded topological modeling. Its significance is the formulation of graph construction as a learning problem with a generative model and parameter-estimation procedure. The stated contribution is foundational: it develops a way to approach the relationship between prototypes, their connections, and the points they represent, rather than claiming a complete solution to topological learning.
summary.tldr: A generative model built on a Delaunay graph uses expectation-maximization to take an initial step toward statistically learning point-set topology.

title: Learning Topology with the Generative Gaussian Graph and the EM Algorithm

abstract: Fair discriminative pedestrian finders are now available. In fact, these pedestrian finders make most errors on pedestrians in configurations that are uncommon in the training data, for example, mounting a bicycle. This is undesirable. However, the human configuration can itself be estimated discriminatively using structure learning. We demonstrate a pedestrian finder which first finds the most likely human pose in the window using a discriminative procedure trained with structure learning on a small dataset. We then present features (local histogram of oriented gradient and local PCA of gradient) based on that configuration to an SVM classifier. We show, using the INRIA Person dataset, that estimates of configuration significantly improve the accuracy of a discriminative pedestrian finder.

paragraphs: Pedestrian detectors can struggle when a person's configuration is uncommon in their training data, such as when someone is mounting a bicycle. This paper investigates whether explicitly estimating body configuration can improve detection. The approach makes pose estimation part of the detector rather than relying only on the appearance of an image window.

For each window, a discriminative procedure first estimates the most likely human pose. This procedure is trained through structure learning on a small dataset. The estimated configuration then determines features passed to an SVM classifier, including local histograms of oriented gradients and local principal components of gradients. Pose therefore influences how the classifier receives evidence about the candidate person.

Experiments on the INRIA Person dataset show that configuration estimates significantly improve detection accuracy. This finding supports using estimated body arrangement to inform a discriminative pedestrian classifier. The demonstrated result is improved overall accuracy on that dataset; the motivation is the difficulty posed by configurations that appear infrequently in training.
summary.tldr: Estimating human pose before extracting classification features significantly improves pedestrian detection accuracy on the INRIA Person dataset.

title: Configuration Estimates Improve Pedestrian Finding

abstract: We consider the problem of extracting smooth low-dimensional neural trajectories'' that summarize the activity recorded simultaneously from tens to hundreds of neurons on individual experimental trials. Beyond the benefit of visualizing the high-dimensional noisy spiking activity in a compact denoised form, such trajectories can offer insight into the dynamics of the neural circuitry underlying the recorded activity. Current methods for extracting neural trajectories involve a two-stage process: the data are first denoised'' by smoothing over time, then a static dimensionality reduction technique is applied. We first describe extensions of the two-stage methods that allow the degree of smoothing to be chosen in a principled way, and account for spiking variability that may vary both across neurons and across time. We then present a novel method for extracting neural trajectories, Gaussian-process factor analysis (GPFA), which unifies the smoothing and dimensionality reduction operations in a common probabilistic framework. We applied these methods to the activity of 61 neurons recorded simultaneously in macaque premotor and motor cortices during reach planning and execution. By adopting a goodness-of-fit metric that measures how well the activity of each neuron can be predicted by all other recorded neurons, we found that GPFA provided a better characterization of the population activity than the two-stage methods. From the extracted single-trial neural trajectories, we directly observed a convergence in neural state during motor planning, an effect suggestive of attractor dynamics that was shown indirectly by previous studies.

Existing approaches first smooth activity over time and then apply a separate, static dimensionality-reduction method.

The authors improve those two-stage approaches by choosing smoothing in a principled way and accounting for spiking variability across neurons and time. They then introduce Gaussian-process factor analysis, which combines smoothing and dimensionality reduction in one probabilistic framework. This makes the temporal and low-dimensional descriptions parts of a unified model.

summary.tldr: GPFA jointly smooths and reduces neural population activity, improving its characterization and revealing planning-related state convergence suggestive of attractor dynamics.

title: Gaussian-process factor analysis for low-dimensional single-trial analysis of neural population activity

abstract: Recent proposals suggest that large, generic neuronal networks could store memory traces of past input sequences in their instantaneous state. Such a proposal raises important theoretical questions about the duration of these memory traces and their dependence on network size, connectivity and signal statistics. Prior work, in the case of gaussian input sequences and linear neuronal networks, shows that the duration of memory traces in a network cannot exceed the number of neurons (in units of the neuronal time constant), and that no network can out-perform an equivalent feedforward network. However a more ethologically relevant scenario is that of sparse input sequences. In this scenario, we show how linear neural networks can essentially perform compressed sensing (CS) of past inputs, thereby attaining a memory capacity that {\it exceeds} the number of neurons. This enhanced capacity is achieved by a class of ``orthogonal recurrent networks and not by feedforward networks or generic recurrent networks. We exploit techniques from the statistical physics of disordered systems to analytically compute the decay of memory traces in such networks as a function of network size, signal sparsity and integration time. Alternately, viewed purely from the perspective of CS, this work introduces a new ensemble of measurement matrices derived from dynamical systems, and provides a theoretical analysis of their asymptotic performance."

paragraphs: A neural network's present state can retain traces of past inputs. Earlier analysis of linear networks driven by Gaussian input sequences placed a limit on memory duration tied to the number of neurons, measured in neuronal time constants. This paper examines how that picture changes when the input sequence is sparse.

For sparse inputs, the authors show that linear neural networks can effectively perform compressed sensing of their past inputs. A class of orthogonal recurrent networks can thereby achieve memory capacity exceeding the number of neurons. The enhancement depends on both the signal structure and the network class: the abstract does not attribute it to feedforward networks or generic recurrent networks.

The results connect short-term memory capacity to the structure of both inputs and recurrent dynamics.
summary.tldr: For sparse inputs, orthogonal recurrent linear networks can use dynamical compressed sensing to achieve memory capacity beyond their neuron count.

title: Short-term memory in neuronal networks through dynamical compressed sensing

abstract: Multi-task prediction models are widely being used to couple regressors or classification models by sharing information across related tasks. A common pitfall of these models is that they assume that the output tasks are independent conditioned on the inputs. Here, we propose a multi-task Gaussian process approach to model both the relatedness between regressors as well as the task correlations in the residuals, in order to more accurately identify true sharing between regressors. The resulting Gaussian model has a covariance term that is the sum of Kronecker products, for which efficient parameter inference and out of sample prediction are feasible. On both synthetic examples and applications to phenotype prediction in genetics, we find substantial benefits of modeling structured noise compared to established alternatives.

The resulting Gaussian model has a covariance term that is the sum of Kronecker products, for which efficient parameter inference and out of sample prediction are feasible. paragraphs: Multi-task prediction shares information among related prediction problems. The paper highlights a common assumption that can interfere with this goal: task outputs are treated as independent once the inputs are accounted for. Correlations can still remain in the residuals, the portions of outputs that the regressors do not explain.

The proposed Gaussian process model represents both relationships among regressors and correlations among residuals. Modeling these two sources of dependence is intended to identify more accurately which information should genuinely be shared between regressors. Shared unexplained variation therefore receives its own place in the model.

The resulting covariance is expressed as a sum of Kronecker products, with efficient parameter inference and prediction on new observations remaining feasible. Experiments on synthetic examples and genetic phenotype prediction show substantial benefits over established alternatives. These findings support the practical importance of modeling structured noise in the evaluated settings. The methodological contribution is to combine a richer account of cross-task dependence with computations that still allow the model to be fitted and used for prediction.
summary.tldr: A multi-task Gaussian process models both shared regressors and correlated residuals, improving prediction in synthetic and genetics applications.

title: It is all in the noise: Efficient multi-task Gaussian process inference with structured residuals

abstract: In the mixture models problem it is assumed that there are $K$ distributions $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{K}$ and one gets to observe a sample from a mixture of these distributions with unknown coefficients. The goal is to associate instances with their generating distributions, or to identify the parameters of the hidden distributions. In this work we make the assumption that we have access to several samples drawn from the same $K$ underlying distributions, but with different mixing weights. As with topic modeling, having multiple samples is often a reasonable assumption. Instead of pooling the data into one sample, we prove that it is possible to use the differences between the samples to better recover the underlying structure. We present algorithms that recover the underlying structure under milder assumptions than the current state of art when either the dimensionality or the separation is high. The methods, when applied to topic modeling, allow generalization to words not present in the training data.

paragraphs: A mixture model describes observations generated by several hidden distributions, with unknown proportions determining their contributions. This paper assumes access to several sample collections that share the same underlying distributions but have different mixing weights. The question is whether those differences can help identify the hidden structure.

The authors prove that preserving differences between sample collections can improve recovery compared with pooling everything into a single sample. They present algorithms that recover the underlying structure under milder assumptions than the state of the art when either dimensionality or separation is high. The shared components and varying proportions are therefore useful sources of information, not merely incidental features of data collection.

The paper also connects the methods to topic modeling, where multiple collections with differing mixtures are often a reasonable assumption. In that application, the methods allow generalization to words absent from the training data. The contribution shows how variation across related samples can make latent distributions easier to recover, with the recovery claims tied to the stated high-dimensionality or high-separation regimes.
summary.tldr: Differences in mixing weights across samples help recover shared hidden distributions under milder assumptions in high-dimensional or well-separated settings.

title: Using multiple samples to learn mixture models

abstract: We introduce a generic scheme for accelerating first-order optimization methods in the sense of Nesterov, which builds upon a new analysis of the accelerated proximal point algorithm. Our approach consists of minimizing a convex objective by approximately solving a sequence of well-chosen auxiliary problems, leading to faster convergence. This strategy applies to a large class of algorithms, including gradient descent, block coordinate descent, SAG, SAGA, SDCA, SVRG, Finito/MISO, and their proximal variants. For all of these methods, we provide acceleration and explicit support for non-strongly convex objectives. In addition to theoretical speed-up, we also show that acceleration is useful in practice, especially for ill-conditioned problems where we measure significant improvements.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a general way to accelerate algorithms that minimize convex objectives using first-order information. Its starting point is a new analysis of the accelerated proximal point algorithm. The goal is to make a broad collection of existing optimization methods converge faster through a shared procedure.

The procedure replaces direct optimization with a sequence of carefully chosen auxiliary problems. An existing algorithm approximately solves each auxiliary problem, and the surrounding scheme turns those approximate solutions into accelerated progress on the original objective. Allowing approximate solutions is central: the method is designed to work with practical optimization routines rather than requiring exact answers at every stage.

The analysis covers gradient descent, block coordinate descent, several incremental methods, and their proximal variants. It provides acceleration with explicit support for objectives that are not strongly convex. Experiments also show practical improvements, especially on ill-conditioned problems. These findings support using the scheme as a broadly applicable accelerator within the convex settings studied.
summary.tldr: Catalyst accelerates many convex optimization methods by approximately solving a carefully constructed sequence of auxiliary problems.

title: A Universal Catalyst for First-Order Optimization

abstract: Learned region sparsity has achieved state-of-the-art performance in classification tasks by exploiting and integrating a sparse set of local information into global decisions. The underlying mechanism resembles how people sample information from an image with their eye movements when making similar decisions. In this paper we incorporate the biologically plausible mechanism of Inhibition of Return into the learned region sparsity model, thereby imposing diversity on the selected regions. We investigate how these mechanisms of sparsity and diversity relate to visual attention by testing our model on three different types of visual search tasks. We report state-of-the-art results in predicting the locations of human gaze fixations, even though our model is trained only on image-level labels without object location annotations. Notably, the classification performance of the extended model remains the same as the original. This work suggests a new computational perspective on visual attention mechanisms and shows how the inclusion of attention-based mechanisms can improve computer vision techniques.

The paper connects this selective use of visual information to how people move their eyes while making decisions. It asks whether a model built for classification can also account for where people look during visual search.

The authors add Inhibition of Return, a biologically plausible attention mechanism, to encourage diversity among the selected regions. Sparsity controls how much local information is used, while diversity encourages the selected set to cover different regions. The resulting model is tested on three types of visual search task to examine how these two mechanisms relate to human attention.

The model achieves reported state-of-the-art performance in predicting gaze fixation locations despite training only with image-level labels and no object-location annotations. Its classification performance remains unchanged from the original model. The findings suggest that selective, diverse region use can explain aspects of gaze behavior while preserving classification ability, linking an attention-inspired modification to both visual prediction and a computational account of human information sampling.
summary.tldr: Adding diversity to sparse region selection predicts human gaze from image-level training labels while preserving classification performance.

title: Learned Region Sparsity and Diversity Also Predicts Visual Attention

abstract: We establish a new connection between value and policy based reinforcement learning (RL) based on a relationship between softmax temporal value consistency and policy optimality under entropy regularization. Specifically, we show that softmax consistent action values correspond to optimal entropy regularized policy probabilities along any action sequence, regardless of provenance. From this observation, we develop a new RL algorithm, Path Consistency Learning (PCL), that minimizes a notion of soft consistency error along multi-step action sequences extracted from both on- and off-policy traces. We examine the behavior of PCL in different scenarios and show that PCL can be interpreted as generalizing both actor-critic and Q-learning algorithms. We subsequently deepen the relationship by showing how a single model can be used to represent both a policy and the corresponding softmax state values, eliminating the need for a separate critic. The experimental evaluation demonstrates that PCL significantly outperforms strong actor-critic and Q-learning baselines across several benchmarks.

paragraphs: Value-based reinforcement learning estimates how worthwhile actions are, while policy-based learning represents how actions should be chosen. This paper connects the two through entropy regularization and a softmax form of temporal consistency. It shows that action values satisfying this consistency relationship correspond to optimal entropy-regularized policy probabilities along any action sequence, regardless of how that sequence was obtained.

The authors turn this relationship into Path Consistency Learning, or PCL. The algorithm minimizes a soft consistency error across sequences of multiple actions. It can use both on-policy traces, generated by the current policy, and off-policy traces. This makes the theoretical connection directly useful as a training objective over different sources of experience.

The paper interprets PCL as generalizing actor-critic and Q-learning approaches. It also shows how one model can represent both a policy and its associated softmax state values, removing the need for a separate critic. Across several benchmarks, the reported evaluation finds significant improvements over strong actor-critic and Q-learning baselines.
summary.tldr: Path Consistency Learning connects values and policies through entropy-regularized consistency and learns from both on-policy and off-policy action sequences.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Value and Policy Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Identifying the top-K frequent items is one of the most common and important operations in large data processing systems. As a result, several solutions have been proposed to solve this problem approximately. In this paper, we identify that in modern distributed settings with both multi-node as well as multi-core parallelism, existing algorithms, although theoretically sound, are suboptimal from the performance perspective. In particular, for identifying top-K frequent items, Count-Min Sketch (CMS) has fantastic update time but lack the important property of reducibility which is needed for exploiting available massive data parallelism. On the other end, popular Frequent algorithm (FA) leads to reducible summaries but the update costs are significant. In this paper, we present Topkapi, a fast and parallel algorithm for finding top-K frequent items, which gives the best of both worlds, i.e., it is reducible as well as efficient update time similar to CMS. Topkapi possesses strong theoretical guarantees and leads to significant performance gains due to increased parallelism, relative to past work.

paragraphs: Finding the most frequent items is a common operation in large data systems, and approximate summaries can make it efficient. This paper focuses on performance when work is distributed across multiple machines and multiple cores. In that setting, both the cost of updating a summary and the ability to combine summaries matter.

The authors identify a tradeoff in existing approaches. Count-Min Sketch offers fast updates but lacks the reducibility they need for parallel top-K identification. The Frequent algorithm produces reducible summaries, but its updates are costly. Reducibility allows summaries computed on separate portions of data to be combined, making it central to exploiting parallel processing.

Topkapi is designed to provide both reducibility and update efficiency similar to Count-Min Sketch. The paper presents strong theoretical guarantees and reports significant performance gains over earlier work through increased parallelism. Its contribution is to align the properties of the summary algorithm with the practical requirements of distributed and multicore data processing.
summary.tldr: Topkapi combines fast updates with mergeable summaries to accelerate parallel identification of the most frequent items.

title: Topkapi: Parallel and Fast Sketches for Finding Top-K Frequent Elements

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of time series forecasting for non-stationary signals and multiple future steps prediction. To handle this challenging task, we introduce DILATE (DIstortion Loss including shApe and TimE), a new objective function for training deep neural networks. DILATE aims at accurately predicting sudden changes, and explicitly incorporates two terms supporting precise shape and temporal change detection. We introduce a differentiable loss function suitable for training deep neural nets, and provide a custom back-prop implementation for speeding up optimization. We also introduce a variant of DILATE, which provides a smooth generalization of temporally-constrained Dynamic TimeWarping (DTW). Experiments carried out on various non-stationary datasets reveal the very good behaviour of DILATE compared to models trained with the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function, and also to DTW and variants. DILATE is also agnostic to the choice of the model, and we highlight its benefit for training fully connected networks as well as specialized recurrent architectures, showing its capacity to improve over state-of-the-art trajectory forecasting approaches.

To handle this challenging task, we introduce DILATE (DIstortion Loss including shApe and TimE), a new objective function for training deep neural networks. DILATE aims at accurately predicting sudden changes, and explicitly incorporates two terms supporting precise shape and temporal change detection. We introduce a differentiable loss function suitable for training deep neural nets, and provide a custom back-prop implementation for speeding up optimization. We also introduce a variant of DILATE, which provides a smooth generalization of temporally-constrained Dynamic TimeWarping (DTW). Experiments carried out on various non-stationary datasets reveal the very good behaviour of DILATE compared to models trained with the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function, and also to DTW and variants. DILATE is also agnostic to the choice of the model, and we highlight its benefit for training fully connected networks as well as specialized recurrent architectures, showing its capacity to improve over state-of-the-art trajectory forecasting approaches.

paragraphs: Forecasting several future steps is difficult when a signal changes its behavior over time, especially around sudden transitions. The paper introduces DILATE, a training objective that explicitly considers both the shape of a forecast and the timing of its changes. These two components address different aspects of whether a predicted trajectory captures an upcoming event accurately.

DILATE is differentiable, making it suitable for training deep neural networks. The authors provide a custom back-propagation implementation to speed optimization. They also introduce a variant that smoothly generalizes temporally constrained Dynamic Time Warping, connecting the objective to a method for comparing sequences while accounting for their alignment.

Experiments on several non-stationary datasets report favorable results relative to training with mean squared error, Dynamic Time Warping, and its variants. The loss is independent of a specific model architecture, and the paper demonstrates benefits for fully connected networks and specialized recurrent models. It also reports improvements over state-of-the-art trajectory forecasting approaches, supporting the usefulness of explicitly supervising both forecast shape and temporal placement.
summary.tldr: DILATE trains forecasting networks with separate shape and timing terms to improve predictions of changing trajectories.

title: Shape and Time Distortion Loss for Training Deep Time Series Forecasting Models

abstract: Human activities often occur in specific scene contexts, e.g., playing basketball on a basketball court. Training a model using existing video datasets thus inevitably captures and leverages such bias (instead of using the actual discriminative cues). The learned representation may not generalize well to new action classes or different tasks. In this paper, we propose to mitigate scene bias for video representation learning. Specifically, we augment the standard cross-entropy loss for action classification with 1) an adversarial loss for scene types and 2) a human mask confusion loss for videos where the human actors are masked out. These two losses encourage learning representations that are unable to predict the scene types and the correct actions when there is no evidence. We validate the effectiveness of our method by transferring our pre-trained model to three different tasks, including action classification, temporal localization, and spatio-temporal action detection. Our results show consistent improvement over the baseline model without debiasing.

This shortcut can weaken the usefulness of their representations for new actions or other tasks. The paper modifies training to reduce scene bias and encourage representations that depend more on evidence for the human activity.

The method adds two losses to ordinary action-classification training. An adversarial scene loss discourages representations from predicting the scene type. A human-mask confusion loss uses videos with the actors hidden and discourages correct action prediction when the relevant human evidence has been removed. Together, these objectives target both explicit scene information and action predictions supported by actor-free context.

The authors evaluate transfer of the pretrained model to action classification, temporal localization, and spatiotemporal action detection. They report consistent improvements over the baseline trained without debiasing. These results support the usefulness of reducing scene shortcuts for the tested transfer tasks, rather than establishing that contextual information has been completely removed from the representation.
summary.tldr: Training losses that discourage scene prediction and actor-free action recognition improve video-representation transfer across three action-related tasks.

title: Why Can't I Dance in the Mall? Learning to Mitigate Scene Bias in Action Recognition

abstract: We analyse the learning performance of Distributed Gradient Descent in the context of multi-agent decentralised non-parametric regression with the square loss function when i.i.d. samples are assigned to agents. We show that if agents hold sufficiently many samples with respect to the network size, then Distributed Gradient Descent achieves optimal statistical rates with a number of iterations that scales, up to a threshold, with the inverse of the spectral gap of the gossip matrix divided by the number of samples owned by each agent raised to a problem-dependent power. The presence of the threshold comes from statistics. It encodes the existence of a "big data" regime where the number of required iterations does not depend on the network topology. In this regime, Distributed Gradient Descent achieves optimal statistical rates with the same order of iterations as gradient descent run with all the samples in the network. Provided the communication delay is sufficiently small, the distributed protocol yields a linear speed-up in runtime compared to the single-machine protocol. This is in contrast to decentralised optimisation algorithms that do not exploit statistics and only yield a linear speed-up in graphs where the spectral gap is bounded away from zero. Our results exploit the statistical concentration of quantities held by agents and shed new light on the interplay between statistics and communication in decentralised methods. Bounds are given in the standard non-parametric setting with source/capacity assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes distributed gradient descent for decentralized non-parametric regression with squared loss. Agents receive independent, identically distributed samples and communicate through a network. The question is when their joint learning can achieve optimal statistical accuracy while also delivering a runtime benefit over processing all samples on one machine.

When each agent holds sufficiently many samples relative to network size, the method attains optimal statistical rates. Its iteration requirement depends on both sample counts and the network's spectral gap, up to a threshold. Beyond that threshold lies a big-data regime where the required number of iterations no longer depends on network topology.

Under the stated source and capacity assumptions, the analysis explains how statistical concentration can reduce the effect of network structure, revealing conditions where data abundance offsets communication-related difficulty.
summary.tldr: With enough data per agent and sufficiently low communication delay, decentralized regression achieves optimal statistical rates and linear runtime speed-up.

title: Optimal Statistical Rates for Decentralised Non-Parametric Regression with Linear Speed-Up

abstract: In an effort to better understand the different ways in which the discount factor affects the optimization process in reinforcement learning, we designed a set of experiments to study each effect in isolation. Our analysis reveals that the common perception that poor performance of low discount factors is caused by (too) small action-gaps requires revision. We propose an alternative hypothesis that identifies the size-difference of the action-gap across the state-space as the primary cause. We then introduce a new method that enables more homogeneous action-gaps by mapping value estimates to a logarithmic space. We prove convergence for this method under standard assumptions and demonstrate empirically that it indeed enables lower discount factors for approximate reinforcement-learning methods. This in turn allows tackling a class of reinforcement-learning problems that are challenging to solve with traditional methods.

paragraphs: The discount factor affects how reinforcement-learning systems value future rewards, but it also changes the optimization problem. This paper designs experiments to isolate its different effects. The authors revisit the common explanation that low discount factors perform poorly because the differences between action values, called action gaps, become too small.

Their alternative hypothesis emphasizes how much action-gap sizes vary across states. If those differences have very different scales in different parts of the state space, learning can become difficult. The proposed method maps value estimates into logarithmic space to make action gaps more homogeneous, directly addressing this variation in scale.

The authors prove convergence under standard assumptions and empirically show that the method enables lower discount factors in approximate reinforcement learning. They report that this makes a class of problems accessible that traditional methods find challenging. The work therefore connects an experimental reassessment of a familiar optimization explanation to a concrete change in value representation, while treating the proposed cause as a hypothesis.
summary.tldr: Mapping value estimates into logarithmic space makes action gaps more homogeneous and empirically enables lower discount factors in approximate reinforcement learning.

title: Using a Logarithmic Mapping to Enable Lower Discount Factors in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We present an improved method for symbolic regression that seeks to fit data to formulas that are Pareto-optimal, in the sense of having the best accuracy for a given complexity. It improves on the previous state-of-the-art by typically being orders of magnitude more robust toward noise and bad data, and also by discovering many formulas that stumped previous methods. We develop a method for discovering generalized symmetries (arbitrary modularity in the computational graph of a formula) from gradient properties of a neural network fit. We use normalizing flows to generalize our symbolic regression method to probability distributions from which we only have samples, and employ statistical hypothesis testing to accelerate robust brute-force search.

We use normalizing flows to generalize our symbolic regression method to probability distributions from which we only have samples, and employ statistical hypothesis testing to accelerate robust brute-force search.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for mathematical formulas that explain data. AI Feynman 2.0 seeks formulas that balance accuracy against complexity: at a given level of complexity, the aim is to obtain the best fit. This makes the search sensitive to both how well an expression describes observations and how complicated that expression becomes.

The method uses a neural network fitted to the data to uncover structure that can guide formula discovery. Properties of the network's gradients reveal generalized symmetries, expressed as modularity in a formula's computational graph. Identifying such modules gives the symbolic search information about how a larger expression may be organized into related components.

The authors also use normalizing flows to extend the approach to probability distributions available only through samples, and statistical hypothesis tests to accelerate robust brute-force search. They report discovering formulas that earlier methods could not find and typically achieving orders-of-magnitude greater robustness to noise and bad data. These are qualified performance claims, while the broader contribution is a search strategy combining formula structure, statistical testing, and accuracy–complexity trade-offs.
summary.tldr: AI Feynman 2.0 uses learned formula structure and statistical testing to improve symbolic regression while balancing accuracy and complexity.

title: AI Feynman 2.0: Pareto-optimal symbolic regression exploiting graph modularity

abstract: Given a set of items F and a weight function W: F -> (0,1), the problem of sampling seeks to sample an item proportional to its weight. Sampling is a fundamental problem in machine learning. The daunting computational complexity of sampling with formal guarantees leads designers to propose heuristics-based techniques for which no rigorous theoretical analysis exists to quantify the quality of the generated distributions. This poses a challenge in designing a testing methodology to test whether a sampler under test generates samples according to a given distribution. Only recently, Chakraborty and Meel (2019) designed the first scalable verifier, called Barbarik, for samplers in the special case when the weight function W is constant, that is, when the sampler is supposed to sample uniformly from F. The techniques in Barbarik, however, fail to handle general weight functions. The primary contribution of this paper is an affirmative answer to the above challenge: motivated by Barbarik, but using different techniques and analysis, we design Barbarik2, an algorithm to test whether the distribution generated by a sampler is epsilon-close or eta-far from any target distribution. In contrast to black-box sampling techniques that require a number of samples proportional to |F|, Barbarik2 requires only \tilde{O}(Tilt(W, F)^2/eta(eta - 6*epsilon)^3) samples, where the Tilt is the maximum ratio of weights of two points in F. Barbarik2 can handle any arbitrary weight function. We present a prototype implementation of Barbarik2 and use it to test three state-of-the-art samplers.

paragraphs: A weighted sampler should choose each item with probability proportional to its assigned weight. Many practical samplers use heuristics without rigorous distribution-quality guarantees, making verification important. An earlier verifier handled uniform sampling, but its techniques did not extend to general weights. This paper introduces Barbarik2 to address that broader problem.

Barbarik2 tests whether a sampler’s output distribution is within an epsilon tolerance of a target distribution or at least an eta distance away. These are separated testing cases, so the result is not a promise to classify every intermediate discrepancy. The method accepts arbitrary weight functions and uses different techniques and analysis from the earlier uniform verifier.

Its sample bound depends on the tolerances and the squared tilt, the largest ratio between two item weights, rather than directly on the number of items as in the cited black-box approaches. This changes what controls verification cost, although weight imbalance still matters. The authors implement a prototype and apply it to three state-of-the-art samplers.
summary.tldr: Barbarik2 tests weighted samplers against arbitrary target distributions with sample complexity governed by weight ratios and testing tolerances.

title: On Testing of Samplers

abstract: Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) is an essential tool for integral approximation, Bayesian inference, and sampling for simulation in science, etc. In the QMC area, the rank-1 lattice is important due to its simple operation, and nice property for point set construction. However, the construction of the generating vector of the rank-1 lattice is usually time-consuming through an exhaustive computer search. To address this issue, we propose a simple closed-form rank-1 lattice construction method based on group theory. Our method reduces the number of distinct pairwise distance values to generate a more regular lattice. We theoretically prove a lower and an upper bound of the minimum pairwise distance of any non-degenerate rank-1 lattice. Empirically, our methods can generate near-optimal rank-1 lattice compared with Korobov exhaustive search regarding the $l_1$-norm and $l_2$-norm minimum distance. Moreover, experimental results show that our method achieves superior approximation performance on the benchmark integration test problems and the kernel approximation problems.

paragraphs: Quasi-Monte Carlo methods use constructed point sets for tasks such as approximating integrals and sampling in scientific computation. Rank-1 lattices are attractive because their construction and operation are simple once a generating vector is available. Finding that vector, however, can require a time-consuming exhaustive search. This paper proposes a closed-form construction based on group theory.

The construction reduces the number of distinct distances between pairs of points to produce a more regular lattice. The authors also prove lower and upper bounds on the minimum pairwise distance for any non-degenerate rank-1 lattice. These theoretical results characterize an important geometric property of the point sets, alongside the practical method for constructing them.

Empirically, the proposed methods produce near-optimal lattices relative to Korobov exhaustive search when judged by minimum distance in the l1 and l2 norms. Experiments also show superior approximation performance on benchmark integration and kernel approximation problems. The contribution links a simpler construction procedure with favorable geometry and demonstrated approximation quality in the tested problems.
summary.tldr: A group-theoretic closed-form construction produces rank-1 lattices with near-optimal empirical spacing and strong approximation performance.

title: Subgroup-based Rank-1 Lattice Quasi-Monte Carlo

abstract: Conventional Neural Networks can approximate simple arithmetic operations, but fail to generalize beyond the range of numbers that were seen during training. Neural Arithmetic Units aim to overcome this difficulty, but current arithmetic units are either limited to operate on positive numbers or can only represent a subset of arithmetic operations. We introduce the Neural Power Unit (NPU) that operates on the full domain of real numbers and is capable of learning arbitrary power functions in a single layer. The NPU thus fixes the shortcomings of existing arithmetic units and extends their expressivity. We achieve this by using complex arithmetic without requiring a conversion of the network to complex numbers. A simplification of the unit to the RealNPU yields a highly transparent model. We show that the NPUs outperform their competitors in terms of accuracy and sparsity on artificial arithmetic datasets, and that the RealNPU can discover the governing equations of a dynamical system only from data.

The NPU thus fixes the shortcomings of existing arithmetic units and extends their expressivity. We achieve this by using complex arithmetic without requiring a conversion of the network to complex numbers. A simplification of the unit to the RealNPU yields a highly transparent model. paragraphs: Neural networks can fit arithmetic within the numerical range used for training yet struggle to generalize beyond it. Specialized arithmetic units address this problem, but existing units may require positive inputs or represent only some operations. This paper introduces the Neural Power Unit, designed to accept real-number inputs and learn arbitrary power functions in a single layer.

The unit uses complex arithmetic internally without requiring the surrounding network to be converted to complex numbers. This construction expands the range of functions available to an arithmetic unit. The authors also introduce a simplified version, RealNPU, whose structure provides a highly transparent model.

On artificial arithmetic datasets, the authors report better accuracy and sparsity than competing methods. They further demonstrate that RealNPU can discover the governing equations of a dynamical system from data alone. These findings connect the architectural contribution to two uses: learning arithmetic more effectively and producing compact, understandable mathematical descriptions of observed dynamics in the demonstrated setting.
summary.tldr: Neural Power Units use complex arithmetic internally to learn power functions, with a transparent variant demonstrated on dynamical-equation discovery.

title: Neural Power Units

abstract: Macroscopic data aggregated from microscopic events are pervasive in machine learning, such as country-level COVID-19 infection statistics based on city-level data. Yet, many existing approaches for predicting macroscopic behavior only use aggregated data, leaving a large amount of fine-grained microscopic information unused. In this paper, we propose a principled optimization framework for macroscopic prediction by fitting microscopic models based on conditional stochastic optimization. The framework leverages both macroscopic and microscopic information, and adapts to individual microscopic models involved in the aggregation. In addition, we propose efficient learning algorithms with convergence guarantees. In our experiments, we show that the proposed learning framework clearly outperforms other plug-in supervised learning approaches in real-world applications, including the prediction of daily infections of COVID-19 and medicare claims.

The framework leverages both macroscopic and microscopic information, and adapts to individual microscopic models involved in the aggregation. In addition, we propose efficient learning algorithms with convergence guarantees. In our experiments, we show that the proposed learning framework clearly outperforms other plug-in supervised learning approaches in real-world applications, including the prediction of daily infections of COVID-19 and medicare claims.

paragraphs: Many prediction targets summarize smaller-scale events, such as national infection statistics assembled from city-level data. Models trained only on the aggregate can leave useful fine-grained information unused. This paper asks how to use both levels of information when the ultimate goal is to predict the larger-scale quantity.

The authors propose an optimization framework that fits microscopic models for macroscopic prediction using conditional stochastic optimization. It incorporates information at both scales and adapts to the individual microscopic models participating in the aggregation. This ties the fitting of the smaller-scale models to the aggregate prediction objective. The paper also develops efficient learning algorithms with convergence guarantees.

Experiments apply the framework to daily COVID-19 infection prediction and Medicare claims prediction. The authors report clear improvements over other plug-in supervised learning approaches in these real-world applications. The findings support using the relationship between detailed events and their aggregate during model fitting, showing that fine-grained modeling can improve predictions even when the quantity of interest is macroscopic.
summary.tldr: The framework fits microscopic models using information at both scales to improve aggregate predictions, with convergence guarantees and positive real-world results.

title: The Devil is in the Detail: A Framework for Macroscopic Prediction via Microscopic Models

abstract: We consider the task of automated theorem proving, a key AI task. Deep learning has shown promise for training theorem provers, but there are limited human-written theorems and proofs available for supervised learning. To address this limitation, we propose to learn a neural generator that automatically synthesizes theorems and proofs for the purpose of training a theorem prover. Experiments on real-world tasks demonstrate that synthetic data from our approach improves the theorem prover and advances the state of the art of automated theorem proving in Metamath.
