Deep learning has shown promise for training theorem provers, but there are limited human-written theorems and proofs available for supervised learning. To address this limitation, we propose to learn a neural generator that automatically synthesizes theorems and proofs for the purpose of training a theorem prover. Experiments on real-world tasks demonstrate that synthetic data from our approach improves the theorem prover and advances the state of the art of automated theorem proving in Metamath.

paragraphs: Automated theorem proving asks an AI system to establish mathematical statements through proofs. Deep learning has shown promise for training such systems, but supervised learning depends on examples of theorems and their proofs. The paper addresses a practical bottleneck: only a limited supply of human-written examples is available for that training.

The authors propose learning a neural generator that synthesizes both theorems and proofs. Those generated examples are then used to train a theorem prover. The generator therefore serves as a source of training material for the proving task. Producing proofs along with statements is central to the approach because the training data must include demonstrations of how the statements can be established.

Experiments on real-world tasks show that the synthetic data improves the theorem prover. The authors also report advancing the state of the art in automated theorem proving within Metamath. The findings support learned data generation as a way to improve theorem-proving systems when the available human-written training collection is limited.
summary.tldr: A neural generator creates theorem-and-proof training examples that improve automated proving and advance reported results in Metamath.

title: Learning to Prove Theorems by Learning to Generate Theorems

abstract: It is often desirable to reduce the dimensionality of a large dataset by projecting it onto a low-dimensional subspace. Matrix sketching has emerged as a powerful technique for performing such dimensionality reduction very efficiently. Even though there is an extensive literature on the worst-case performance of sketching, existing guarantees are typically very different from what is observed in practice. We exploit recent developments in the spectral analysis of random matrices to develop novel techniques that provide provably accurate expressions for the expected value of random projection matrices obtained via sketching. These expressions can be used to characterize the performance of dimensionality reduction in a variety of common machine learning tasks, ranging from low-rank approximation to iterative stochastic optimization. Our results apply to several popular sketching methods, including Gaussian and Rademacher sketches, and they enable precise analysis of these methods in terms of spectral properties of the data. Empirical results show that the expressions we derive reflect the practical performance of these sketching methods, down to lower-order effects and even constant factors.

Even though there is an extensive literature on the worst-case performance of sketching, existing guarantees are typically very different from what is observed in practice. These expressions can be used to characterize the performance of dimensionality reduction in a variety of common machine learning tasks, ranging from low-rank approximation to iterative stochastic optimization. Empirical results show that the expressions we derive reflect the practical performance of these sketching methods, down to lower-order effects and even constant factors.

paragraphs: Matrix sketching reduces the dimensionality of large datasets by projecting them into smaller subspaces. Although worst-case guarantees are well studied, they often differ substantially from observed performance. This paper seeks more precise descriptions of what random projections do on average, with the structure of the data included in the analysis.

Using developments in random-matrix spectral analysis, the authors derive provably accurate expressions for expected projection matrices produced by sketching. The expressions apply to popular methods including Gaussian and Rademacher sketches. They describe performance through spectral properties of the data, making those properties part of the explanation of how a sketch behaves.

The results can characterize tasks ranging from low-rank approximation to iterative stochastic optimization. Their significance is the level of detail available beyond broad worst-case estimates. In empirical evaluations, the derived expressions track practical behavior even in constant factors and lower-order effects. The work therefore connects rigorous analysis of expected projections with the finer performance differences observed when sketching methods are used.
summary.tldr: Precise expressions for expected sketching projections explain practical performance through data spectra, including observed constant factors and lower-order effects.

title: Precise expressions for random projections: Low-rank approximation and randomized Newton

abstract: The Lipschitz constant of a network plays an important role in many applications of deep learning, such as robustness certification and Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network. We introduce a semidefinite programming hierarchy to estimate the global and local Lipschitz constant of a multiple layer deep neural network. The novelty is to combine a polynomial lifting for ReLU functions derivatives with a weak generalization of Putinar's positivity certificate. This idea could also apply to other, nearly sparse, polynomial optimization problems in machine learning. We empirically demonstrate that our method provides a trade-off with respect to state of the art linear programming approach, and in some cases we obtain better bounds in less time.

We introduce a semidefinite programming hierarchy to estimate the global and local Lipschitz constant of a multiple layer deep neural network. The novelty is to combine a polynomial lifting for ReLU functions derivatives with a weak generalization of Putinar's positivity certificate. This idea could also apply to other, nearly sparse, polynomial optimization problems in machine learning. We empirically demonstrate that our method provides a trade-off with respect to state of the art linear programming approach, and in some cases we obtain better bounds in less time.

paragraphs: A network's Lipschitz constant describes how strongly its output can change relative to changes in its input. Estimating this quantity matters for applications including robustness certification and Wasserstein generative adversarial networks. This paper develops an optimization framework for estimating both global and local Lipschitz constants of multilayer ReLU networks.

The approach introduces a hierarchy of semidefinite programs. Its key construction combines a polynomial lifting of ReLU derivatives with a weak generalization of Putinar's positivity certificate. This translates the derivative-based estimation problem into a form that the proposed optimization hierarchy can address. The authors also suggest that the construction could extend to other nearly sparse polynomial optimization problems in machine learning.

Empirical comparisons reveal a trade-off relative to a state-of-the-art linear programming approach. In some cases, the proposed method obtains better bounds while taking less time. The stated contribution is therefore an additional way to balance bound quality and computation, with demonstrated improvements in particular cases rather than a claim of uniform superiority.
summary.tldr: A semidefinite programming hierarchy estimates ReLU-network Lipschitz constants, sometimes producing better bounds faster than a linear programming approach.

title: Semialgebraic Optimization for Lipschitz Constants of ReLU Networks

abstract: Adversarial learning has demonstrated good performance in the unsupervised domain adaptation setting, by learning domain-invariant representations. However, recent work has shown limitations of this approach when label distributions differ between the source and target domains. In this paper, we propose a new assumption, \textit{generalized label shift} ($\glsa$), to improve robustness against mismatched label distributions. $\glsa$ states that, conditioned on the label, there exists a representation of the input that is invariant between the source and target domains. Under $\glsa$, we provide theoretical guarantees on the transfer performance of any classifier. We also devise necessary and sufficient conditions for $\glsa$ to hold, by using an estimation of the relative class weights between domains and an appropriate reweighting of samples. Our weight estimation method could be straightforwardly and generically applied in existing domain adaptation (DA) algorithms that learn domain-invariant representations, with small computational overhead. In particular, we modify three DA algorithms, JAN, DANN and CDAN, and evaluate their performance on standard and artificial DA tasks. Our algorithms outperform the base versions, with vast improvements for large label distribution mismatches. Our code is available at \url{https://tinyurl.com/y585xt6j}.
originalAbstract: Adversarial learning has demonstrated good performance in the unsupervised domain adaptation setting, by learning domain-invariant representations. However, recent work has shown limitations of this approach when label distributions differ between the source and target domains. In this paper, we propose a new assumption, \textit{generalized label shift} ($\glsa$), to improve robustness against mismatched label distributions. $\glsa$ states that, conditioned on the label, there exists a representation of the input that is invariant between the source and target domains. Under $\glsa$, we provide theoretical guarantees on the transfer performance of any classifier. We also devise necessary and sufficient conditions for $\glsa$ to hold, by using an estimation of the relative class weights between domains and an appropriate reweighting of samples. Our weight estimation method could be straightforwardly and generically applied in existing domain adaptation (DA) algorithms that learn domain-invariant representations, with small computational overhead. In particular, we modify three DA algorithms, JAN, DANN and CDAN, and evaluate their performance on standard and artificial DA tasks. Our algorithms outperform the base versions, with vast improvements for large label distribution mismatches. Our code is available at \url{https://tinyurl.com/y585xt6j}.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers learning from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. Methods that make the domains' representations look alike can struggle when class frequencies differ. This paper addresses that mismatch through generalized label shift: the assumption that a representation exists whose distribution is the same across domains when conditioned on the class label.

This distinction allows overall class proportions to change while requiring alignment within each class. Under the assumption, the authors establish transfer-performance guarantees for any classifier. They also derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the assumption to hold, using estimates of relative class weights and appropriate sample reweighting.

The weight-estimation procedure can be incorporated into existing methods that learn domain-invariant representations with little added computation. The authors modify JAN, DANN, and CDAN and evaluate them on standard and artificial adaptation tasks. The modified versions outperform their originals, with especially large gains when label distributions differ substantially. These results support explicitly accounting for class proportions during representation alignment.
summary.tldr: Class-conditioned alignment and estimated class reweighting improve domain adaptation when source and target label proportions differ.

title: Domain Adaptation with Conditional Distribution Matching and Generalized Label Shift

abstract: We introduce an end-to-end learnable technique to robustly identify feature edges in 3D point cloud data. We represent these edges as a collection of parametric curves (i.e.,~lines, circles, and B-splines). Accordingly, our deep neural network, coined PIE-NET, is trained for parametric inference of edges. The network relies on a "region proposal" architecture, where a first module proposes an over-complete collection of edge and corner points, and a second module ranks each proposal to decide whether it should be considered. We train and evaluate our method on the ABC dataset, a large dataset of CAD models, and compare our results to those produced by traditional (non-learning) processing pipelines, as well as a recent deep learning based edge detector (EC-NET). Our results significantly improve over the state-of-the-art from both a quantitative and qualitative standpoint.

paragraphs: A three-dimensional point cloud describes geometry through sampled points, while feature edges provide a more structured description of that geometry. PIE-NET is an end-to-end learnable method for identifying these edges robustly. It represents the results as parametric curves, including straight lines, circles, and B-splines, rather than treating edge identification solely as a collection of point-level decisions.

The network uses a region-proposal architecture with two stages. The first produces an over-complete set of candidate edge and corner points. The second ranks the proposals to determine which should be retained. This separates generating a broad set of possibilities from deciding which candidates deserve inclusion in the inferred edge structure.

The authors train and evaluate PIE-NET on the ABC dataset of CAD models. They compare it with traditional processing pipelines and the learning-based edge detector EC-NET. The reported improvements are significant in both quantitative measurements and qualitative inspection. The contribution combines learned proposal selection with a curve-based output representation, producing explicit geometric edge descriptions from point-cloud input.
summary.tldr: PIE-NET learns to recover parametric feature curves from point clouds using candidate proposals and learned ranking.

title: PIE-NET: Parametric Inference of Point Cloud Edges

abstract: We introduce REDO, a class-agnostic framework to REconstruct the Dynamic Objects from RGBD or calibrated videos. Compared to prior work, our problem setting is more realistic yet more challenging for three reasons: 1) due to occlusion or camera settings an object of interest may never be entirely visible, but we aim to reconstruct the complete shape; 2) we aim to handle different object dynamics including rigid motion, non-rigid motion, and articulation; 3) we aim to reconstruct different categories of objects with one unified framework. To address these challenges, we develop two novel modules. First, we introduce a canonical 4D implicit function which is pixel-aligned with aggregated temporal visual cues. Second, we develop a 4D transformation module which captures object dynamics to support temporal propagation and aggregation. We study the efficacy of REDO in extensive experiments on synthetic RGBD video datasets SAIL-VOS 3D and DeformingThings4D++, and on real-world video data 3DPW. We find REDO outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic reconstruction methods by a margin. In ablation studies we validate each developed component.

paragraphs: REDO aims to reconstruct complete moving objects from RGBD or calibrated videos, including cases where an object is never fully visible. The framework is designed to handle rigid movement, deformation, and articulated motion across different object categories. Combining those goals makes the reconstruction problem more demanding than recovering a fully observed object with a single type of movement.

The method introduces two cooperating modules. A canonical four-dimensional implicit function represents the object while aligning with image pixels and visual evidence aggregated over time. A separate four-dimensional transformation module captures the object's dynamics. This motion representation supports moving information across time and combining observations, allowing the reconstruction to use evidence distributed across video frames.

The authors evaluate REDO on the synthetic RGBD datasets SAIL-VOS 3D and DeformingThings4D++, as well as real-world 3DPW videos. They report an improvement over state-of-the-art dynamic reconstruction methods and use ablation studies to validate the individual components. The findings support a unified approach to reconstructing dynamic objects under the varied visibility and motion conditions studied.
summary.tldr: REDO combines temporal visual evidence and learned object dynamics to reconstruct complete objects across categories and motion types.

title: Class-agnostic Reconstruction of Dynamic Objects from Videos

abstract: Escaping saddle points is a central research topic in nonconvex optimization. In this paper, we propose a simple gradient-based algorithm such that for a smooth function $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, it outputs an $\epsilon$-approximate second-order stationary point in $\tilde{O}(\log n/\epsilon^{1.75})$ iterations. Compared to the previous state-of-the-art algorithms by Jin et al. with $\tilde{O}(\log^4 n/\epsilon^{2})$ or $\tilde{O}(\log^6 n/\epsilon^{1.75})$ iterations, our algorithm is polynomially better in terms of $\log n$ and matches their complexities in terms of $1/\epsilon$. For the stochastic setting, our algorithm outputs an $\epsilon$-approximate second-order stationary point in $\tilde{O}(\log^{2} n/\epsilon^{4})$ iterations. Technically, our main contribution is an idea of implementing a robust Hessian power method using only gradients, which can find negative curvature near saddle points and achieve the polynomial speedup in $\log n$ compared to the perturbed gradient descent methods. Finally, we also perform numerical experiments that support our results.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a small gradient can occur near a saddle point even when useful downhill directions remain. This paper develops a gradient-based algorithm for reaching an approximate second-order stationary point of a smooth function. That target requires approximate stationarity together with control of negative curvature; it does not establish a global minimum.

The main technique implements a robust Hessian power method using only gradients. It seeks negative curvature near saddle points without requiring the algorithm to access the Hessian directly. This provides a mechanism for finding escape directions and improves the dimension dependence compared with the perturbed gradient descent methods considered in the paper.

For dimension n and accuracy ε, the stated iteration bound is roughly log(n)/ε^1.75, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. The improvement concerns powers of log(n), while retaining the ε dependence of the cited faster-accuracy comparison. In the stochastic setting, the bound is roughly log²(n)/ε^4 under the same notation. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results, complementing the analysis of how gradient information can reveal useful curvature.
summary.tldr: A gradient-only curvature-finding method escapes saddle points with improved logarithmic dependence on problem dimension.

title: Escape saddle points by a simple gradient-descent based algorithm

abstract: We introduce a novel theoretical framework for Return On Investment (ROI) maximization in repeated decision-making. Our setting is motivated by the use case of companies that regularly receive proposals for technological innovations and want to quickly decide whether they are worth implementing. We design an algorithm for learning ROI-maximizing decision-making policies over a sequence of innovation proposals. Our algorithm provably converges to an optimal policy in class $\Pi$ at a rate of order $\min\big\{1/(N\Delta^2),N^{-1/3}\}$, where $N$ is the number of innovations and $\Delta$ is the suboptimality gap in $\Pi$. A significant hurdle of our formulation, which sets it aside from other online learning problems such as bandits, is that running a policy does not provide an unbiased estimate of its performance.

Our algorithm provably converges to an optimal policy in class $\Pi$ at a rate of order $\min\big\{1/(N\Delta^2),N^{-1/3}\}$, where $N$ is the number of innovations and $\Delta$ is the suboptimality gap in $\Pi$. paragraphs: The paper studies repeated decisions aimed at maximizing return on investment. Its motivating situation is a company receiving a sequence of technological innovation proposals and needing to decide quickly whether to implement them. The objective is to learn a good decision-making policy across proposals, rather than evaluate each proposal as an isolated problem.

A central difficulty is that executing a policy does not yield an unbiased estimate of that policy's performance. The authors identify this as a feature that distinguishes their formulation from other online-learning problems, including bandits. Their algorithm therefore addresses learning when the feedback from running a policy cannot simply be treated as an unbiased performance measurement.

The algorithm provably approaches the best policy within a specified policy class. Its convergence rate has order min{1/(NΔ²), N^(-1/3)}, where N counts innovations and Δ is the class's suboptimality gap. This guarantee describes how learning depends on both experience and the gap between policies, while restricting optimality to the chosen class.
summary.tldr: The paper gives an algorithm with a convergence guarantee for learning ROI-maximizing policies despite biased performance feedback.

title: ROI Maximization in Stochastic Online Decision-Making

abstract: Convolutional networks are ubiquitous in deep learning. They are particularly useful for images, as they reduce the number of parameters, reduce training time, and increase accuracy. However, as a model of the brain they are seriously problematic, since they require weight sharing - something real neurons simply cannot do. Consequently, while neurons in the brain can be locally connected (one of the features of convolutional networks), they cannot be convolutional. Locally connected but non-convolutional networks, however, significantly underperform convolutional ones. This is troublesome for studies that use convolutional networks to explain activity in the visual system. Here we study plausible alternatives to weight sharing that aim at the same regularization principle, which is to make each neuron within a pool react similarly to identical inputs. The most natural way to do that is by showing the network multiple translations of the same image, akin to saccades in animal vision. However, this approach requires many translations, and doesn't remove the performance gap. We propose instead to add lateral connectivity to a locally connected network, and allow learning via Hebbian plasticity. This requires the network to pause occasionally for a sleep-like phase of "weight sharing". This method enables locally connected networks to achieve nearly convolutional performance on ImageNet and improves their fit to the ventral stream data, thus supporting convolutional networks as a model of the visual stream.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks gain efficiency and accuracy by sharing weights across locations, but the paper argues that this mechanism is problematic as a model of biological neurons. Locally connected networks avoid literal weight sharing yet perform substantially worse. The authors therefore seek a more biologically plausible way to encourage similar responses to identical inputs across a pool of neurons.

They first consider training with multiple translations of each image, resembling changes in visual input caused by saccades. This requires many translations and does not close the performance gap. Their proposed alternative adds lateral connections to a locally connected network and uses Hebbian plasticity, with occasional sleep-like phases that encourage a functional analogue of weight sharing.

The resulting locally connected networks achieve nearly convolutional performance on ImageNet and fit ventral-stream data better. These findings support the idea that some benefits of convolution-like regularization can arise through a different learning mechanism. The method therefore offers a bridge between the practical success of convolutional networks and efforts to explain visual-system activity, while retaining the paper's framing as progress toward biological plausibility.
summary.tldr: Lateral connections and sleep-like Hebbian learning bring locally connected networks close to convolutional accuracy while improving their fit to visual-system data.

title: Towards Biologically Plausible Convolutional Networks

abstract: Stochastic processes are random variables with values in some space of paths. However, reducing a stochastic process to a path-valued random variable ignores its filtration, i.e. the flow of information carried by the process through time. By conditioning the process on its filtration, we introduce a family of higher order kernel mean embeddings (KMEs) that generalizes the notion of KME to capture additional information related to the filtration. We derive empirical estimators for the associated higher order maximum mean discrepancies (MMDs) and prove consistency. We then construct a filtration-sensitive kernel two-sample test able to capture information that gets missed by the standard MMD test. In addition, leveraging our higher order MMDs we construct a family of universal kernels on stochastic processes that allows to solve real-world calibration and optimal stopping problems in quantitative finance (such as the pricing of American options) via classical kernel-based regression methods. Finally, adapting existing tests for conditional independence to the case of stochastic processes, we design a causal-discovery algorithm to recover the causal graph of structural dependencies among interacting bodies solely from observations of their multidimensional trajectories.

paragraphs: A stochastic process describes a random trajectory, but its complete path does not by itself capture how information becomes available over time. That evolving information is its filtration. This paper develops representations that account for this distinction, which matters when a task depends on what can be known at a particular moment.

The authors condition processes on their filtrations to construct higher-order kernel mean embeddings. From these representations, they derive higher-order maximum mean discrepancies and empirical estimators with consistency guarantees. A resulting two-sample test can detect filtration-related information that a standard MMD test misses, extending what kernel-based comparisons can distinguish between stochastic processes.

The framework also yields universal kernels for regression on stochastic processes. The authors use these for financial calibration and optimal stopping problems, including American option pricing, where the timing of information is relevant to decisions. Finally, they adapt conditional independence tests to processes and develop a causal-discovery algorithm for recovering structural dependencies among interacting bodies from observed multidimensional trajectories.
summary.tldr: Higher-order kernel embeddings capture how information unfolds in stochastic processes, supporting richer statistical tests, regression, and causal discovery.

title: Higher Order Kernel Mean Embeddings to Capture Filtrations of Stochastic Processes

abstract: Teacher-student models provide a framework in which the typical-case performance of high-dimensional supervised learning can be described in closed form. The assumptions of Gaussian i.i.d. input data underlying the canonical teacher-student model may, however, be perceived as too restrictive to capture the behaviour of realistic data sets. In this paper, we introduce a Gaussian covariate generalisation of the model where the teacher and student can act on different spaces, generated with fixed, but generic feature maps. While still solvable in a closed form, this generalization is able to capture the learning curves for a broad range of realistic data sets, thus redeeming the potential of the teacher-student framework. Our contribution is then two-fold: first, we prove a rigorous formula for the asymptotic training loss and generalisation error. Second, we present a number of situations where the learning curve of the model captures the one of a realistic data set learned with kernel regression and classification, with out-of-the-box feature maps such as random projections or scattering transforms, or with pre-learned ones - such as the features learned by training multi-layer neural networks. We discuss both the power and the limitations of the framework.

paragraphs: Teacher-student models offer a mathematical setting for describing typical learning performance in high dimensions. Their appeal is that performance can sometimes be expressed in closed form. However, the standard assumption of independent Gaussian inputs can seem too restrictive to explain learning curves observed on realistic datasets.

This paper generalizes the framework using a Gaussian covariate model in which teacher and student can operate in different spaces. Fixed but generic feature maps generate those spaces. The construction retains mathematical tractability while allowing a broader range of representations. The authors prove a rigorous formula for asymptotic training loss and generalization error.

They also present situations where the model’s predicted learning curve captures the curve obtained on realistic data. These examples cover kernel regression and classification with random projections, scattering transforms, and features previously learned by multilayer neural networks. The findings show that a solvable Gaussian framework can describe useful aspects of learning beyond its simplest input assumptions. The theoretical formula is asymptotic, and the reported agreements concern the situations examined rather than every possible dataset or feature map.
summary.tldr: A generalized Gaussian teacher-student model gives rigorous asymptotic error formulas and captures learning curves for several realistic datasets and feature representations.

title: Learning curves of generic features maps for realistic datasets with a teacher-student model

abstract: Domain generalization (DG) methods aim to achieve generalizability to an unseen target domain by using only training data from the source domains. Although a variety of DG methods have been proposed, a recent study shows that under a fair evaluation protocol, called DomainBed, the simple empirical risk minimization (ERM) approach works comparable to or even outperforms previous methods. Unfortunately, simply solving ERM on a complex, non-convex loss function can easily lead to sub-optimal generalizability by seeking sharp minima. In this paper, we theoretically show that finding flat minima results in a smaller domain generalization gap. We also propose a simple yet effective method, named Stochastic Weight Averaging Densely (SWAD), to find flat minima. SWAD finds flatter minima and suffers less from overfitting than does the vanilla SWA by a dense and overfit-aware stochastic weight sampling strategy. SWAD shows state-of-the-art performances on five DG benchmarks, namely PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, TerraIncognita, and DomainNet, with consistent and large margins of +1.6% averagely on out-of-domain accuracy. We also compare SWAD with conventional generalization methods, such as data augmentation and consistency regularization methods, to verify that the remarkable performance improvements are originated from by seeking flat minima, not from better in-domain generalizability. Last but not least, SWAD is readily adaptable to existing DG methods without modification; the combination of SWAD and an existing DG method further improves DG performances. Source code is available at https://github.com/khanrc/swad.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to perform well on an unseen target domain using only source-domain training data. This paper starts from evidence that ordinary empirical risk minimization can rival specialized methods under fair evaluation. It asks how the solution found during training affects generalization, focusing on the difference between sharp and flat minima.

The authors theoretically connect flat minima with a smaller domain generalization gap. Their method, Stochastic Weight Averaging Densely, or SWAD, uses dense sampling of model weights with an overfitting-aware strategy. Compared with standard stochastic weight averaging, it finds flatter minima and suffers less from overfitting, providing a practical mechanism for pursuing the paper’s theoretical motivation.

SWAD achieves reported state-of-the-art performance on five domain-generalization benchmarks, with an average out-of-domain accuracy improvement of 1.6%. Comparisons with data augmentation and consistency regularization support attributing the gains to seeking flat minima rather than simply improving in-domain generalization. SWAD can also be combined with existing domain-generalization methods without modifying them, and the reported combination further improves performance.
summary.tldr: SWAD uses dense, overfitting-aware weight averaging to find flatter minima and improve generalization to unseen domains.

title: SWAD: Domain Generalization by Seeking Flat Minima

abstract: Neural Module Networks (NMNs) aim at Visual Question Answering (VQA) via composition of modules that tackle a sub-task. NMNs are a promising strategy to achieve systematic generalization, i.e., overcoming biasing factors in the training distribution. However, the aspects of NMNs that facilitate systematic generalization are not fully understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that the degree of modularity of the NMN have large influence on systematic generalization. In a series of experiments on three VQA datasets (VQA-MNIST, SQOOP, and CLEVR-CoGenT), our results reveal that tuning the degree of modularity, especially at the image encoder stage, reaches substantially higher systematic generalization. These findings lead to new NMN architectures that outperform previous ones in terms of systematic generalization.

NMNs are a promising strategy to achieve systematic generalization, i.e., overcoming biasing factors in the training distribution. However, the aspects of NMNs that facilitate systematic generalization are not fully understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that the degree of modularity of the NMN have large influence on systematic generalization. These findings lead to new NMN architectures that outperform previous ones in terms of systematic generalization.

paragraphs: Neural module networks answer questions about images by composing components that handle subtasks. This makes them promising for systematic generalization: succeeding beyond the biasing patterns present in the training distribution. The paper investigates which aspects of that modular construction actually support this ability, focusing on how much of the network should be divided into modules.

The authors examine the degree of modularity through experiments on VQA-MNIST, SQOOP, and CLEVR-CoGenT. Their results show that changing this degree has a large effect on systematic generalization. The image encoder, which turns the visual input into a representation for later processing, is a particularly influential place to tune modularity. This makes the organization of visual processing an important architectural choice.

These findings lead to new module-network architectures that outperform previous architectures on systematic generalization. The conclusion is that tuning the extent of modularity can substantially improve results in the evaluated settings. The evidence highlights the degree and placement of modular structure as design decisions that deserve explicit attention.
summary.tldr: Tuning how modular visual question-answering networks are, especially their image encoders, substantially improves systematic generalization in the evaluated datasets.

title: How Modular should Neural Module Networks Be for Systematic Generalization?

abstract: Many instances of algorithmic bias are caused by subpopulation shifts. For example, ML models often perform worse on demographic groups that are underrepresented in the training data. In this paper, we study whether enforcing algorithmic fairness during training improves the performance of the trained model in the \emph{target domain}. On one hand, we conceive scenarios in which enforcing fairness does not improve performance in the target domain. In fact, it may even harm performance. On the other hand, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions under which enforcing algorithmic fairness leads to the Bayes model in the target domain. We also illustrate the practical implications of our theoretical results in simulations and on real data.

For example, ML models often perform worse on demographic groups that are underrepresented in the training data. In this paper, we study whether enforcing algorithmic fairness during training improves the performance of the trained model in the \emph{target domain}. On one hand, we conceive scenarios in which enforcing fairness does not improve performance in the target domain. In fact, it may even harm performance. On the other hand, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions under which enforcing algorithmic fairness leads to the Bayes model in the target domain. We also illustrate the practical implications of our theoretical results in simulations and on real data.

paragraphs: A model trained on one population may perform differently when the proportions of demographic groups change. Groups with little representation in training data can receive worse predictions. This paper asks whether imposing algorithmic fairness during training helps the resulting model perform well in the target population where it will be used.

The answer is conditional. The authors construct scenarios in which enforcing fairness fails to improve target-domain performance, and others in which it can make performance worse. These examples establish that a fairness intervention does not automatically correct the predictive consequences of a subpopulation shift. The relationship between the training and target populations matters.

The paper also derives necessary and sufficient conditions under which enforcing fairness produces the target domain’s Bayes model, the optimal prediction rule for that domain. This gives a precise theoretical characterization of when the intervention succeeds in that sense. Simulations and real-data analyses illustrate the practical implications, connecting the formal conditions to observed behavior under population changes.
summary.tldr: Enforcing fairness can help or harm prediction under subpopulation shift, and the paper characterizes when it yields the target-domain Bayes model.

title: Does enforcing fairness mitigate biases caused by subpopulation shift?

abstract: Probability discrepancy measure is a fundamental construct for numerous machine learning models such as weakly supervised learning and generative modeling. However, most measures overlook the fact that the distributions are not the end-product of learning, but are the basis of downstream predictor. Therefore it is important to warp the probability discrepancy measure towards the end tasks, and we hence propose a new bi-level optimization based approach so that the two distributions are compared not uniformly against the entire hypothesis space, but only with respect to the optimal predictor for the downstream end task. When applied to margin disparity discrepancy and contrastive domain discrepancy, our method significantly improves the performance in unsupervised domain adaptation, and enjoys a much more principled training process.

paragraphs: Measures of discrepancy between probability distributions help machine learning systems compare data sources. The paper argues that such comparisons should account for the prediction task those distributions will support. A difference that matters across a broad collection of possible predictors need not have the same significance for the predictor used in the downstream task.

The authors introduce a bilevel optimization approach that makes the discrepancy task-dependent. Instead of comparing two distributions uniformly against the entire hypothesis space, the method compares them with respect to the optimal downstream predictor. The nested optimization links how the predictor is chosen with how the distributions are judged to differ.

The approach is applied to margin disparity discrepancy and contrastive domain discrepancy in unsupervised domain adaptation. The authors report significant performance improvements and describe the resulting training process as more principled. The practical meaning is that distribution comparison becomes tied to the purpose of adaptation: supporting a useful predictor, with the reported applications providing evidence for this task-focused design.
summary.tldr: A bilevel approach tailors distribution discrepancy to the optimal downstream predictor and improves the reported unsupervised domain adaptation results.

title: Implicit Task-Driven Probability Discrepancy Measure for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: 3D object tracking in point clouds is still a challenging problem due to the sparsity of LiDAR points in dynamic environments. In this work, we propose a Siamese voxel-to-BEV tracker, which can significantly improve the tracking performance in sparse 3D point clouds. Specifically, it consists of a Siamese shape-aware feature learning network and a voxel-to-BEV target localization network. The Siamese shape-aware feature learning network can capture 3D shape information of the object to learn the discriminative features of the object so that the potential target from the background in sparse point clouds can be identified. To this end, we first perform template feature embedding to embed the template's feature into the potential target and then generate a dense 3D shape to characterize the shape information of the potential target. For localizing the tracked target, the voxel-to-BEV target localization network regresses the target's 2D center and the z-axis center from the dense bird's eye view (BEV) feature map in an anchor-free manner. Concretely, we compress the voxelized point cloud along z-axis through max pooling to obtain a dense BEV feature map, where the regression of the 2D center and the z-axis center can be performed more effectively. Extensive evaluation on the KITTI tracking dataset shows that our method significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods by a large margin. Code is available at https://github.com/fpthink/V2B.

paragraphs: Tracking an object through LiDAR measurements is difficult when only a few points describe its surface. This paper introduces a tracker that combines learning an object's three-dimensional shape with locating it in a bird's-eye-view representation. These two components address complementary questions: which points belong to the target, and where the target is.

The shape-learning component brings information from a template into a potential target's features, then generates a dense three-dimensional shape. This gives the tracker a richer description than the sparse observations alone provide. The localization component groups points into voxels and compresses them along the vertical axis using max pooling, producing a dense feature map viewed from above.

From that map, the method directly predicts both the target's horizontal center and its vertical center without using anchors. Evaluations on the KITTI tracking dataset report a substantial improvement over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The result supports combining shape information and dense spatial features to improve tracking when the original point cloud is sparse.
summary.tldr: A tracker combines dense shape learning with bird's-eye-view localization to improve object tracking in sparse LiDAR point clouds.

title: 3D Siamese Voxel-to-BEV Tracker for Sparse Point Clouds

abstract: Model quantization has emerged as an indispensable technique to accelerate deep learning inference. Although researchers continue to push the frontier of quantization algorithms, existing quantization work is often unreproducible and undeployable. This is because researchers do not choose consistent training pipelines and ignore the requirements for hardware deployments. In this work, we propose Model Quantization Benchmark (MQBench), a first attempt to evaluate, analyze, and benchmark the reproducibility and deployability for model quantization algorithms. We choose multiple different platforms for real-world deployments, including CPU, GPU, ASIC, DSP, and evaluate extensive state-of-the-art quantization algorithms under a unified training pipeline. MQBench acts like a bridge to connect the algorithm and the hardware. We conduct a comprehensive analysis and find considerable intuitive or counter-intuitive insights. By aligning up the training settings, we find existing algorithms have about-the-same performance on the conventional academic track. While for the hardware-deployable quantization, there is a huge accuracy gap and still a long way to go. Surprisingly, no existing algorithm wins every challenge in MQBench, and we hope this work could inspire future research directions.

paragraphs: Model quantization is used to accelerate neural-network inference, but an algorithm's reported performance may not translate cleanly into a reproducible, deployable system. This paper attributes that gap to inconsistent training procedures and insufficient attention to hardware requirements. MQBench brings those two issues into the evaluation of quantization methods.

The benchmark compares advanced quantization algorithms under a unified training pipeline and considers deployment on CPUs, GPUs, ASICs, and DSPs. This connects the algorithmic comparison to the platforms on which models are intended to run. The shared training procedure also makes it possible to reassess apparent differences between methods under aligned experimental conditions.

With training settings aligned, the authors find roughly similar performance among existing algorithms on the conventional academic track. Hardware-deployable quantization, however, shows a large accuracy gap, and no evaluated algorithm wins every MQBench challenge. These findings suggest that academic comparisons alone do not settle practical method selection. Reproducibility and hardware compatibility expose important dimensions of performance that require further work.
summary.tldr: MQBench finds similar academic performance under aligned training settings but substantial accuracy challenges when quantization must satisfy hardware deployment requirements.

title: MQBench: Towards Reproducible and Deployable Model Quantization Benchmark

abstract: The performance of trained neural networks is robust to harsh levels of pruning. Coupled with the ever-growing size of deep learning models, this observation has motivated extensive research on learning sparse models. In this work, we focus on the task of controlling the level of sparsity when performing sparse learning. Existing methods based on sparsity-inducing penalties involve expensive trial-and-error tuning of the penalty factor, thus lacking direct control of the resulting model sparsity. In response, we adopt a constrained formulation: using the gate mechanism proposed by Louizos et al. (2018), we formulate a constrained optimization problem where sparsification is guided by the training objective and the desired sparsity target in an end-to-end fashion. Experiments on CIFAR-{10, 100}, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet using WideResNet and ResNet{18, 50} models validate the effectiveness of our proposal and demonstrate that we can reliably achieve pre-determined sparsity targets without compromising on predictive performance.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks retain only part of their available parameters or connections. This paper focuses on controlling how sparse a trained model becomes. Many existing methods encourage sparsity through an extra penalty in the training objective, but choosing its strength requires trial and error because it does not directly specify the final sparsity.

The authors formulate training as a constrained optimization problem with a desired sparsity target. They use an existing gating mechanism to support sparsification, allowing the prediction objective and the target to guide learning together. The practical distinction is that the user specifies the desired model sparsity directly, rather than repeatedly adjusting a penalty and checking what sparsity it produces.

Experiments span CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet with WideResNet and ResNet architectures. In these evaluations, the method reliably reaches predetermined sparsity targets without compromising predictive performance. The findings support constrained training as a practical way to make model sparsity controllable while preserving the predictive quality demonstrated in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A constrained training formulation directly targets neural-network sparsity and reliably meets those targets without sacrificing predictive performance in the reported experiments.

title: Controlled Sparsity via Constrained Optimization or: How I Learned to Stop Tuning Penalties and Love Constraints

abstract: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising direction for training agents that are capable of solving multiple tasks and reach a diverse set of objectives. How to \textit{specify} and \textit{ground} these goals in such a way that we can both reliably reach goals during training as well as generalize to new goals during evaluation remains an open area of research. Defining goals in the space of noisy, high-dimensional sensory inputs is one possibility, yet this poses a challenge for training goal-conditioned agents, or even for generalization to novel goals. We propose to address this by learning compositional representations of goals and processing the resulting representation via a discretization bottleneck, for coarser specification of goals, through an approach we call DGRL. We show that discretizing outputs from goal encoders through a bottleneck can work well in goal-conditioned RL setups, by experimentally evaluating this method on tasks ranging from maze environments to complex robotic navigation and manipulation tasks. Additionally, we show a theoretical result which bounds the expected return for goals not observed during training, while still allowing for specifying goals with expressive combinatorial structure.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains an agent to pursue different objectives using a goal supplied as input. A central difficulty is deciding how to express that goal. Directly using noisy, high-dimensional sensory observations can make learning difficult and can also hinder the agent's ability to pursue goals it has not encountered during training.

The proposed method, DGRL, learns compositional goal representations and then passes them through a discretization bottleneck. This produces a coarser description of the objective while retaining a structure in which components can be combined. The approach focuses on the goal representation as a way to make both training and generalization more manageable.

Experiments span maze environments and more complex robotic navigation and manipulation tasks, showing that discretizing goal-encoder outputs can work well in these settings. The paper also derives a bound on expected return for goals absent from training while allowing expressive combinations of goal components. Together, the empirical and theoretical results support discrete, compositional representations as a useful abstraction for this learning problem.
summary.tldr: DGRL combines compositional goal representations with discretization to support learning and generalization in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

title: Discrete Compositional Representations as an Abstraction for Goal Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) has achieved great success in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in practical applications. However, CTDE-based methods typically suffer from poor zero-shot generalization ability with dynamic team composition and varying partial observability. To tackle these issues, we propose a spontaneously grouping mechanism, termed Self-Organized Group (SOG), which is featured with conductor election (CE) and message summary (MS). In CE, a certain number of conductors are elected every $T$ time-steps to temporally construct groups, each with conductor-follower consensus where the followers are constrained to only communicate with their conductor. In MS, each conductor summarize and distribute the received messages to all affiliate group members to hold a unified scheduling. SOG provides zero-shot generalization ability to the dynamic number of agents and the varying partial observability. Sufficient experiments on mainstream multi-agent benchmarks exhibit superiority of SOG.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent systems often train centrally and then let agents act separately. Such methods can struggle to generalize immediately when team membership changes or agents have different amounts of observable information. Self-Organized Group addresses these issues by organizing agents into temporary communication groups.

The mechanism has two parts: conductor election and message summary. At regular intervals of T time steps, a selected set of conductors forms temporary groups. Followers communicate only with their own conductor. Each conductor summarizes the incoming messages and distributes the summary to its group, supporting coordinated scheduling among the members.

This structure makes group formation and information exchange part of the coordination mechanism, rather than assuming a permanently fixed team arrangement. The paper reports zero-shot generalization to changing numbers of agents and varying partial observability. Experiments on mainstream multi-agent benchmarks show superior performance for the proposed approach. The findings support periodically reorganized, summarized communication as a practical way to handle the kinds of team and observation changes studied.
summary.tldr: Self-Organized Group uses elected conductors and summarized messages to coordinate agents and generalize to changing teams and observability.

title: Self-Organized Group for Cooperative Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose a variational model, iterative Structural Inference of Directed Graphs (iSIDG), to infer the existence of directed interactions from observational agents’ features over a time period in a dynamical system. First, the iterative process in our model feeds the learned interactions back to encourage our model to eliminate indirect interactions and to emphasize directional representation during learning. Second, we show that extra regularization terms in the objective function for smoothness, connectiveness, and sparsity prompt our model to infer a more realistic structure and to further eliminate indirect interactions. We evaluate iSIDG on various datasets including biological networks, simulated fMRI data, and physical simulations to demonstrate that our model is able to precisely infer the existence of interactions, and is significantly superior to baseline models.

Second, we show that extra regularization terms in the objective function for smoothness, connectiveness, and sparsity prompt our model to infer a more realistic structure and to further eliminate indirect interactions. paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer directed interactions among agents from observations of their features over time. Its model, iSIDG, uses a variational approach to recover this structure in dynamical systems. A central concern is separating direct interactions from indirect relationships that can also appear in the observations.

The model repeatedly feeds its learned interactions back into the inference process. This feedback is intended to suppress indirect interactions and strengthen the representation of direction. Additional objective terms encourage smoothness, connectedness, and sparsity. The authors show that these terms promote more realistic structures and further reduce inferred indirect interactions.

Evaluation covers biological networks, simulated fMRI data, and physical simulations. The reported results show precise interaction inference and significant improvements over baseline models. The contribution combines iterative feedback with structural regularization, giving the model two complementary ways to refine the graph it learns. These findings support the approach across several kinds of dynamical-system data included in the evaluation.
summary.tldr: iSIDG iteratively refines directed interaction graphs and uses structural regularization to reduce indirect connections.

title: Iterative Structural Inference of Directed Graphs

abstract: Improving the accuracy of deep neural networks on out-of-distribution (OOD) data is critical to an acceptance of deep learning in real world applications. It has been observed that accuracies on in-distribution (ID) versus OOD data follow a linear trend and models that outperform this baseline are exceptionally rare (and referred to as ``effectively robust”). Recently, some promising approaches have been developed to improve OOD robustness: model pruning, data augmentation, and ensembling or zero-shot evaluating large pretrained models. However, there still is no clear understanding of the conditions on OOD data and model properties that are required to observe effective robustness. We approach this issue by conducting a comprehensive empirical study of diverse approaches that are known to impact OOD robustness on a broad range of natural and synthetic distribution shifts of CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. In particular, we view the "effective robustness puzzle" through a Fourier lens and ask how spectral properties of both models and OOD data correlate with OOD robustness. We find this Fourier lens offers some insight into why certain robust models, particularly those from the CLIP family, achieve OOD robustness. However, our analysis also makes clear that no known metric is consistently the best explanation of OOD robustness. Thus, to aid future research into the OOD puzzle, we address the gap in publicly-available models with effective robustness by introducing a set of pretrained CIFAR-10 models---$RobustNets$---with varying levels of OOD robustness.

summary.tldr: Fourier analysis partly explains exceptional distribution-shift robustness, but no examined metric consistently explains it best.

title: Models Out of Line: A Fourier Lens on Distribution Shift Robustness

abstract: This paper studies the problem of real-world video super-resolution (VSR) for animation videos, and reveals three key improvements for practical animation VSR. First, recent real-world super-resolution approaches typically rely on degradation simulation using basic operators without any learning capability, such as blur, noise, and compression. In this work, we propose to learn such basic operators from real low-quality animation videos, and incorporate the learned ones into the degradation generation pipeline. Such neural-network-based basic operators could help to better capture the distribution of real degradations. Second, a large-scale high-quality animation video dataset, AVC, is built to facilitate comprehensive training and evaluations for animation VSR. Third, we further investigate an efficient multi-scale network structure. It takes advantage of the efficiency of unidirectional recurrent networks and the effectiveness of sliding-window-based methods. Thanks to the above delicate designs, our method, AnimeSR, is capable of restoring real-world low-quality animation videos effectively and efficiently, achieving superior performance to previous state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: AnimeSR addresses the restoration of low-quality animation videos at higher resolution. Its starting point is that training data must reflect the damage found in actual videos. Existing approaches commonly simulate degradation with fixed blur, noise, and compression operations. The paper instead learns basic degradation operators from real low-quality animation footage and incorporates them into the simulation pipeline.

These learned operators could capture real degradation patterns more faithfully, giving the restoration model more relevant examples to learn from. The work also introduces AVC, a large collection of high-quality animation videos for training and evaluation. Together, the learned degradation process and the dataset address how to construct useful training material for animation super-resolution.

The third contribution is an efficient network with multiple processing scales. It combines advantages of unidirectional recurrent processing and sliding-window methods. The authors report that the resulting AnimeSR system restores real-world animation effectively and efficiently, outperforming previous leading methods. The contribution therefore spans training-data construction, evaluation resources, and model design.
summary.tldr: AnimeSR combines learned video degradations, a high-quality animation dataset, and an efficient network to improve real-world animation super-resolution.

title: AnimeSR: Learning Real-World Super-Resolution Models for Animation Videos

abstract: U-Net architectures are ubiquitous in state-of-the-art deep learning, however their regularisation properties and relationship to wavelets are understudied. In this paper, we formulate a multi-resolution framework which identifies U-Nets as finite-dimensional truncations of models on an infinite-dimensional function space. We provide theoretical results which prove that average pooling corresponds to projection within the space of square-integrable functions and show that U-Nets with average pooling implicitly learn a Haar wavelet basis representation of the data. We then leverage our framework to identify state-of-the-art hierarchical VAEs (HVAEs), which have a U-Net architecture, as a type of two-step forward Euler discretisation of multi-resolution diffusion processes which flow from a point mass, introducing sampling instabilities. We also demonstrate that HVAEs learn a representation of time which allows for improved parameter efficiency through weight-sharing. We use this observation to achieve state-of-the-art HVAE performance with half the number of parameters of existing models, exploiting the properties of our continuous-time formulation.

paragraphs: U-Nets process information at multiple resolutions, but the mathematical implications of this structure are not fully understood. This paper develops a framework that treats a finite U-Net as a truncated version of a model operating on an infinite-dimensional space of functions. That perspective connects architectural choices to established mathematical operations.

The authors prove that average pooling acts as a projection in the space of square-integrable functions. They also show that U-Nets using average pooling implicitly learn a representation in a Haar wavelet basis. These results give a precise interpretation to how the network handles information across resolutions, rather than treating pooling as merely an implementation detail.

The framework also interprets hierarchical variational autoencoders with U-Net architectures as two-step forward Euler discretizations of multiresolution diffusion processes starting from a point mass, which introduce sampling instabilities. The authors further find that these models learn a representation of time that supports sharing weights. Using this observation, they report state-of-the-art hierarchical VAE performance with half as many parameters as existing models.
summary.tldr: A multiresolution interpretation of U-Nets connects average pooling to wavelets and enables hierarchical VAEs with substantially fewer parameters.

title: A Multi-Resolution Framework for U-Nets with Applications to Hierarchical VAEs

abstract: In this work, we present a unified framework for multi-modality 3D object detection, named UVTR. The proposed method aims to unify multi-modality representations in the voxel space for accurate and robust single- or cross-modality 3D detection. To this end, the modality-specific space is first designed to represent different inputs in the voxel feature space. Different from previous work, our approach preserves the voxel space without height compression to alleviate semantic ambiguity and enable spatial connections. To make full use of the inputs from different sensors, the cross-modality interaction is then proposed, including knowledge transfer and modality fusion. In this way, geometry-aware expressions in point clouds and context-rich features in images are well utilized for better performance and robustness. The transformer decoder is applied to efficiently sample features from the unified space with learnable positions, which facilitates object-level interactions. In general, UVTR presents an early attempt to represent different modalities in a unified framework. It surpasses previous work in single- or multi-modality entries. The proposed method achieves leading performance in the nuScenes test set for both object detection and the following object tracking task. Code is made publicly available at https://github.com/dvlab-research/UVTR.

UVTR brings these inputs into a unified voxel feature space to support detection with either a single modality or multiple modalities. Each input first receives a modality-specific representation within that shared spatial framework.

The method preserves height in the voxel representation instead of compressing it away. This is intended to reduce semantic ambiguity and retain spatial connections. Cross-modality interaction then supports both knowledge transfer and feature fusion, allowing the method to use complementary information from different sensors. A transformer decoder samples the unified features at learned positions and enables interactions at the object level.

The reported results surpass previous work in both single-modality and multimodality settings. UVTR also achieves leading performance on the nuScenes test set for detection and the subsequent tracking task. The contribution is a common spatial representation that supports sensor interaction and transformer-based object reasoning, with empirical gains spanning detection configurations and tracking.
summary.tldr: UVTR unifies image and point-cloud features in an uncompressed-height voxel space for transformer-based 3D detection and tracking.

title: Unifying Voxel-based Representation with Transformer for 3D Object Detection

abstract: We study a Markov matching market involving a planner and a set of strategic agents on the two sides of the market.At each step, the agents are presented with a dynamical context, where the contexts determine the utilities. The planner controls the transition of the contexts to maximize the cumulative social welfare, while the agents aim to find a myopic stable matching at each step. Such a setting captures a range of applications including ridesharing platforms. We formalize the problem by proposing a reinforcement learning framework that integrates optimistic value iteration with maximum weight matching. The proposed algorithm addresses the coupled challenges of sequential exploration, matching stability, and function approximation. We prove that the algorithm achieves sublinear regret.

paragraphs: A matching market can evolve over time, with current decisions affecting the conditions under which future matches occur. This paper studies a planner and strategic agents on two sides of such a market. At each step, the current context determines agents' utilities, while the planner controls how contexts transition to maximize cumulative social welfare.

The agents seek a stable matching based on the current situation, giving them a shorter-term objective than the planner. The proposed reinforcement learning framework combines optimistic value iteration with maximum-weight matching. It brings sequential planning and matching into one algorithm so that learning about future consequences can coexist with the requirement for stability at each step.

The analysis addresses exploration, matching stability, and function approximation together, and proves that the algorithm achieves sublinear regret. This means its cumulative regret grows more slowly than the interaction horizon. The framework captures settings such as ridesharing platforms, where matching decisions occur repeatedly within changing conditions. Its contribution is a formal approach to learning long-term planning behavior while accounting for agents' immediate matching incentives.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning framework combines long-term welfare planning with stable matching in dynamic markets and achieves provably sublinear regret.

title: Learn to Match with No Regret: Reinforcement Learning in Markov Matching Markets

abstract: The research area of algorithms with predictions has seen recent success showing how to incorporate machine learning into algorithm design to improve performance when the predictions are correct, while retaining worst-case guarantees when they are not. Most previous work has assumed that the algorithm has access to a single predictor. However, in practice, there are many machine learning methods available, often with incomparable generalization guarantees, making it hard to pick a best method a priori. In this work we consider scenarios where multiple predictors are available to the algorithm and the question is how to best utilize them. Ideally, we would like the algorithm's performance to depend on the quality of the {\em best} predictor. However, utilizing more predictions comes with a cost, since we now have to identify which prediction is best. We study the use of multiple predictors for a number of fundamental problems, including matching, load balancing, and non-clairvoyant scheduling, which have been well-studied in the single predictor setting. For each of these problems we introduce new algorithms that take advantage of multiple predictors, and prove bounds on the resulting performance.

paragraphs: Algorithms with predictions use learned forecasts to improve decisions while seeking worst-case protection when forecasts are unreliable. Much of this research assumes access to one predictor. This paper considers the more practical situation in which several predictors are available and their relative quality cannot easily be determined in advance.

The central challenge is that a collection of predictions brings both opportunity and an identification cost. An algorithm would ideally perform according to the strongest predictor in the collection, but it must somehow determine which predictions deserve attention. Simply having more forecasts does not settle how to use them effectively. The paper makes this selection problem part of algorithm design.

The authors develop algorithms for matching, load balancing, and non-clairvoyant scheduling, and prove performance bounds for each setting. These results extend problems previously studied with a single predictor to prediction portfolios. The contribution is a set of problem-specific methods and guarantees for exploiting multiple forecasts, rather than an unconditional claim that access to more predictors always improves performance.
summary.tldr: The paper develops algorithms and performance bounds for using multiple predictors while accounting for the cost of identifying useful predictions.

title: Algorithms with Prediction Portfolios

abstract: PointNet++ is one of the most influential neural architectures for point cloud understanding. Although the accuracy of PointNet++ has been largely surpassed by recent networks such as PointMLP and Point Transformer, we find that a large portion of the performance gain is due to improved training strategies, i.e. data augmentation and optimization techniques, and increased model sizes rather than architectural innovations. Thus, the full potential of PointNet++ has yet to be explored. In this work, we revisit the classical PointNet++ through a systematic study of model training and scaling strategies, and offer two major contributions. First, we propose a set of improved training strategies that significantly improve PointNet++ performance. For example, we show that, without any change in architecture, the overall accuracy (OA) of PointNet++ on ScanObjectNN object classification can be raised from 77.9% to 86.1%, even outperforming state-of-the-art PointMLP. Second, we introduce an inverted residual bottleneck design and separable MLPs into PointNet++ to enable efficient and effective model scaling and propose PointNeXt, the next version of PointNets. PointNeXt can be flexibly scaled up and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both 3D classification and segmentation tasks. For classification, PointNeXt reaches an overall accuracy of 87.7 on ScanObjectNN, surpassing PointMLP by 2.3%, while being 10x faster in inference. For semantic segmentation, PointNeXt establishes a new state-of-the-art performance with 74.9% mean IoU on S3DIS (6-fold cross-validation), being superior to the recent Point Transformer. The code and models are available at https://github.com/guochengqian/pointnext.

title: PointNeXt: Revisiting PointNet++ with Improved Training and Scaling Strategies

abstract: Although two-stage Vector Quantized (VQ) generative models allow for synthesizing high-fidelity and high-resolution images, their quantization operator encodes similar patches within an image into the same index, resulting in a repeated artifact for similar adjacent regions using existing decoder architectures. To address this issue, we propose to incorporate the spatially conditional normalization to modulate the quantized vectors so as to insert spatially variant information to the embedded index maps, encouraging the decoder to generate more photorealistic images. Moreover, we use multichannel quantization to increase the recombination capability of the discrete codes without increasing the cost of model and codebook. Additionally, to generate discrete tokens at the second stage, we adopt a Masked Generative Image Transformer (MaskGIT) to learn an underlying prior distribution in the compressed latent space, which is much faster than the conventional autoregressive model. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed modulated VQGAN is able to greatly improve the reconstructed image quality as well as provide high-fidelity image generation.

paragraphs: MoVQ addresses repeated visual artifacts in two-stage image generators that represent image patches using discrete codes. Similar patches can receive the same code, and existing decoders can produce repeated patterns in nearby regions as a result. The paper aims to retain this compact representation while improving the images reconstructed from it.

Its central change is spatially conditional normalization, which modulates the quantized vectors with information that varies across image locations. This gives the decoder spatial variation to work with even when patches share a discrete index. The intended effect is to encourage more photorealistic images by enriching the information available during decoding.

The method also uses multichannel quantization to expand how discrete codes can be recombined without increasing model or codebook cost. For the second stage, it adopts MaskGIT to learn the distribution of tokens in the compressed representation. The abstract describes this token-generation approach as much faster than conventional autoregressive modeling.

Experiments on two benchmark datasets report substantially improved reconstruction quality and high-fidelity image generation. These findings support the value of modulating quantized representations: the reported gains concern both recovering an image from its compressed codes and producing images through the full generative process.
summary.tldr: MoVQ enriches discrete image codes with spatial variation to reduce repeated artifacts and improve reconstruction and generation quality.

title: MoVQ: Modulating Quantized Vectors for High-Fidelity Image Generation

abstract: Value decomposition multi-agent reinforcement learning methods learn the global value function as a mixing of each agent's individual utility functions. Coordination graphs (CGs) represent a higher-order decomposition by incorporating pairwise payoff functions and thus is supposed to have a more powerful representational capacity. However, CGs decompose the global value function linearly over local value functions, severely limiting the complexity of the value function class that can be represented. In this paper, we propose the first non-linear coordination graph by extending CG value decomposition beyond the linear case. One major challenge is to conduct greedy action selections in this new function class to which commonly adopted DCOP algorithms are no longer applicable. We study how to solve this problem when mixing networks with LeakyReLU activation are used. An enumeration method with a global optimality guarantee is proposed and motivates an efficient iterative optimization method with a local optimality guarantee. We find that our method can achieve superior performance on challenging multi-agent coordination tasks like MACO.
