paragraphs: Estimating depth from one image requires recovering both the overall scene layout and small geometric details. Models trained on large, diverse datasets often capture the layout reliably but miss detail. Diffusion-based approaches can recover finer structure, yet their less diverse three-dimensional training data can leave them struggling with geometrically complex scenes.

BetterDepth combines these strengths by refining the depth prediction of an existing model. That prediction supplies the global layout, while a conditional diffusion process repeatedly uses the input image to improve detail. Global pre-alignment and local patch masking during training help the refiner respect its supplied depth structure while learning to add finer features. The depth-estimation objective is affine-invariant.

Despite training on small synthetic datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across diverse public datasets and scenes encountered in the wild. They also show that the refiner can improve other depth models without additional retraining. This makes the result useful as a reusable refinement component, with the original estimator and the diffusion model contributing complementary geometric capabilities.
summary.tldr: BetterDepth refines existing depth predictions with diffusion to improve fine detail while preserving global geometry, without retraining for each supported estimator.

title: BetterDepth: Plug-and-Play Diffusion Refiner for Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation

abstract: Hybrid Reinforcement Learning (RL), where an agent learns from both an offline dataset and online explorations in an unknown environment, has garnered significant recent interest. A crucial question posed by Xie et al. (2022) is whether hybrid RL can improve upon the existing lower bounds established in purely offline and purely online RL without relying on the single-policy concentrability assumption. While Li et al. (2023) provided an affirmative answer to this question in the tabular PAC RL case, the question remains unsettled for both the regret-minimizing RL case and the non-tabular case. In this work, building upon recent advancements in offline RL and reward-agnostic exploration, we develop computationally efficient algorithms for both PAC and regret-minimizing RL with linear function approximation, without requiring concentrability on the entire state-action space. We demonstrate that these algorithms achieve sharper error or regret bounds that are no worse than, and can improve on, the optimal sample complexity in offline RL (the first algorithm, for PAC RL) and online RL (the second algorithm, for regret-minimizing RL) in linear Markov decision processes (MDPs), regardless of the quality of the behavior policy. To our knowledge, this work establishes the tightest theoretical guarantees currently available for hybrid RL in linear MDPs.

paragraphs: Hybrid reinforcement learning combines an existing dataset with new exploration in an unknown environment. This paper asks whether the combination can improve on sample requirements established for learning exclusively offline or online. It addresses linear Markov decision processes, extending the theoretical question beyond settings represented by tables.

The authors develop computationally efficient algorithms for two objectives. The first seeks a sufficiently accurate policy with a probability guarantee, known as PAC learning. The second minimizes regret accumulated during learning. The algorithms build on offline learning and reward-agnostic exploration without requiring concentrability across the entire state-action space.

For the PAC algorithm, the error guarantees are no worse than, and can improve upon, optimal offline sample complexity. For the regret-minimizing algorithm, the analogous comparison is with optimal online sample complexity. These comparisons hold regardless of the quality of the behavior policy that generated the offline data. The contribution establishes that combining data sources can provide theoretical advantages in linear MDPs, without claiming a strict improvement in every instance.
summary.tldr: The paper gives efficient hybrid-RL algorithms for linear MDPs whose guarantees can improve on offline or online sample complexity regardless of behavior-policy quality.

title: Hybrid Reinforcement Learning Breaks Sample Size Barriers In Linear MDPs

abstract: We analyze the error rates of the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm with leapfrog integrator for Bayesian neural network inference. We show that due to the non-differentiability of activation functions in the ReLU family, leapfrog HMC for networks with these activation functions has a large local error rate of $\Omega(\epsilon)$ rather than the classical error rate of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^3)$. This leads to a higher rejection rate of the proposals, making the method inefficient. We then verify our theoretical findings through empirical simulations as well as experiments on a real-world dataset that highlight the inefficiency of HMC inference on ReLU-based neural networks compared to analytical networks.
originalAbstract: We analyze the error rates of the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm with leapfrog integrator for Bayesian neural network inference. We show that due to the non-differentiability of activation functions in the ReLU family, leapfrog HMC for networks with these activation functions has a large local error rate of $\Omega(\epsilon)$ rather than the classical error rate of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^3)$. This leads to a higher rejection rate of the proposals, making the method inefficient. We then verify our theoretical findings through empirical simulations as well as experiments on a real-world dataset that highlight the inefficiency of HMC inference on ReLU-based neural networks compared to analytical networks.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo uses simulated movement to propose samples for Bayesian inference. This paper studies its leapfrog implementation for neural networks whose activation functions belong to the ReLU family. The key concern is the activation’s lack of differentiability, which changes the numerical behavior of the simulation used to construct sampling proposals.

The authors show that the local error has a lower bound of order epsilon for these networks, rather than the classical upper bound of order epsilon cubed. Here, epsilon is the integrator’s step size. This is a substantial deterioration in how numerical error behaves as steps become smaller. The resulting proposals are rejected more often, making the inference procedure inefficient.

Simulations and experiments on a real-world dataset support the theoretical analysis and compare ReLU-based networks with analytic networks. The findings connect an architectural choice directly to the behavior of an inference algorithm: activation nonsmoothness affects the integrator, which affects proposal acceptance. The result concerns leapfrog HMC with ReLU-family activations, the specific combination analyzed and tested in the paper.
summary.tldr: ReLU nondifferentiability worsens leapfrog HMC’s local error and increases proposal rejection in Bayesian neural-network inference.

title: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on ReLU Neural Networks is Inefficient

abstract: Train-time data poisoning attacks threaten machine learning models by introducing adversarial examples during training, leading to misclassification. Current defense methods often reduce generalization performance, are attack-specific, and impose significant training overhead. To address this, we introduce a set of universal data purification methods using a stochastic transform, $\Psi(x)$, realized via iterative Langevin dynamics of Energy-Based Models (EBMs), Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs), or both. These approaches purify poisoned data with minimal impact on classifier generalization. Our specially trained EBMs and DDPMs provide state-of-the-art defense against various attacks (including Narcissus, Bullseye Polytope, Gradient Matching) on CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and CINIC-10, without needing attack or classifier-specific information. We discuss performance trade-offs and show that our methods remain highly effective even with poisoned or distributionally shifted generative model training data.

paragraphs: Training-data poisoning introduces adversarial examples that can make a learned model misclassify inputs. Existing defenses can reduce generalization, depend on the particular attack, or add substantial training overhead. PureGen addresses this problem by purifying training data through generative-model dynamics, aiming to remove harmful alterations while retaining useful information for classification.

The authors propose stochastic transformations implemented with iterative Langevin dynamics of energy-based models, denoising diffusion probabilistic models, or combinations of the two. These specially trained generative models process poisoned data without requiring attack-specific or classifier-specific information. The approach therefore seeks a shared purification mechanism across different poisoning settings.

Experiments report state-of-the-art defenses against attacks including Narcissus, Bullseye Polytope, and Gradient Matching on CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and CINIC-10, with minimal impact on classifier generalization. The paper also examines performance trade-offs and finds the methods remain highly effective when the generative models' own training data are poisoned or distributionally shifted. These claims describe the evaluated settings rather than a guarantee against every attack.
summary.tldr: PureGen uses generative-model dynamics to purify poisoned training data without attack- or classifier-specific information.

title: PureGen: Universal Data Purification for Train-Time Poison Defense via Generative Model Dynamics

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) generate functionally correct solutions but often fall short in code efficiency, a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. In this paper, we introduce a novel test-time iterative optimization framework to address this, employing a closed-loop system where LLMs iteratively refine code based on empirical performance feedback from an execution sandbox. We explore three training strategies: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Group Relative Policy Optimization~(GRPO). Experiments on our Venus dataset and the APPS benchmark show that SFT and DPO rapidly saturate in efficiency gains. In contrast, GRPO, using reinforcement learning (RL) with execution feedback, continuously optimizes code performance, significantly boosting both pass@1 (from 47% to 62%) and the likelihood of outperforming human submissions in efficiency (from 31% to 45%). Our work demonstrates effective test-time code efficiency improvement and critically reveals the power of RL in teaching LLMs to truly self-improve code efficiency. We released our code and data at https://github.com/Elfsong/Afterburner.

paragraphs: Afterburner addresses a gap between writing code that works and writing code that runs efficiently. Its approach makes optimization an iterative process: a language model produces or revises code, an execution sandbox measures its performance, and the model uses that feedback to make another revision. Optimization therefore continues at test time.

The paper compares three ways to train models for this feedback loop: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and Group Relative Policy Optimization, a reinforcement learning method. The central question is whether training produces a model that can keep benefiting from measured execution feedback across successive attempts.

On the Venus dataset and APPS benchmark, the first two strategies quickly reach a plateau in efficiency improvements, while the reinforcement learning approach continues improving performance. Reported pass@1 rises from 47% to 62%, and the likelihood of exceeding human submissions in efficiency rises from 31% to 45%. These results support training models to use execution feedback as an ongoing optimization signal.
summary.tldr: Afterburner uses reinforcement learning and execution feedback to teach language models to iteratively improve code efficiency.

title: Afterburner: Reinforcement Learning Facilitates Self-Improving Code Efficiency Optimization

abstract: Learning editable high-resolution scene representations for dynamic scenes is an open problem with applications across the domains from autonomous driving to creative editing - the most successful approaches today make a trade-off between editability and supporting scene complexity: neural atlases represent dynamic scenes as two deforming image layers, foreground and background, which are editable in 2D, but break down when multiple objects occlude and interact. In contrast, scene graph models make use of annotated data such as masks and bounding boxes from autonomous-driving datasets to capture complex 3D spatial relationships, but their implicit volumetric node representations are challenging to edit view-consistently. We propose Neural Atlas Graphs (NAGs), a hybrid high-resolution scene representation, where every graph node is a view-dependent neural atlas, facilitating both 2D appearance editing and 3D ordering and positioning of scene elements. Fit at test-time, NAGs achieve state-of-the-art quantitative results on the Waymo Open Dataset - by 5 dB PSNR increase compared to existing methods - and make environmental editing possible in high resolution and visual quality - creating counterfactual driving scenarios with new backgrounds and edited vehicle appearance. We find that the method also generalizes beyond driving scenes and compares favorably - by more than 7 dB in PSNR - to recent matting and video editing baselines on the DAVIS video dataset with a diverse set of human and animal-centric scenes. Project Page: https://princeton-computational-imaging.github.io/nag/

paragraphs: Dynamic scenes are difficult to represent in a way that supports both complex interactions and straightforward editing. Two-layer neural atlases make appearance editable in two dimensions but struggle when several objects overlap and interact. Scene graphs capture richer spatial relationships, yet their volumetric representations can be difficult to edit consistently across views.

Neural Atlas Graphs combine these ideas by assigning a view-dependent neural atlas to every graph node. The resulting representation supports two-dimensional appearance changes alongside three-dimensional ordering and positioning of scene elements. It is fitted at test time and enables high-resolution edits such as replacing driving-scene backgrounds or changing vehicle appearance.

On the Waymo Open Dataset, the authors report state-of-the-art quantitative results, including a five-decibel PSNR improvement over existing methods. They also evaluate human- and animal-centered videos in DAVIS, reporting more than a seven-decibel advantage over recent matting and video-editing baselines. These findings show that the hybrid representation supports both editable driving scenes and a broader collection of dynamic video content.
summary.tldr: Neural Atlas Graphs combine editable image-based nodes with three-dimensional scene organization, improving reconstruction quality and enabling complex dynamic-scene edits.

title: Neural Atlas Graphs for Dynamic Scene Decomposition and Editing

abstract: We present SimpleStories, a large synthetic story dataset in simple language, consisting of 2 million samples each in English and Japanese. Through parameterizing prompts at multiple levels of abstraction, we achieve control over story characteristics at scale, inducing syntactic and semantic diversity. Ablations on a newly trained tiny model suite then show improved sample efficiency and model interpretability in comparison with the TinyStories dataset. We open-source all constituent parts of model creation, hoping to enable novel ways to study the end-to-end training process. As a byproduct, we move the frontier with regards to the fewest-parameter language model that outputs grammatical English.

Through parameterizing prompts at multiple levels of abstraction, we achieve control over story characteristics at scale, inducing syntactic and semantic diversity. Ablations on a newly trained tiny model suite then show improved sample efficiency and model interpretability in comparison with the TinyStories dataset. paragraphs: SimpleStories is a synthetic dataset of stories written in simple language, containing two million examples in English and another two million in Japanese. Its central idea is to control story generation through prompts parameterized at several levels of abstraction. This provides a way to shape story characteristics while producing varied sentence structures and meanings at scale.

The authors train a suite of tiny language models and use ablation experiments to study the resulting dataset. Compared with TinyStories, they report improved sample efficiency and model interpretability. These findings suggest that how synthetic stories are specified can affect both the amount of training data needed and how understandable the resulting small models are.

The work also releases all constituent parts of model creation to support investigation of the end-to-end training process. As an additional outcome, the authors report advancing the frontier for the fewest-parameter language model capable of producing grammatical English. The contribution therefore combines controlled multilingual training data with experiments on compact models and resources for studying their creation.
summary.tldr: SimpleStories uses controlled synthetic stories to improve tiny-model sample efficiency and interpretability compared with TinyStories.

title: Parameterized Synthetic Text Generation with SimpleStories

abstract: We study online convex optimization on $\ell_p$-balls in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $p > 2$. While always sub-linear, the optimal regret exhibits a shift between the high-dimensional setting ($d > T$), when the dimension $d$ is greater than the time horizon $T$ and the low-dimensional setting ($d \leq T$). We show that Follow-the-Regularised-Leader (FTRL) with time-varying regularisation which is adaptive to the dimension regime is anytime optimal for all dimension regimes. Motivated by this, we ask whether it is possible to obtain anytime optimality of FTRL with fixed non-adaptive regularisation. Our main result establishes that for separable regularisers, adaptivity in the regulariser is necessary, and that any fixed regulariser will be sub-optimal in one of the two dimension regimes. Finally, we provide lower bounds which rule out sub-linear regret bounds for the linear bandit problem in sufficiently high-dimension for all $\ell_p$-balls with $p \geq 1$.
originalAbstract: We study online convex optimization on $\ell_p$-balls in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $p > 2$. We show that Follow-the-Regularised-Leader (FTRL) with time-varying regularisation which is adaptive to the dimension regime is anytime optimal for all dimension regimes. Motivated by this, we ask whether it is possible to obtain anytime optimality of FTRL with fixed non-adaptive regularisation. Our main result establishes that for separable regularisers, adaptivity in the regulariser is necessary, and that any fixed regulariser will be sub-optimal in one of the two dimension regimes. Finally, we provide lower bounds which rule out sub-linear regret bounds for the linear bandit problem in sufficiently high-dimension for all $\ell_p$-balls with $p \geq 1$.

paragraphs: This paper studies online convex optimization when decisions lie in an lp-ball with p greater than two. Performance is measured by regret, the accumulated shortfall against a comparison decision. Although optimal regret remains sublinear, its behavior changes depending on whether the number of dimensions exceeds the number of interaction rounds.

The authors show that Follow-the-Regularised-Leader can remain optimal at any stopping time by using time-varying regularization that adapts to this dimensional regime. They then ask whether a fixed regularizer could achieve the same result. For separable regularizers, they prove it cannot: any fixed choice is suboptimal in at least one of the two regimes.

This establishes a specific necessity result for adaptive regularization within the studied class, rather than a claim about every possible regularizer. The paper also supplies lower bounds for linear bandits on lp-balls with p at least one. In sufficiently high dimensions, these bounds rule out sublinear regret, identifying a separate barrier in the bandit setting.
summary.tldr: For separable FTRL regularizers on lp-balls with p greater than two, adaptation is necessary for optimal performance across dimensional regimes.

title: On the necessity of adaptive regularisation: Optimal anytime online learning on $\boldsymbol{\ell_p}$-balls

abstract: Local SGD, or Federated Averaging, is one of the most widely used algorithms for distributed optimization. Although it often outperforms alternatives such as mini-batch SGD, existing theory has not fully explained this advantage under realistic assumptions about data heterogeneity. Recent work has suggested that a second-order heterogeneity assumption may suffice to justify the empirical gains of local SGD. We confirm this conjecture by establishing new upper and lower bounds on the convergence of local SGD. These bounds demonstrate how a low second-order heterogeneity, combined with third-order smoothness, enables local SGD to interpolate between heterogeneous and homogeneous regimes while maintaining communication efficiency. Our main technical contribution is a refined analysis of the consensus error, a central quantity in such results. We validate our theory with experiments on a distributed linear regression task.

paragraphs: Local SGD, also called Federated Averaging, allows distributed workers to perform local optimization before coordinating. Although it often works better than alternatives such as mini-batch SGD, explaining that advantage becomes difficult when workers hold different data. This paper investigates whether similarity in second-order properties can explain the gains despite such heterogeneity.

The authors establish new upper and lower convergence bounds. Their results show how low second-order heterogeneity, together with third-order smoothness, lets local SGD interpolate between heterogeneous and homogeneous regimes while retaining communication efficiency. These conditions concern how local optimization landscapes vary and how smoothly their curvature changes; both are part of the stated theoretical result.

The central technical step is a finer analysis of consensus error, which tracks disagreement among the distributed iterates. Experiments on distributed linear regression support the theory. The contribution clarifies when differences across workers can coexist with effective local training, providing a conditional explanation of empirical advantages rather than a claim that local SGD always outperforms its alternatives.
summary.tldr: Refined convergence bounds explain local SGD’s advantages under low second-order heterogeneity and third-order smoothness.

title: Revisiting Consensus Error: A Fine-grained Analysis of Local SGD under Second-order Data Heterogeneity

abstract: Alignment with human preferences is commonly framed using a universal reward function, even though human preferences are inherently heterogeneous. We formalize this heterogeneity by introducing user types and examine the limits of the homogeneity assumption. We show that aligning to heterogeneous preferences with a single policy is best achieved using the average reward across user types. However, this requires additional information about annotators. We examine improvements under different information settings, focusing on direct alignment methods. We find that minimal information can yield first-order improvements, while full feedback from each user type leads to consistent learning of the optimal policy. Surprisingly, however, no sample-efficient consistent direct loss exists in this latter setting. These results reveal a fundamental tension between consistency and sample efficiency in direct policy alignment.

paragraphs: Preference alignment often represents human judgments through a single universal reward function. This paper examines what changes when people have systematically different preferences. The authors formalize those differences using user types and study how direct alignment methods behave when the available feedback contains varying amounts of information about those types.

For the problem of learning one policy, their analysis identifies the average reward across user types as the appropriate objective. Learning this objective, however, requires additional information about annotators. Treating all feedback as though it came from one homogeneous preference source can therefore obscure information that matters for finding the best shared policy.

The results distinguish improvements from stronger guarantees. Minimal information about preference heterogeneity can yield first-order improvements, while full feedback from every user type permits consistent learning of the optimal policy. Yet, even in that richer setting, the authors show that no sample-efficient consistent direct loss exists. This exposes a theoretical tension: enough information can make consistent learning possible without making it achievable through a sample-efficient direct loss.
summary.tldr: Accounting for differing user preferences improves direct alignment, but the paper establishes a tension between consistent learning and sample efficiency.

title: Direct Alignment with Heterogeneous Preferences

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge but are vulnerable to corpus poisoning and contamination attacks, which can compromise output integrity. Existing defenses often apply aggressive filtering, leading to unnecessary loss of valuable information and reduced reliability in generation. To address this problem, we propose a two-stage semantic filtering and conflict-free framework for trustworthy RAG. In the first stage, we perform a joint filter with semantic and cluster-based filtering which is guided by the Entity-intent-relation extractor (EIRE). EIRE extracts entities, latent objectives, and entity relations from both the user query and filtered documents, scores their semantic relevance, and selectively adds valuable documents into the clean retrieval database. In the second stage, we proposed an EIRE-guided conflict-aware filtering module, which analyzes semantic consistency between the query, candidate answers, and retrieved knowledge before final answer generation, filtering out internal and external contradictions that could mislead the model. Through this two-stage process, SeCon-RAG effectively preserves useful knowledge while mitigating conflict contamination, achieving significant improvements in both generation robustness and output trustworthiness. Extensive experiments across various LLMs and datasets demonstrate that the proposed SeCon-RAG markedly outperforms state-of-the-art defense methods.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies language models with external information, but poisoned or contaminated documents can distort their answers. Filtering aggressively can create another problem by discarding useful knowledge. SeCon-RAG addresses this trade-off through two stages that examine semantic relevance and contradictions, aiming to preserve helpful material while reducing contamination’s influence on generation.

This component identifies entities, underlying objectives, and relationships in the query and documents, then scores relevance to selectively admit valuable documents into the clean retrieval database. The process uses the meaning and relationships within information to guide what is retained.

The second stage checks consistency among the query, candidate answers, and retrieved knowledge before final generation. It removes internal and external contradictions that could mislead the model. Across multiple language models and datasets, the authors report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art defenses in robustness and trustworthiness. The findings support combining selective knowledge retention with a later consistency check.
summary.tldr: SeCon-RAG combines selective semantic filtering with contradiction checks to improve robustness while retaining useful retrieved knowledge.

title: SeCon-RAG: A Two-Stage Semantic Filtering and Conflict-Free Framework for Trustworthy RAG

abstract: Mathematicians have long employed decomposition techniques to prove inequalities, yet automating this process remains a significant challenge in computational mathematics. We introduce IneqSearch, a hybrid reasoning system that integrates symbolic computation with large language models (LLMs) to address this challenge. IneqSearch reformulates inequality proving as a structured search problem: identifying appropriate combinations of theorems that decompose expressions into non-negative components. The system combines a symbolic solver for deductive reasoning with an LLM-based agent for constructive proof exploration, effectively implementing methodologies observed in formal mathematical practice. A key contribution of IneqSearch is its iterative learning mechanism that systematically incorporates newly proven results into its theorem database, enabling knowledge acquisition during practice that enhances its capabilities without requiring human intervention. In empirical evaluation on 437 Olympiad-level inequalities, IneqSearch successfully proves 342 problems, significantly outperforming existing methods and demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating symbolic and neural approaches for mathematical reasoning.

IneqSearch turns that task into a structured search problem supported by both symbolic computation and a language model.

Their shared objective is to discover theorem combinations that produce the required non-negative decomposition. This ties the language model’s exploration to explicit mathematical transformations that contribute to a proof.

IneqSearch also adds newly proven results to its theorem database through an iterative learning mechanism. This lets later proof searches draw on knowledge accumulated during earlier practice without human intervention. In an evaluation of 437 Olympiad-level inequalities, the system proves 342 and significantly outperforms existing methods. The findings support combining guided exploration, symbolic deduction, and a growing collection of reusable results.
summary.tldr: IneqSearch combines symbolic deduction, LLM-guided exploration, and accumulated theorems to prove 342 of 437 evaluated Olympiad inequalities.

title: IneqSearch: Hybrid Reasoning for Olympiad Inequality Proofs

abstract: Multi-bit quantization networks enable flexible deployment of deep neural networks by supporting multiple precision levels within a single model. However, existing approaches suffer from significant training overhead as full-dataset updates are repeated for each supported bit-width, resulting in a cost that scales linearly with the number of precisions. Additionally, extra fine-tuning stages are often required to support additional or intermediate precision options, further compounding the overall training burden. To address this issue, we propose two techniques that greatly reduce the training overhead without compromising model utility: (i) Weight bias correction enables shared batch normalization and eliminates the need for fine-tuning by neutralizing quantization-induced bias across bit-widths and aligning activation distributions; and (ii) Bit-wise coreset sampling strategy allows each child model to train on a compact, informative subset selected via gradient-based importance scores by exploiting the implicit knowledge transfer phenomenon. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-1K with both ResNet and ViT architectures demonstrate that our method achieves competitive or superior accuracy while reducing training time up to 7.88×.

paragraphs: A multi-bit quantization network supports several numerical precision levels within one model, providing flexibility at deployment. Training can be expensive because existing approaches repeatedly update each precision variant on the full dataset. Supporting additional or intermediate precisions can also require further fine-tuning. This paper addresses both sources of training overhead.

Its first technique corrects weight bias introduced by quantization. By aligning activation distributions across bit-widths, the method enables shared batch normalization and removes the need for the extra fine-tuning stage described in the abstract. The second technique assigns each precision variant a compact, informative training subset. These subsets are selected using gradient-based importance scores, taking advantage of implicit knowledge transfer among the variants.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-1K with ResNet and Vision Transformer architectures. The method achieves competitive or better accuracy while delivering training speedups of up to 7.88 times. The findings indicate that repeated full-dataset training can be substantially reduced in the evaluated settings by combining precision alignment with selective use of training examples.
summary.tldr: Weight bias correction and precision-specific data subsets reduce multi-bit network training costs, with reported speedups of up to 7.88 times.

title: Efficient Multi-bit Quantization Network Training via Weight Bias Correction and Bit-wise Coreset Sampling

abstract: In this paper, we establish global non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for the BFGS quasi-Newton method without requiring strong convexity or the Lipschitz continuity of the gradient or Hessian. Instead, we consider the setting where the objective function is strictly convex and strongly self-concordant. For an arbitrary initial point and any arbitrary positive-definite initial Hessian approximation, we prove global linear and superlinear convergence guarantees for BFGS when the step size is determined using a line search scheme satisfying the weak Wolfe conditions. Moreover, all our global guarantees are affine-invariant, with the convergence rates depending solely on the initial error and the strongly self-concordant constant. Our results extend the global non-asymptotic convergence theory of BFGS beyond traditional assumptions and, for the first time, establish affine-invariant convergence guarantees—aligning with the inherent affine invariance of the BFGS method.

paragraphs: BFGS is an optimization method that maintains an approximation to an objective's curvature. This paper establishes convergence guarantees under a different set of assumptions from those commonly used in its analysis. The objective must be strictly convex and strongly self-concordant, but the analysis does not require strong convexity or Lipschitz continuity of either the gradient or Hessian.

Under these conditions, the authors prove global linear and superlinear convergence guarantees. The results allow an arbitrary starting point and any positive-definite initial Hessian approximation, provided step sizes come from a line search satisfying the weak Wolfe conditions. The guarantees are non-asymptotic, meaning they describe convergence quantitatively rather than only characterizing behavior in an eventual limit.

A central feature is affine invariance: changing coordinates through an invertible affine transformation does not alter the guarantees. The stated rates depend only on the initial error and the strong self-concordance constant. This aligns the analysis with BFGS's own coordinate invariance and extends its global convergence theory beyond traditional assumptions, while retaining the paper's specific conditions on the objective and line search.
summary.tldr: The paper proves affine-invariant global convergence guarantees for BFGS on strictly convex, strongly self-concordant objectives with weak-Wolfe line searches.

title: Affine-Invariant Global Non-Asymptotic Convergence Analysis of BFGS under Self-Concordance

abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training samples (i.e., forget data) from a trained model while preserving its performance on the remaining samples (i.e., retain data). Existing approximate unlearning approaches, such as fine-tuning or negative gradient, often suffer from either insufficient forgetting or significant degradation on retain data. In this paper, we introduce Unlearning-Aware Minimization (UAM), a novel min–max optimization framework for machine unlearning. UAM perturbs model parameters to maximize the forget loss and then leverages the corresponding gradients to minimize the retain loss. We derive an efficient optimization method for this min-max problem, which enables effective removal of forget data and uncovers better optima that conventional methods fail to reach. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UAM outperforms existing methods across diverse benchmarks, including image classification datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet) and multiple-choice question-answering benchmarks for large language models (WMDP-Bio, WMDP-Cyber).

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples while preserving a model’s performance on the examples that remain. Approximate methods can fail in either direction: they may leave too much of the unwanted influence or damage useful performance. Unlearning-Aware Minimization treats these competing requirements as a coupled optimization problem.

The method uses a min–max framework. It first perturbs model parameters to increase loss on the data designated for forgetting, then uses the associated gradients to reduce loss on retained data. The authors derive an efficient way to optimize this objective. The design makes the retain-data update explicitly account for parameter changes that target forgetting.

Experiments cover image classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet, along with language-model multiple-choice question answering on WMDP-Bio and WMDP-Cyber. The authors report better performance than existing methods and access to favorable optima that conventional approaches miss. These findings support jointly optimizing forgetting and retention as a way to improve approximate unlearning across the evaluated vision and language tasks.
summary.tldr: Unlearning-Aware Minimization couples forgetting-oriented parameter perturbations with retained-data optimization to improve approximate machine unlearning.

title: Unlearning-Aware Minimization

abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS) plays a critical role in molecular identification, significantly advancing scientific discovery. However, structure elucidation from MS data remains challenging due to the scarcity of annotated spectra. While large-scale pretraining has proven effective in addressing data scarcity in other domains, applying this paradigm to mass spectrometry is hindered by the complexity and heterogeneity of raw spectral signals. To address this, we propose MS-BART, a unified modeling framework that maps mass spectra and molecular structures into a shared token vocabulary, enabling cross-modal learning through large-scale pretraining on reliably computed fingerprint–molecule datasets. Multi-task pretraining objectives further enhance MS-BART's generalization by jointly optimizing denoising and translation task. The pretrained model is subsequently transferred to experimental spectra through finetuning on fingerprint predictions generated with MIST, a pre-trained spectral inference model, thereby enhancing robustness to real-world spectral variability. While finetuning alleviates the distributional difference, MS-BART still suffers molecular hallucination and requires further alignment. We therefore introduce a chemical feedback mechanism that guides the model toward generating molecules closer to the reference structure. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MS-BART achieves SOTA performance across 5/12 key metrics on MassSpecGym and NPLIB1 and is faster by one order of magnitude than competing diffusion-based methods, while comprehensive ablation studies systematically validate the model's effectiveness and robustness. We provide the data and code at [https://github.com/OpenDFM/MS-BART](https://github.com/OpenDFM/MS-BART).

abstract: Video Question Answering (VideoQA) task serves as a critical playground for evaluating whether foundation models can effectively perceive, understand, and reason about dynamic real-world scenarios. However, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with simultaneously ensuring the ability to model spatial relationships between video frames and to understand the causal dynamics of temporal evolution on complex and reasoning-intensive VideoQA. In this work, we equip MLLM with a comprehensive and extensible Video Toolkit, to enhance MLLM’s spatiotemporal reasoning capabilities as well as guarantee the harmony between the quantity and diversity of tools. To better control the tool invocation sequence and avoid toolchain shortcut issues, we propose a Spatiotemporal Reasoning Framework (STAR) that strategically schedules temporal and spatial tools, thereby progressively localizing the key area in the video. Our STAR framework enhances GPT-4o using lightweight tools, achieving an 8.2% gain on VideoMME and 4.6% on LongVideoBench. We believe that our proposed Video Toolkit and STAR framework make an important step towards building autonomous and intelligent video analysis assistants. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/fansunqi/VideoTool.

paragraphs: Answering difficult questions about video requires reasoning about both spatial relationships and events unfolding over time. Multimodal language models can struggle to handle these together, especially for questions involving complex temporal dynamics. This paper adds an extensible Video Toolkit to support those capabilities through specialized tools.

The accompanying Spatiotemporal Reasoning Framework, called STAR, controls when spatial and temporal tools are invoked. It schedules them strategically so that reasoning progressively localizes the relevant part of the video. summary.tldr: STAR strategically schedules spatial and temporal video tools, improving GPT-4o's performance on two video question-answering benchmarks.

title: Tool-Augmented Spatiotemporal Reasoning for Streamlining Video Question Answering Task

abstract: Federated Class Incremental Learning (FCIL) aims to collaboratively process continuously increasing incoming tasks across multiple clients. Among various approaches, data replay has become a promising solution, which can alleviate forgetting by reintroducing representative samples from previous tasks. However, their performance is typically limited by class imbalance, both within the replay buffer due to limited global awareness and between replayed and newly arrived classes. To address this issue, we propose a class-wise balancing data replay method for FCIL (FedCBDR), which employs a global coordination mechanism for class-level memory construction and reweights the learning objective to alleviate the aforementioned imbalances. Specifically, FedCBDR has two key components: 1) the global-perspective data replay module reconstructs global representations of prior task knowledge in a privacy-preserving manner, which then guides a class-aware and importance-sensitive sampling strategy to achieve balanced replay; 2) Subsequently, to handle class imbalance across tasks, the task-aware temperature scaling module adaptively adjusts the temperature of logits at both class and instance levels based on task dynamics, which reduces the model’s overconfidence in majority classes while enhancing its sensitivity to minority classes. Experimental results verified that FedCBDR achieves balanced class-wise sampling under heterogeneous data distributions and improves generalization under task imbalance between earlier and recent tasks, yielding a 2%-15% Top-1 accuracy improvement over six state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: FedCBDR tackles forgetting when multiple clients collaboratively learn a growing collection of classes. Replaying examples from earlier tasks can preserve old knowledge, but replay introduces two balancing problems. The stored examples may unevenly represent classes, and the older classes represented through replay may be overwhelmed by newly arriving classes during subsequent learning.

The method first coordinates memory construction using a global perspective. It reconstructs representations of earlier knowledge while preserving privacy, then uses those representations to guide sampling that considers both class membership and example importance. This addresses the limited view available to individual clients, helping replay reflect the broader distribution of knowledge across the collaborative system.

A second component adjusts the temperature of prediction logits at both class and instance levels according to task dynamics. This reduces overconfidence in majority classes and increases sensitivity to minority classes. Experiments report balanced sampling under heterogeneous client data and improved generalization when earlier and recent tasks are imbalanced. Across comparisons with six state-of-the-art methods, the reported Top-1 accuracy improvements range from 2% to 15%.
summary.tldr: FedCBDR balances replayed classes and adjusts prediction temperatures to reduce forgetting and class imbalance in federated incremental learning.

title: Class-wise Balancing Data Replay for Federated Class-Incremental Learning

abstract: Numerous models have been developed for scanpath and saliency prediction, which are typically trained on scanpaths, which model eye movement as a sequence of discrete fixation points connected by saccades, while the rich information contained in the raw trajectories is often discarded. Moreover, most existing approaches fail to capture the variability observed among human subjects viewing the same image. They generally predict a single scanpath of fixed, pre-defined length, which conflicts with the inherent diversity and stochastic nature of real-world visual attention. To address these challenges, we propose DiffEye, a diffusion-based training framework designed to model continuous and diverse eye movement trajectories during free viewing of natural images. Our method builds on a diffusion model conditioned on visual stimuli and introduces a novel component, namely Corresponding Positional Embedding (CPE), which aligns spatial gaze information with the patch-based semantic features of the visual input. By leveraging raw eye-tracking trajectories rather than relying on scanpaths, DiffEye captures the inherent variability in human gaze behavior and generates high-quality, realistic eye movement patterns, despite being trained on a comparatively small dataset. The generated trajectories can also be converted into scanpaths and saliency maps, resulting in outputs that more accurately reflect the distribution of human visual attention. DiffEye is the first method to tackle this task on natural images using a diffusion model while fully leveraging the richness of raw eye-tracking data. Our extensive evaluation shows that DiffEye not only achieves state-of-the-art performance in scanpath generation but also enables, for the first time, the generation of continuous eye movement trajectories. Project webpage: https://diff-eye.github.io/

abstract: Recent studies have uncovered an interesting phenomenon: unimodal foundation models tend to learn convergent representations, regardless of differences in architecture, training objectives, or data modalities. However, these representations are essentially internal abstractions of samples that characterize samples independently, leading to limited expressiveness. In this paper, we propose The Indra Representation Hypothesis, inspired by the philosophical metaphor of Indra’s Net. We argue that representations from unimodal foundation models are converging to implicitly reflect a shared relational structure underlying reality, akin to the relational ontology of Indra’s Net. We formalize this hypothesis using the V-enriched Yoneda embedding from category theory, defining the Indra representation as a relational profile of each sample with respect to others. This formulation is shown to be unique, complete, and structure-preserving under a given cost function. We instantiate the Indra representation using angular distance and evaluate it in cross-model and cross-modal scenarios involving vision, language, and audio. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Indra representations consistently enhance robustness and alignment across architectures and modalities, providing a theoretically grounded and practical framework for training-free alignment of unimodal foundation models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jianglin954/Indra.

paragraphs: Different foundation models can learn similar representations despite differences in architecture, objectives, and modality. This paper proposes that the convergence reflects a shared relational structure: samples acquire meaning partly through their relationships to other samples. The Indra Representation Hypothesis develops this view beyond treating each sample's internal representation as an independent abstraction.

The authors formalize a sample's representation as its relational profile with respect to other samples, using the V-enriched Yoneda embedding from category theory. Under a given cost function, they show that this formulation is unique, complete, and structure-preserving. Those mathematical properties apply to the specified formulation; the broader claim about what foundation models converge toward is presented as a hypothesis.

For practical evaluation, the authors instantiate the relational representation with angular distance. Experiments involving vision, language, and audio report consistent improvements in robustness and alignment across architectures and modalities. The resulting approach aligns unimodal foundation models without training. Its contribution connects a relational explanation of representational convergence to a concrete transformation that improves cross-model and cross-modal alignment in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Indra represents samples through their relationships to others, providing a theoretically grounded, training-free approach that improves multimodal alignment in experiments.

title: The Indra Representation Hypothesis for Multimodal Alignment

abstract: Today’s deep learning architectures are primarily based on perceptron models, which do not capture the oscillatory dynamics characteristic of biological neurons. Although oscillatory systems have recently gained attention for their closer resemblance to neural behavior, they still fall short of modeling the intricate spatio-temporal interactions observed in natural neural circuits. In this paper, we propose a bio-inspired oscillatory state system (BioOSS) designed to emulate the wave-like propagation dynamics critical to neural processing, particularly in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), where complex activity patterns emerge. BioOSS comprises two interacting populations of neurons: p neurons, which represent simplified membrane-potential-like units inspired by pyramidal cells in cortical columns, and o neurons, which govern propagation velocities and modulate the lateral spread of activity. Through local interactions, these neurons produce wave-like propagation patterns. The model incorporates trainable parameters for damping and propagation speed, enabling flexible adaptation to task-specific spatio-temporal structures. We evaluate BioOSS on both synthetic and real-world tasks, demonstrating superior performance and enhanced interpretability compared to alternative architectures.

Local interactions between these populations generate wave-like activity patterns, while trainable damping and propagation-speed parameters let the dynamics adapt to a task.

The authors evaluate BioOSS on synthetic and real-world tasks and report better performance and interpretability than alternative architectures. The proposed value lies in making spatial propagation and temporal evolution explicit parts of computation. Its biological framing supplies the design inspiration; the stated empirical finding is that this architecture improves the tested learning tasks and makes its behavior more interpretable.
summary.tldr: BioOSS uses interacting neuron populations with trainable wave dynamics, reporting improved task performance and interpretability.

title: BioOSS: A Bio-Inspired Oscillatory State System with Spatio-Temporal Dynamics

abstract: Adversarial examples reveal critical vulnerabilities in deep neural networks by exploiting their sensitivity to imperceptible input perturbations. While adversarial training remains the predominant defense strategy, it often incurs significant computational cost and may compromise clean-data accuracy. In this work, we investigate an architectural approach to adversarial robustness by embedding group-equivariant convolutions—specifically, rotation- and scale-equivariant layers—into standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs). These layers encode symmetry priors that align model behavior with structured transformations in the input space, promoting smoother decision boundaries and greater resilience to adversarial attacks. We propose and evaluate two symmetry-aware architectures: a parallel design that processes standard and equivariant features independently before fusion, and a cascaded design that applies equivariant operations sequentially. Theoretically, we demonstrate that such models reduce hypothesis space complexity, regularize gradients, and yield tighter certified robustness bounds under the CLEVER (Cross Lipschitz Extreme Value for nEtwork Robustness) framework. Empirically, our models consistently improve adversarial robustness and generalization across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR-10C under both FGSM and PGD attacks, without requiring adversarial training. These findings underscore the potential of symmetry-enforcing architectures as efficient and principled alternatives to data augmentation-based defenses.

paragraphs: Small input changes can cause neural networks to make incorrect predictions even when those changes are hard to perceive. This paper investigates whether building transformation symmetries into a convolutional network can improve its resistance to such attacks. The approach uses layers whose behavior follows rotations and changes in scale in a structured way.

The authors compare two architectures. One processes ordinary features and symmetry-aware features in parallel before combining them; the other applies equivariant operations in sequence. Their theoretical analysis connects these architectural constraints to reduced model complexity, more controlled gradients, and tighter certified robustness bounds within the CLEVER framework. These connections explain how symmetry can influence sensitivity to input changes.

On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR-10C, the models improve robustness and generalization under FGSM and PGD attacks without adversarial training. The findings support symmetry-aware architecture as a promising way to improve robustness while avoiding the training procedure used by the predominant defense approach. The empirical claim concerns the evaluated datasets and attacks.
summary.tldr: Rotation- and scale-equivariant layers improve adversarial robustness in the reported evaluations without requiring adversarial training.

title: Bridging Symmetry and Robustness: On the Role of Equivariance in Enhancing Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have demonstrated strong performance in generative modeling, particularly in image synthesis, making them a compelling choice for molecular conformer generation. However, applying DiTs to molecules introduces novel challenges, such as integrating discrete molecular graph information with continuous 3D geometry, handling Euclidean symmetries, and designing conditioning mechanisms that generalize across molecules of varying sizes and structures. We propose DiTMC, a framework that adapts DiTs to address these challenges through a modular architecture that separates the processing of 3D coordinates from conditioning on atomic connectivity. To this end, we introduce two complementary graph-based conditioning strategies that integrate seamlessly with the DiT architecture. These are combined with different attention mechanisms, including both standard non-equivariant and SO(3)-equivariant formulations, enabling flexible control over the trade-off between between accuracy and computational efficiency. Experiments on standard conformer generation benchmarks (GEOM-QM9, -DRUGS, -XL) demonstrate that DiTMC achieves state-of-the-art precision and physical validity. Our results highlight how architectural choices and symmetry priors affect sample quality and efficiency, suggesting promising directions for large-scale generative modeling of molecular structures. Code is available at [https://github.com/ML4MolSim/dit_mc](https://github.com/ML4MolSim/dit_mc).

paragraphs: Generating molecular conformers requires producing three-dimensional coordinates consistent with atomic connectivity. Adapting diffusion transformers to this task introduces challenges involving discrete molecular graphs, continuous geometry, spatial symmetries, and variation in molecular size and structure. DiTMC addresses these challenges through a modular architecture that separates coordinate processing from conditioning on the molecular graph.

The framework introduces two complementary graph-based conditioning strategies. It combines them with attention mechanisms that include standard non-equivariant and SO(3)-equivariant versions, the latter explicitly respecting rotational symmetry. These alternatives make architectural and symmetry choices available for controlling the trade-off between generation accuracy and computational efficiency.

On GEOM-QM9, GEOM-DRUGS, and GEOM-XL, DiTMC achieves state-of-the-art precision and physical validity in the reported experiments. The study also examines how architectural decisions and symmetry priors affect sample quality and efficiency. Its contribution therefore includes both a strong conformer generator and evidence about how to adapt diffusion transformers to molecular geometry across varying structures and sizes.
summary.tldr: DiTMC combines graph conditioning and geometric attention choices to generate molecular conformers with strong precision and physical validity.

title: Sampling 3D Molecular Conformers with Diffusion Transformers

abstract: We introduce a data capture system and a new dataset, HO-Cap, for 3D reconstruction and pose tracking of hands and objects in videos. The system leverages multiple RGB-D cameras and a HoloLens headset for data collection, avoiding the use of expensive 3D scanners or motion capture systems. We propose a semiautomatic method for annotating the shape and pose of hands and objects in the collected videos, significantly reducing the annotation time and cost compared to manual labeling. With this system, we captured a video dataset of humans performing various single- and dual-hand manipulation tasks, including simple pick-and-place actions, handovers between hands, and using objects according to their affordance. This dataset can serve as human demonstrations for research in embodied AI and robot manipulation. Our capture setup and annotation framework will be made available to the community for reconstructing 3D shapes of objects and human hands, as well as tracking their poses in videos.

paragraphs: HO-Cap provides a capture system and video dataset for reconstructing the shapes of hands and objects and tracking their poses during interaction. The setup combines multiple cameras that record color and depth with a HoloLens headset. It avoids relying on expensive 3D scanners or motion-capture systems for data collection.

The authors also introduce a semiautomatic annotation method for the recorded shapes and poses. They report that this reduces labeling time and cost substantially compared with manual annotation. The capture and annotation components work together to make detailed hand-object interaction data less burdensome to produce.

The dataset contains people manipulating objects with one or two hands, including picking and placing, transferring objects between hands, and using objects according to their functions. These recordings can serve as human demonstrations for embodied AI and robot-manipulation research. The authors state that the capture setup and annotation framework will be made available, extending the contribution beyond the collected videos to a reusable process for creating and tracking 3D interaction data.
summary.tldr: HO-Cap combines accessible capture hardware and semiautomatic annotation to collect 3D hand-object interaction demonstrations.

title: HO-Cap: A Capture System and Dataset for 3D Reconstruction and Pose Tracking of Hand-Object Interaction

abstract: Many kernels for discretely structured data in the literature are designed within the framework of the convolution kernel and its generalization, the mapping kernel. The two most important advantages to use this framework is an easy-to-check criteria of positive definiteness and efficient computation based on the dynamic programming methodology of the resulting kernels. On the other hand, the recent theory of partitionable kernels reveals that the known kernels only take advantage of a very small portion of the potential of the framework. In fact, we have good opportunities to find novel and important kernels in the unexplored area. In this paper, we shed light on a novel important class of kernels within the framework: We give a mathematical characterization of the class, show a parametric method to optimize kernels of the class to specific problems, based on this characterization, and present some experimental results, which show the new kernels are promising in both accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Kernels provide a way to compare structured objects for learning. Many kernels for discrete structures come from convolution kernels or their broader mapping-kernel framework. That framework is attractive because it provides criteria for checking positive definiteness and supports efficient computation through dynamic programming. These properties make mathematically valid comparisons easier to construct and use.

The paper argues that familiar kernels occupy only a small part of what this framework permits. Building on the theory of partitionable kernels, it identifies a previously unexplored class and gives a mathematical characterization of it. This turns an open design opportunity into a defined family of possible kernels.

The authors then use that characterization to develop a parameterized way of adapting kernels in the class to particular problems. Their experiments suggest that the resulting kernels are promising in both accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution therefore combines a broader mathematical design space with a practical way to search within it, rather than presenting only one fixed similarity function.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes a new class of structured-data kernels and develops a parameterized method for adapting them to specific problems.

title: A New Frontier of Kernel Design for Structured Data

abstract: First steps towards a mathematical theory of deep convolutional neural networks for feature extraction were made—for the continuous-time case—in Mallat, 2012, and Wiatowski and Bölcskei, 2015. This paper considers the discrete case, introduces new convolutional neural network architectures, and proposes a mathematical framework for their analysis. Specifically, we establish deformation and translation sensitivity results of local and global nature, and we investigate how certain structural properties of the input signal are reflected in the corresponding feature vectors. Our theory applies to general filters and general Lipschitz-continuous non-linearities and pooling operators. Experiments on handwritten digit classification and facial landmark detection—including feature importance evaluation—complement the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical framework for deep convolutional feature extraction in the discrete setting. Earlier theoretical work discussed in the abstract concerned continuous-time signals. Moving to discrete inputs brings the analysis to a different setting and accompanies the introduction of new convolutional network architectures.

The analysis examines how extracted features respond when an input is translated or deformed, with results covering both local and global behavior. It also studies how structural properties of an input appear in its feature vector. These questions connect a network's internal representation to meaningful changes and patterns in the signal it receives.

The framework accommodates general filters and nonlinearities and pooling operators that satisfy Lipschitz continuity. That condition specifies the class of operations covered by the theory. Experiments on handwritten digit classification and facial landmark detection, including feature importance evaluation, complement the mathematical results. The contribution thus joins architectural proposals with an account of feature sensitivity and structure, supported by evaluations on two recognition-related tasks.
summary.tldr: New discrete convolutional architectures come with theory describing feature sensitivity to transformations and how input structure appears in learned representations.

title: Discrete Deep Feature Extraction: A Theory and New Architectures

abstract: Mixed-initiative classifier training, where the human teacher can choose which items to label or to label items chosen by the computer, has enjoyed empirical success but without a rigorous statistical learning theoretical justification. We analyze the label complexity of a simple mixed-initiative training mechanism using teach- ing dimension and active learning. We show that mixed-initiative training is advantageous com- pared to either computer-initiated (represented by active learning) or human-initiated classifier training. The advantage exists across all human teaching abilities, from optimal to completely unhelpful teachers. We further improve classifier training by educating the human teachers. This is done by showing, or explaining, optimal teaching sets to the human teachers. We conduct Mechanical Turk human experiments on two stylistic classifier training tasks to illustrate our approach.

paragraphs: Mixed-initiative classifier training lets a human choose examples to label or answer labeling requests chosen by the computer. The paper seeks a statistical learning explanation for the empirical success of combining those two sources of initiative. Its focus is label complexity: the labeling effort required by the training mechanism.

The analysis combines teaching dimension and active learning to study a simple mixed-initiative mechanism. It establishes an advantage over either computer-led active learning or human-led training alone. Within the analyzed setting, that advantage spans teaching abilities from optimal to completely unhelpful, making teacher quality an explicit part of the theoretical result.

The authors also improve training by educating human teachers, showing or explaining optimal teaching sets to them. Mechanical Turk experiments on two stylistic classification tasks illustrate this approach. The work therefore addresses both how to combine human and computer choices and how to help people choose more informative examples. Its theoretical result concerns the analyzed mechanism, while the human experiments illustrate the proposed teacher-education strategy.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes label-complexity advantages for a mixed human–computer training mechanism and explores teaching people to provide better examples.

title: The Label Complexity of Mixed-Initiative Classifier Training

abstract: Deep nets generalize well despite having more parameters than the number of training samples. Recent works try to give an explanation using PAC-Bayes and Margin-based analyses, but do not as yet result in sample complexity bounds better than naive parameter counting. The current paper shows generalization bounds that are orders of magnitude better in practice. These rely upon new succinct reparametrizations of the trained net — a compression that is explicit and efficient. These yield generalization bounds via a simple compression-based framework introduced here. Our results also provide some theoretical justification for widespread empirical success in compressing deep nets. Analysis of correctness of our compression relies upon some newly identified noise stability properties of trained deep nets, which are also experimentally verified. The study of these properties and resulting generalization bounds are also extended to convolutional nets, which had eluded earlier attempts on proving generalization.

paragraphs: Deep networks can generalize well even when their parameter counts exceed the number of training examples. This paper seeks stronger mathematical explanations of that behavior. It observes that earlier PAC-Bayes and margin-based analyses had not yet produced sample-complexity bounds better than simply counting parameters, and develops a compression-based framework instead.

The approach explicitly and efficiently compresses a trained network into a more succinct parameterization. That compact representation supports generalization bounds reported to be orders of magnitude better in practice. The mathematical explanation therefore depends on the trained network's capacity for compression, giving a role to properties that raw parameter counting does not capture.

To establish that the compression works, the authors identify noise-stability properties of trained networks and verify them experimentally. They also extend the study of these properties and the resulting bounds to convolutional networks. Alongside the improved guarantees, the analysis offers theoretical support for the empirical success of network compression by connecting stable trained behavior to a smaller effective description.
summary.tldr: Efficient compression and noise-stability properties yield substantially stronger practical generalization bounds for trained deep networks.

title: Stronger Generalization Bounds for Deep Nets via a Compression Approach

abstract: We argue that the estimation of mutual information between high dimensional continuous random variables can be achieved by gradient descent over neural networks. We present a Mutual Information Neural Estimator (MINE) that is linearly scalable in dimensionality as well as in sample size, trainable through back-prop, and strongly consistent. We present a handful of applications on which MINE can be used to minimize or maximize mutual information. We apply MINE to improve adversarially trained generative models. We also use MINE to implement the Information Bottleneck, applying it to supervised classification; our results demonstrate substantial improvement in flexibility and performance in these settings.

We present a Mutual Information Neural Estimator (MINE) that is linearly scalable in dimensionality as well as in sample size, trainable through back-prop, and strongly consistent. We present a handful of applications on which MINE can be used to minimize or maximize mutual information. We apply MINE to improve adversarially trained generative models. We also use MINE to implement the Information Bottleneck, applying it to supervised classification; our results demonstrate substantial improvement in flexibility and performance in these settings.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures how much information two random variables share. The paper addresses estimating it when the variables are continuous and high-dimensional. It presents the Mutual Information Neural Estimator, or MINE, which turns this estimation problem into one that can be trained through gradient descent over a neural network.

MINE is trainable with backpropagation and scales linearly with both dimensionality and sample size. The authors also establish strong consistency, giving the estimator an asymptotic reliability property as more data become available. These features make the estimate suitable for integration into learning procedures that seek either to increase or to decrease mutual information.

The paper demonstrates this integration in adversarial generative modeling and supervised classification. In the latter setting, MINE is used to implement the Information Bottleneck. The authors report substantial improvements in flexibility and performance in these applications. The contribution therefore combines an estimator with evidence that mutual-information objectives can be made useful within neural-network training.
summary.tldr: MINE estimates mutual information with neural networks and enables information-based objectives in generative modeling and classification.

title: Mutual Information Neural Estimation

abstract: We establish novel generalization bounds for learning algorithms that converge to global minima. We derive black-box stability results that only depend on the convergence of a learning algorithm and the geometry around the minimizers of the empirical risk function. The results are shown for non-convex loss functions satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) and the quadratic growth (QG) conditions, which we show arise for 1-layer neural networks with leaky ReLU activations and deep neural networks with linear activations. We use our results to establish the stability of first-order methods such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD), gradient descent (GD), randomized coordinate descent (RCD), and the stochastic variance reduced gradient method (SVRG), in both the PL and the strongly convex setting. Our results match or improve state-of-the-art generalization bounds and can easily extend to similar optimization algorithms. Finally, although our results imply comparable stability for SGD and GD in the PL setting, we show that there exist simple quadratic models with multiple local minima where SGD is stable but GD is not.

This provides a route to guarantees that can apply across optimization methods rather than requiring an entirely separate analysis for each one.

The nonconvex results use the Polyak-Lojasiewicz and quadratic growth conditions. The authors show these conditions arise for one-layer networks with leaky ReLU activations and deep networks with linear activations. They establish stability results for SGD, gradient descent, randomized coordinate descent, and SVRG in the PL and strongly convex settings, matching or improving existing generalization bounds.

The comparison between stochastic and ordinary gradient descent has a meaningful qualification. Although the results imply comparable stability in the PL setting, the authors construct simple quadratic models with multiple local minima where SGD is stable and gradient descent is not. This shows that the relationship between the algorithms' stability depends on the optimization setting.
summary.tldr: Convergence and loss geometry yield generalization guarantees for several optimizers, while examples reveal setting-dependent stability differences between SGD and GD.

title: Stability and Generalization of Learning Algorithms that Converge to Global Optima

abstract: We consider the setting where we wish to perform ranking for hundreds of thousands of users which is common in recommender systems and web search ranking. Learning a single ranking function is unlikely to capture the variability across all users while learning a ranking function for each person is time-consuming and requires large amounts of data from each user. To address this situation, we propose a Factorization RankSVM algorithm which learns a series of k basic ranking functions and then constructs for each user a local ranking function that is a combination of them. We develop a fast algorithm to reduce the time complexity of gradient descent solver by exploiting the low-rank structure, and the resulting algorithm is much faster than existing methods. Furthermore, we prove that the generalization error of the proposed method can be significantly better than training individual RankSVMs. Finally, we present some interesting patterns in the principal ranking functions learned by our algorithms.

paragraphs: Personalized ranking becomes difficult when a system serves hundreds of thousands of users. One shared ranking function may miss differences between users, while a separate function for every person is expensive to learn and demands substantial individual data. This paper addresses that tension through a low-rank representation of ranking functions.

Factorization RankSVM learns a collection of k basic ranking functions. Each user's ranking function is then built as a combination of those shared components. This provides a way to express individual variation while learning common structure across users, rather than estimating every user's ranking model independently.

The authors exploit the low-rank structure to accelerate the gradient descent solver and report a method much faster than existing approaches. They also prove that its generalization error can be significantly better than that of separate RankSVM models; this is a possible advantage established by their analysis, rather than an unconditional claim. Patterns in the learned principal ranking functions offer an additional view of the shared structure.
summary.tldr: Factorization RankSVM builds personalized rankings from shared basic functions, improving computational efficiency and potentially generalization.

title: Extreme Learning to Rank via Low Rank Assumption

abstract: The classical Multinomial Logit (MNL) is a behavioral model for user choice. In this model, a user is offered a slate of choices (a subset of a finite universe of $n$ items), and selects exactly one item from the slate, each with probability proportional to its (positive) weight. Given a set of observed slates and choices, the likelihood-maximizing item weights are easy to learn at scale, and easy to interpret. However, the model fails to represent common real-world behavior. As a result, researchers in user choice often turn to mixtures of MNLs, which are known to approximate a large class of models of rational user behavior. Unfortunately, the only known algorithms for this problem have been heuristic in nature. In this paper we give the first polynomial-time algorithms for exact learning of uniform mixtures of two MNLs. Interestingly, the parameters of the model can be learned for any $n$ by sampling the behavior of random users only on slates of sizes 2 and 3; in contrast, we show that slates of size 2 are insufficient by themselves.
