paragraphs: A multinomial logit model assigns each item a positive weight and predicts choices in proportion to those weights among the offered items. It is easy to fit and interpret, but a single model cannot express some common choice behavior. Mixtures offer greater flexibility, although the abstract describes earlier learning approaches for them as heuristic.

The paper provides polynomial-time algorithms for exact learning of uniform mixtures of two multinomial logit models. The uniform, two-component setting is central to the result: it gives a precise class of mixtures for which the authors establish an efficient learning procedure with a formal guarantee.

A striking finding concerns the choice sets needed to learn the parameters. For any number of items, sampling random users' choices from sets containing only two or three items suffices. Sets of two items alone are shown to be insufficient. This identifies a meaningful difference between pairwise choice information and information from triples, linking the learning guarantee to the structure of the observations available.
summary.tldr: Uniform mixtures of two multinomial logits can be learned exactly in polynomial time using choice sets of sizes two and three.

title: Learning a Mixture of Two Multinomial Logits

abstract: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) is introduced to expand the commonly used analytic variational distribution family, by mixing the variational parameter with a flexible distribution. This mixing distribution can assume any density function, explicit or not, as long as independent random samples can be generated via reparameterization. Not only does SIVI expand the variational family to incorporate highly flexible variational distributions, including implicit ones that have no analytic density functions, but also sandwiches the evidence lower bound (ELBO) between a lower bound and an upper bound, and further derives an asymptotically exact surrogate ELBO that is amenable to optimization via stochastic gradient ascent. With a substantially expanded variational family and a novel optimization algorithm, SIVI is shown to closely match the accuracy of MCMC in inferring the posterior in a variety of Bayesian inference tasks.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior using a chosen family of distributions. This paper broadens that family by treating its parameters as draws from another, more flexible distribution. The resulting mixture can represent richer posterior shapes, including implicit distributions without an analytic density function.

The mixing distribution need not have an explicit density, but it must support independent sampling through reparameterization. This flexibility creates an optimization challenge because the evidence lower bound can become difficult to work with directly. The authors address it by constructing lower and upper bounds on that objective and deriving an asymptotically exact surrogate suitable for stochastic gradient ascent.

The method therefore combines a more expressive approximation family with a way to optimize it. Across a variety of Bayesian inference tasks, the authors report posterior inference accuracy close to that of MCMC. This empirical finding supports the usefulness of the expanded family and optimization method together, while the surrogate’s exactness is specifically an asymptotic result.
summary.tldr: Semi-implicit variational inference combines flexible parameter mixtures with an optimizable surrogate objective, closely matching MCMC accuracy in reported tasks.

title: Semi-Implicit Variational Inference

abstract: We address the problem of planning in an environment with deterministic dynamics and stochastic discounted rewards under a limited numerical budget where the ranges of both rewards and noise are unknown. We introduce PlaTypOOS, an adaptive, robust, and efficient alternative to the OLOP (open-loop optimistic planning) algorithm. Whereas OLOP requires a priori knowledge of the ranges of both rewards and noise, PlaTypOOS dynamically adapts its behavior to both. This allows PlaTypOOS to be immune to two vulnerabilities of OLOP: failure when given underestimated ranges of noise and rewards and inefficiency when these are overestimated. PlaTypOOS additionally adapts to the global smoothness of the value function. PlaTypOOS acts in a provably more efficient manner vs. OLOP when OLOP is given an overestimated reward and show that in the case of no noise, PlaTypOOS learns exponentially faster.

paragraphs: The paper considers planning with deterministic state dynamics, stochastic discounted rewards, and a limited computation budget. The reward range and noise range are unknown. These unknown scales create difficulties for OLOP, an optimistic planning algorithm that requires both ranges in advance: underestimates can cause failure, while overestimates can waste computation.

The proposed alternative, PlaTypOOS, adapts dynamically to reward and noise scales. This removes the two stated vulnerabilities associated with supplying incorrect ranges to OLOP. The algorithm also adjusts to the global smoothness of the value function, making its planning behavior responsive to another property of the problem rather than relying only on fixed advance information.

The authors prove an efficiency advantage over OLOP when OLOP receives an overestimated reward range. They also show exponentially faster learning in the noiseless case. These improvements have specific conditions: the planning setting retains deterministic dynamics, and the strongest speed claim applies when noise is absent. The broader contribution is adaptive planning when relevant numerical scales are unknown.
summary.tldr: PlaTypOOS adapts to unknown reward and noise scales, with conditional efficiency advantages over OLOP and exponentially faster learning without noise.

title: Scale-free adaptive planning for deterministic dynamics & discounted rewards

abstract: We consider the problem of nonparametric regression in the high-dimensional setting in which $P \gg N$. We study the use of overlapping group structures to improve prediction and variable selection. These structures arise commonly when analyzing DNA microarray data, where genes can naturally be grouped according to genetic pathways. We incorporate overlapping group structure into a Bayesian additive regression trees model using a prior constructed so that, if a variable from some group is used to construct a split, this increases the probability that subsequent splits will use predictors from the same group. We refer to our model as an overlapping group Bayesian additive regression trees (OG-BART) model, and our prior on the splits an overlapping group Dirichlet (OG-Dirichlet) prior. Like the sparse group lasso, our prior encourages sparsity both within and between groups. We study the correlation structure of the prior, illustrate the proposed methodology on simulated data, and apply the methodology to gene expression data to learn which genetic pathways are predictive of breast cancer tumor metastasis.

paragraphs: When predictors greatly outnumber observations, information about how predictors are related can help guide regression and variable selection. The paper studies overlapping groups, such as genes that belong to shared biological pathways. Overlap matters because a predictor can participate in several meaningful groups rather than fitting into one exclusive category.

The authors incorporate these relationships into a Bayesian additive regression trees model. Their prior makes a predictor’s use in a tree split increase the probability that later splits select predictors from the same group. The resulting OG-BART model uses an overlapping group Dirichlet prior that encourages sparsity both across groups and among predictors within groups.

The paper studies correlations induced by this prior, illustrates the method on simulated data, and applies it to gene-expression data involving breast cancer tumor metastasis. That application identifies genetic pathways predictive of metastasis. The approach makes grouping information part of the model’s selection preferences, allowing related predictors to influence one another while retaining pressure toward a selective set of groups and variables.
summary.tldr: OG-BART uses overlapping predictor groups to guide tree splits and encourage sparse selection within and across groups.

title: Incorporating Grouping Information into Bayesian Decision Tree Ensembles

abstract: Motivated by the recent potential of mass customization brought by whole-garment knitting machines, we introduce the new problem of automatic machine instruction generation using a single image of the desired physical product, which we apply to machine knitting. We propose to tackle this problem by directly learning to synthesize regular machine instructions from real images. We create a cured dataset of real samples with their instruction counterpart and propose to use synthetic images to augment it in a novel way. We theoretically motivate our data mixing framework and show empirical results suggesting that making real images look more synthetic is beneficial in our problem setup.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the task of generating machine instructions from a single image of a desired physical product, focusing on machine knitting. The motivation is the customization potential of whole-garment knitting machines. The learning problem is to connect the visible appearance of a knitted sample with instructions that describe how to manufacture it.

The authors propose learning this mapping directly from real images to regular machine instructions. They create paired data containing real samples and their corresponding instructions, then augment those data with synthetic images. These paired examples establish the connection between appearance and manufacturing commands, while the synthetic images become part of the training framework.

A central contribution is the way real and synthetic data are mixed. The authors give a theoretical motivation for their framework and report empirical evidence suggesting that making real images look more synthetic helps in this setting. The finding is specific and qualified: it supports that direction of image transformation for the studied inverse-knitting problem, rather than establishing a universal rule for combining synthetic and real data.
summary.tldr: The paper learns knitting instructions from product images and finds evidence that making real images more synthetic improves its data-mixing approach.

title: Neural Inverse Knitting: From Images to Manufacturing Instructions

abstract: We consider the use of decision trees for decision-making problems under the predict-then-optimize framework. That is, we would like to first use a decision tree to predict unknown input parameters of an optimization problem, and then make decisions by solving the optimization problem using the predicted parameters. A natural loss function in this framework is to measure the suboptimality of the decisions induced by the predicted input parameters, as opposed to measuring loss using input parameter prediction error. This natural loss function is known in the literature as the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss, and we propose a tractable methodology called SPO Trees (SPOTs) for training decision trees under this loss. SPOTs benefit from the interpretability of decision trees, providing an interpretable segmentation of contextual features into groups with distinct optimal solutions to the optimization problem of interest. We conduct several numerical experiments on synthetic and real data including the prediction of travel times for shortest path problems and predicting click probabilities for news article recommendation. We demonstrate on these datasets that SPOTs simultaneously provide higher quality decisions and significantly lower model complexity than other machine learning approaches (e.g., CART) trained to minimize prediction error.

paragraphs: Many prediction systems supply inputs to a later optimization problem. Predicted travel times, for example, help determine a shortest path. In this setting, prediction errors matter through the decisions they cause: reducing numerical error alone need not produce the best decision. The paper trains decision trees with this downstream purpose explicitly in view.

Its method, SPO Trees or SPOTs, uses Smart Predict-then-Optimize loss, which measures the suboptimality of decisions made using predicted parameters. The authors propose a tractable way to train trees under this objective. The resulting tree also provides an interpretable grouping of contextual features into regions associated with distinct optimal decisions.

On these datasets, SPOTs produce better decisions with substantially lower model complexity than approaches such as CART trained to minimize prediction error. The findings support aligning tree training with the quality of the eventual optimization decision while preserving an understandable decision structure.
summary.tldr: SPO Trees train interpretable decision trees to improve downstream optimization decisions rather than merely reduce prediction error.

title: Decision Trees for Decision-Making under the Predict-then-Optimize Framework

abstract: The neural plausibility of backpropagation has long been disputed, primarily for its use of non-local weight transport — the biologically dubious requirement that one neuron instantaneously measure the synaptic weights of another. Until recently, attempts to create local learning rules that avoid weight transport have typically failed in the large-scale learning scenarios where backpropagation shines, e.g. ImageNet categorization with deep convolutional networks. Here, we investigate a recently proposed local learning rule that yields competitive performance with backpropagation and find that it is highly sensitive to metaparameter choices, requiring laborious tuning that does not transfer across network architecture. Our analysis indicates the underlying mathematical reason for this instability, allowing us to identify a more robust local learning rule that better transfers without metaparameter tuning. Nonetheless, we find a performance and stability gap between this local rule and backpropagation that widens with increasing model depth. We then investigate several non-local learning rules that relax the need for instantaneous weight transport into a more biologically-plausible "weight estimation" process, showing that these rules match state-of-the-art performance on deep networks and operate effectively in the presence of noisy updates. Taken together, our results suggest two routes towards the discovery of neural implementations for credit assignment without weight symmetry: further improvement of local rules so that they perform consistently across architectures and the identification of biological implementations for non-local learning mechanisms.

paragraphs: Backpropagation's biological plausibility is challenged by weight transport: the requirement that a neuron access another neuron's synaptic weights. This paper investigates learning rules that avoid instantaneous weight transport while still supporting large-scale learning. It considers both local rules and non-local mechanisms based on estimating weights.

The authors first examine a recently proposed local rule with competitive performance and find that it depends heavily on tuning choices that do not transfer across architectures. They do not establish that the proposed mechanisms are implemented by biological neural systems.
summary.tldr: The paper improves local learning without weight symmetry and finds that non-local weight-estimation rules can match strong deep-network performance.

title: Two Routes to Scalable Credit Assignment without Weight Symmetry

abstract: Domain shift is a fundamental problem in visual recognition which typically arises when the source and target data follow different distributions. The existing domain adaptation approaches which tackle this problem work in the "closed-set" setting with the assumption that the source and the target data share exactly the same classes of objects. In this paper, we tackle a more realistic problem of the "open-set" domain shift where the target data contains additional classes that were not present in the source data. More specifically, we introduce an end-to-end Progressive Graph Learning (PGL) framework where a graph neural network with episodic training is integrated to suppress underlying conditional shift and adversarial learning is adopted to close the gap between the source and target distributions. Compared to the existing open-set adaptation approaches, our approach guarantees to achieve a tighter upper bound of the target error. Extensive experiments on three standard open-set benchmarks evidence that our approach significantly outperforms the state-of-the-arts in open-set domain adaptation.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation addresses the mismatch between the data used to learn a model and the data it later encounters. In open-set adaptation, the target data also contain classes absent from the source. This makes the problem broader than aligning two distributions that contain exactly the same object categories.

The paper introduces Progressive Graph Learning, an end-to-end framework combining a graph neural network with adversarial learning. Episodic training of the graph component is used to suppress conditional shift, while adversarial learning reduces the gap between source and target distributions. The framework therefore combines mechanisms aimed at different aspects of the mismatch.

The authors establish a tighter upper bound on target error than existing open-set adaptation approaches. They also report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on three standard open-set benchmarks. The bound and experiments provide distinct support: one improves the theoretical characterization of target error, while the other demonstrates better observed performance in settings that include previously unseen target classes.
summary.tldr: Progressive Graph Learning combines episodic graph training and adversarial adaptation to handle target domains containing additional classes.

title: Progressive Graph Learning for Open-Set Domain Adaptation

abstract: In this paper we propose a scalable, unsupervised approach for detecting anomalies in the Internet of Things (IoT). Complex devices are connected daily and eagerly generate vast streams of multidimensional telemetry. These devices often operate in distinct modes based on external conditions (day/night, occupied/vacant, etc.), and to prevent complete or partial system outage, we would like to recognize as early as possible when these devices begin to operate outside the normal modes. We propose an unsupervised anomaly detection method that creates a negative sample from the positive, observed sample, and trains a classifier to distinguish between positive and negative samples. Using the Concentration Phenomenon, we explain why such a classifier ought to establish suitable decision boundaries between normal and anomalous regions, and show how Integrated Gradients can attribute the anomaly to specific dimensions within the anomalous state vector. We have demonstrated that negative sampling with random forest or neural network classifiers yield significantly higher AUC scores compared to state-of-the-art approaches against benchmark anomaly detection datasets, and a multidimensional, multimodal dataset from real climate control devices. Finally, we describe how negative sampling with neural network classifiers have been successfully deployed at large scale to predict failures in real time in over 15,000 climate-control and power meter devices in 145 office buildings within the California Bay Area.

paragraphs: Connected devices produce telemetry with many measurements and multiple normal operating modes, such as occupied and vacant conditions. This paper proposes an unsupervised method for detecting departures from those modes. It creates artificial negative samples from observed positive samples, then trains a classifier to distinguish the two groups. The resulting classification problem provides a route to anomaly detection.

The authors use the concentration phenomenon to explain why this construction should produce useful boundaries between normal and anomalous regions. They also apply Integrated Gradients to attribute an anomalous state to particular measurement dimensions. This adds an explanatory component: the detector can identify which parts of the state vector contribute to its assessment.

The evidence therefore spans benchmark discrimination, multidimensional operating data, and an operational deployment.
summary.tldr: Classifying observed telemetry against generated negative samples enables scalable anomaly detection with measurement-level explanations and demonstrated device deployment.

title: Interpretable, Multidimensional, Multimodal Anomaly Detection with Negative Sampling for Detection of Device Failure

abstract: We study few-shot supervised domain adaptation (DA) for regression problems, where only a few labeled target domain data and many labeled source domain data are available. Many of the current DA methods base their transfer assumptions on either parametrized distribution shift or apparent distribution similarities, e.g., identical conditionals or small distributional discrepancies. However, these assumptions may preclude the possibility of adaptation from intricately shifted and apparently very different distributions. To overcome this problem, we propose mechanism transfer, a meta-distributional scenario in which a data generating mechanism is invariant among domains. This transfer assumption can accommodate nonparametric shifts resulting in apparently different distributions while providing a solid statistical basis for DA. We take the structural equations in causal modeling as an example and propose a novel DA method, which is shown to be useful both theoretically and experimentally. Our method can be seen as the first attempt to fully leverage the invariance of structural causal models for DA.

However, these assumptions may preclude the possibility of adaptation from intricately shifted and apparently very different distributions. To overcome this problem, we propose mechanism transfer, a meta-distributional scenario in which a data generating mechanism is invariant among domains. This transfer assumption can accommodate nonparametric shifts resulting in apparently different distributions while providing a solid statistical basis for DA. We take the structural equations in causal modeling as an example and propose a novel DA method, which is shown to be useful both theoretically and experimentally. Our method can be seen as the first attempt to fully leverage the invariance of structural causal models for DA.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression when many labeled examples are available from a source domain but only a few from the target domain. Transferring knowledge is difficult when the two observed distributions look very different. Assumptions based on small distributional differences or specific forms of shift can rule out such cases.

The proposed alternative is mechanism transfer: assume that a data-generating mechanism remains invariant across domains. This moves the basis for transfer from apparent similarity in the observed data to shared structure in how the data arise. The framework can accommodate nonparametric shifts that produce visibly different distributions while still providing a statistical basis for adaptation.

The authors develop a concrete adaptation method using structural equations from causal modeling as the shared mechanism. They establish theoretical usefulness and provide experimental support. The contribution is a way to make use of a few target labels when distributional resemblance is weak, provided that the assumed invariant generating mechanism connects the domains.
summary.tldr: Mechanism transfer supports few-shot regression adaptation by assuming shared causal generating structure across domains with potentially very different distributions.

title: Few-shot Domain Adaptation by Causal Mechanism Transfer

abstract: We study the exploration problem with approximate linear action-value functions in episodic reinforcement learning under the notion of low inherent Bellman error, a condition normally employed to show convergence of approximate value iteration. First we relate this condition to other common frameworks and show that it is strictly more general than the low rank (or linear) MDP assumption of prior work. Second we provide an algorithm with a high probability regret bound $\widetilde O(\sum_{t=1}^H d_t \sqrt{K} + \sum_{t=1}^H \sqrt{d_t} \IBE K)$ where $H$ is the horizon, $K$ is the number of episodes, $\IBE$ is the value if the inherent Bellman error and $d_t$ is the feature dimension at timestep $t$. In addition, we show that the result is unimprovable beyond constants and logs by showing a matching lower bound. This has two important consequences: 1) it shows that exploration is possible using only \emph{batch assumptions} with an algorithm that achieves the optimal statistical rate for the setting we consider, which is more general than prior work on low-rank MDPs 2) the lack of closedness (measured by the inherent Bellman error) is only amplified by $\sqrt{d_t}$ despite working in the online setting. Finally, the algorithm reduces to the celebrated \textsc{LinUCB} when $H=1$ but with a different choice of the exploration parameter that allows handling misspecified contextual linear bandits. While computational tractability questions remain open for the MDP setting, this enriches the class of MDPs with a linear representation for the action-value function where statistically efficient reinforcement learning is possible.

title: Learning Near Optimal Policies with Low Inherent Bellman Error

abstract: We propose unsupervised embedding adaptation for the downstream few-shot classification task. Based on findings that deep neural networks learn to generalize before memorizing, we develop Early-Stage Feature Reconstruction (ESFR) — a novel adaptation scheme with feature reconstruction and dimensionality-driven early stopping that finds generalizable features. Incorporating ESFR consistently improves the performance of baseline methods on all standard settings, including the recently proposed transductive method. ESFR used in conjunction with the transductive method further achieves state-of-the-art performance on mini-ImageNet, tiered-ImageNet, and CUB; especially with 1.2% 2.0% improvements in accuracy over the previous best performing method on 1-shot setting.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification depends on representations that remain useful when only a small number of labeled examples are available. This paper proposes adapting those representations through an unsupervised procedure. Its starting point is the observation that deep networks learn generalizable patterns before they begin memorizing the data used for training.

Early-Stage Feature Reconstruction, or ESFR, combines feature reconstruction with an early-stopping rule driven by dimensionality. The aim is to obtain features from the useful early phase of learning. Stopping is therefore part of the adaptation method itself, helping select a representation that generalizes rather than simply continuing reconstruction training.

Adding ESFR consistently improves the tested baseline methods across all standard settings reported in the abstract, including a recently proposed transductive method. Combined with that method, ESFR achieves state-of-the-art results on mini-ImageNet, tiered-ImageNet, and CUB, with highlighted gains in one-shot classification. The findings support unsupervised representation adaptation as a useful addition to few-shot methods, particularly when the adaptation process deliberately targets early-stage generalization.
summary.tldr: ESFR adapts features through unsupervised reconstruction and dimensionality-driven early stopping, improving reported few-shot classification performance.

title: Unsupervised Embedding Adaptation via Early-Stage Feature Reconstruction for Few-Shot Classification

abstract: We study the identification of direct and indirect causes on time series with latent variables, and provide a constrained-based causal feature selection method, which we prove that is both sound and complete under some graph constraints. Our theory and estimation algorithm require only two conditional independence tests for each observed candidate time series to determine whether or not it is a cause of an observed target time series. Furthermore, our selection of the conditioning set is such that it improves signal to noise ratio. We apply our method on real data, and on a wide range of simulated experiments, which yield very low false positive and relatively low false negative rates.

paragraphs: This paper asks which observed time series are direct or indirect causes of an observed target series when some variables remain hidden. The presence of latent variables makes causal feature selection more demanding than simply finding predictive associations. The authors propose a constraint-based method that uses conditional-independence relationships to decide whether a candidate series is a cause.

Under specified graph constraints, the method is proved sound and complete. These guarantees mean that the causal selection procedure is correct and comprehensive within the graph setting covered by the theory. Both the theoretical procedure and the estimation algorithm require only two conditional-independence tests for each observed candidate time series.

The method also chooses its conditioning set in a way that improves the signal-to-noise ratio. This makes the choice of variables used in the tests part of the approach’s contribution. Applications to real data and a broad range of simulations yield very low false-positive rates and relatively low false-negative rates, supporting the method’s practical effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Under graph constraints, two conditional-independence tests per candidate suffice for sound and complete causal time-series feature selection.

title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for causal feature selection in time series with latent common causes

abstract: We systematize the approach to the investigation of deep neural network landscapes by basing it on the geometry of the space of implemented functions rather than the space of parameters. Grouping classifiers into equivalence classes, we develop a standardized parameterization in which all symmetries are removed, resulting in a toroidal topology. On this space, we explore the error landscape rather than the loss. This lets us derive a meaningful notion of the flatness of minimizers and of the geodesic paths connecting them. Using different optimization algorithms that sample minimizers with different flatness we study the mode connectivity and relative distances. Testing a variety of state-of-the-art architectures and benchmark datasets, we confirm the correlation between flatness and generalization performance; we further show that in function space flatter minima are closer to each other and that the barriers along the geodesics connecting them are small. We also find that minimizers found by variants of gradient descent can be connected by zero-error paths composed of two straight lines in parameter space, i.e. polygonal chains with a single bend. We observe similar qualitative results in neural networks with binary weights and activations, providing one of the first results concerning the connectivity in this setting. Our results hinge on symmetry removal, and are in remarkable agreement with the rich phenomenology described by some recent analytical studies performed on simple shallow models.

paragraphs: Different neural network parameter settings can represent equivalent classifiers, complicating comparisons of minima and their surrounding flat regions. This paper organizes the landscape around implemented functions. By grouping equivalent classifiers and removing symmetries, the authors construct a standardized parameterization with toroidal topology. They then examine prediction error on that space rather than the training loss.

This construction supports definitions of flatness and shortest geometric paths between minimizers. Across the tested architectures and datasets, the authors confirm a correlation between flatness and generalization. They also find that flatter minima lie closer together in function space and that the error barriers along connecting geodesic paths are small.

Networks with binary weights and activations show similar qualitative behavior. These observations concern the studied settings and depend on removing symmetries, which is central to making the geometric comparisons meaningful.
summary.tldr: Removing classifier symmetries reveals relationships between flatness, generalization, and low-error connections among neural network minima.

title: Deep Networks on Toroids: Removing Symmetries Reveals the Structure of Flat Regions in the Landscape Geometry

abstract: We consider an online learning problem with one-sided feedback, in which the learner is able to observe the true label only for positively predicted instances. On each round, $k$ instances arrive and receive classification outcomes according to a randomized policy deployed by the learner, whose goal is to maximize accuracy while deploying individually fair policies. We first present a novel auditing scheme, capable of utilizing feedback from dynamically-selected panels of multiple, possibly inconsistent, auditors regarding fairness violations. In particular, we show how our proposed auditing scheme allows for algorithmically exploring the resulting accuracy-fairness frontier, with no need for additional feedback from auditors. We then present an efficient reduction from our problem of online learning with one-sided feedback and a panel reporting fairness violations to the contextual combinatorial semi-bandit problem (Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi, 2009; Gyorgy et al., 2007), allowing us to leverage algorithms for contextual combinatorial semi-bandits to establish multi-criteria no regret guarantees in our setting, simultaneously for accuracy and fairness. Our results eliminate two potential sources of bias from prior work: the “hidden outcomes” that are not available to an algorithm operating in the full information setting, and human biases that might be present in any single human auditor, but can be mitigated by selecting a well-chosen panel.

paragraphs: This paper studies online classification when true labels become visible only for instances receiving positive predictions. On each round, several instances arrive, and a randomized policy assigns outcomes. The learner must pursue accuracy while deploying individually fair policies, despite receiving an incomplete picture of the consequences of its decisions.

The authors introduce an auditing scheme that accepts fairness-violation feedback from dynamically selected panels of auditors. Panel members may disagree, so the framework does not require a single consistent judgment source. The scheme also allows algorithms to explore the tradeoff between accuracy and fairness without requesting additional auditor feedback for that exploration.

An efficient reduction connects the problem to contextual combinatorial semi-bandits, enabling simultaneous no-regret guarantees for accuracy and fairness. The approach directly accommodates hidden outcomes instead of assuming unavailable labels are visible. It also allows a well-chosen panel to mitigate biases that might affect a single auditor. These contributions address two distinct difficulties: selective access to outcome labels and reliance on human judgments about fairness.
summary.tldr: The paper combines panel-based fairness auditing with bandit learning to pursue accuracy and individual fairness when only positive predictions reveal labels.

title: Individually Fair Learning with One-Sided Feedback

abstract: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) provides valuable prior knowledge that is often discarded in regression tasks in machine learning. We show that the independences arising from the presence of collider structures in DAGs provide meaningful inductive biases, which constrain the regression hypothesis space and improve predictive performance. We introduce collider regression, a framework to incorporate probabilistic causal knowledge from a collider in a regression problem. When the hypothesis space is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, we prove a strictly positive generalisation benefit under mild assumptions and provide closed-form estimators of the empirical risk minimiser. Experiments on synthetic and climate model data demonstrate performance gains of the proposed methodology.

paragraphs: A causal graph can contain useful information even when the immediate task is prediction. This paper studies how regression can benefit from probabilistic knowledge encoded in directed acyclic graphs. It focuses on independence relationships associated with collider structures and uses them to restrict the functions a regression model considers.

The proposed framework, collider regression, turns this knowledge into an inductive bias. Constraining the hypothesis space gives learning additional guidance beyond fitting the observed examples. The key idea is that graph-derived independence information can help distinguish useful predictive functions within a regression problem.

For hypothesis spaces that are reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, the authors prove a strictly positive generalisation benefit under mild assumptions. They also derive closed-form estimators for empirical risk minimisation, connecting the theoretical argument to an explicit estimation procedure. Experiments on synthetic data and climate-model data show predictive gains. The findings support using particular forms of causal knowledge to improve regression, with the formal guarantee tied to the specified function space and assumptions.
summary.tldr: Collider regression uses causal independence information to constrain prediction functions and delivers a provable generalisation benefit under stated assumptions.

title: Returning The Favour: When Regression Benefits From Probabilistic Causal Knowledge

abstract: Modern deep neural networks have achieved impressive performance on tasks from image classification to natural language processing. Surprisingly, these complex systems with massive amounts of parameters exhibit the same structural properties in their last-layer features and classifiers across canonical datasets when training until convergence. In particular, it has been observed that the last-layer features collapse to their class-means, and those class-means are the vertices of a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF). This phenomenon is known as Neural Collapse (NC). Recent papers have theoretically shown that NC emerges in the global minimizers of training problems with the simplified “unconstrained feature model”. In this context, we take a step further and prove the NC occurrences in deep linear networks for the popular mean squared error (MSE) and cross entropy (CE) losses, showing that global solutions exhibit NC properties across the linear layers. Furthermore, we extend our study to imbalanced data for MSE loss and present the first geometric analysis of NC under bias-free setting. Our results demonstrate the convergence of the last-layer features and classifiers to a geometry consisting of orthogonal vectors, whose lengths depend on the amount of data in their corresponding classes. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical analyses on synthetic and practical network architectures with both balanced and imbalanced scenarios.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a striking geometric pattern in trained classifiers: features from the same class concentrate at their class mean, and the means form a highly regular simplex arrangement. Earlier theory established such behavior in a simplified model with unconstrained features. This paper advances the analysis to deep linear networks, where the layers impose an explicit network structure.

For mean squared error and cross-entropy losses, the authors prove that global solutions exhibit neural-collapse properties across the linear layers. This connects the geometry to a multilayer training problem rather than only to independently chosen features. The result concerns global solutions of these deep linear models, keeping the mathematical conclusion tied to the setting actually analyzed.

For imbalanced data, the paper studies mean squared error in a bias-free setting. The resulting last-layer feature and classifier geometry consists of orthogonal vectors whose lengths depend on class sample counts. Experiments on synthetic and practical architectures support the theoretical analyses under balanced and imbalanced conditions, illustrating how class imbalance changes the geometry associated with collapse.
summary.tldr: The paper proves neural-collapse structure in deep linear networks and characterizes a class-size-dependent geometry for imbalanced, bias-free MSE training.

title: Neural Collapse in Deep Linear Networks: From Balanced to Imbalanced Data

abstract: In this paper, we study the $k$-clustering problems with outliers in distributed setting. The current best results for the distributed $k$-center problem with outliers have quadratic local running time with communication cost dependent on the aspect ratio $\Delta$ of the given instance, which may constraint the scalability of the algorithms for handling large-scale datasets. To achieve better communication cost for the problem with faster local running time, we propose an inliers-recalling sampling method, which avoids guessing the optimal radius of the given instance, and can achieve a 4-round bi-criteria $(14(1+\epsilon),1+\epsilon)$-approximation with linear local running time in the data size and communication cost independent of the aspect ratio. To obtain a more practical algorithm for the problem, we propose another space-narrowing sampling method, which automatically adjusts the sample size to adapt to different outliers distributions on each machine, and can achieve a 2-round bi-criteria $(14(1+\epsilon),1+\epsilon)$-approximation with communication cost independent of the number of outliers. We show that, if the data points are randomly partitioned across machines, our proposed sampling-based methods can be extended to the $k$-median/means problems with outliers, and can achieve $(O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2}),1+\epsilon)$-approximation with communication cost independent of the number of outliers. Empirical experiments suggest that the proposed 2-round distributed algorithms outperform other state-of-the-art algorithms.

To achieve better communication cost for the problem with faster local running time, we propose an inliers-recalling sampling method, which avoids guessing the optimal radius of the given instance, and can achieve a 4-round bi-criteria $(14(1+\epsilon),1+\epsilon)$-approximation with linear local running time in the data size and communication cost independent of the aspect ratio. paragraphs: Clustering distributed data becomes harder when some points are treated as outliers. Earlier distributed k-center methods required quadratic local running time and communication that depended on the dataset’s aspect ratio. This paper introduces sampling strategies intended to reduce computation and communication while retaining approximation guarantees.

The first strategy, inliers-recalling sampling, avoids guessing the optimal clustering radius. It uses four communication rounds, has local running time linear in data size, and removes aspect-ratio dependence from communication. The second, space-narrowing sampling, adapts sample sizes to the distribution of outliers on each machine. It uses two rounds and has communication cost independent of the number of outliers.

Both k-center methods provide a bicriteria guarantee: they approximate clustering quality while allowing a controlled increase in the outlier budget. The methods also extend to k-median and k-means with outliers when points are randomly partitioned across machines. That partition assumption qualifies the extension. Experiments suggest that the proposed two-round algorithms outperform other state-of-the-art methods, supporting their practical promise alongside the formal guarantees.
summary.tldr: Adaptive sampling reduces distributed clustering costs while preserving bicriteria approximation guarantees for handling outliers.

title: Fast Algorithms for Distributed k-Clustering with Outliers

abstract: We design differentially private regret-minimizing algorithms in the online convex optimization (OCO) framework. Unlike recent results, our algorithms and analyses do not require smoothness, thus yielding the first private regret bounds with an optimal leading-order term for non-smooth loss functions. Additionally, even for smooth losses, the resulting regret guarantees improve upon previous results in terms their dependence of dimension. Our results provide the best known rates for DP-OCO in all practical regimes of the privacy parameter, barring when it is exceptionally small. The principal innovation in our algorithm design is the use of sampling from strongly log-concave densities which satisfy the Log-Sobolev Inequality. The resulting concentration of measure allows us to obtain a better trade-off for the dimension factors than prior work, leading to improved results. Following previous works on DP-OCO, the proposed algorithm explicitly limits the number of switches via rejection sampling. Thus, independently of privacy constraints, the algorithm also provides improved results for online convex optimization with a switching budget.

paragraphs: The paper develops differentially private algorithms for online convex optimization, where decisions are made sequentially as loss functions arrive. Their objective is to keep regret low: the accumulated loss relative to the best fixed decision in hindsight. The central advance is obtaining stronger privacy-preserving regret guarantees without requiring smooth loss functions.

Removing the smoothness requirement extends the guarantees to losses whose slopes can change abruptly. The authors establish the first private regret bounds with an optimal leading-order term for non-smooth losses. This claim concerns the leading term, rather than every part of the bound. For smooth losses, the guarantees also improve how regret depends on the problem’s dimension.

The main technical ingredient is sampling from strongly log-concave probability densities that satisfy the Log-Sobolev Inequality. This property provides concentration guarantees, controlling how much samples fluctuate. The analysis uses that concentration to obtain a better trade-off among dimension-dependent factors. The abstract reports the best known rates across practical privacy-parameter regimes, with an exception when that parameter is exceptionally small.

The algorithm also uses rejection sampling to explicitly limit how often its decision changes. This connects the privacy result to online optimization with a switching budget, where the number of allowed changes is constrained. The authors obtain improved guarantees for that setting independently of privacy requirements.
summary.tldr: The paper improves private online convex optimization regret guarantees without requiring smooth losses, while also improving guarantees under a switching budget.

title: Improved Differentially Private and Lazy Online Convex Optimization: Lower Regret without Smoothness Requirements

abstract: Both the marginal contributions needed for the computation of Shapley values and the graph produced by Pearl-Verma theorem rely on the choice of an ordering of the variables. For Shapley values, the marginal contributions are averaged over all orderings, while in causal inference methods, the typical approach is to select orderings producing a graph with a minimal number of edges. We reconcile both approaches by reinterpreting them from a maximum entropy perspective. Namely, Shapley values assume no prior knowledge about the orderings and treat them as equally likely, while causal inference approaches apply Occam’s razor and consider only orderings producing the simplest explanatory graphs. We find that the blind application of Occam’s razor to Shapley values does not produce fully satisfactory explanations. Hence, we propose two variations of Shapley values based on entropy maximization to appropriately incorporate prior information about the model. Hence, we propose a variation of Shapley values based on entropy maximization to appropriately incorporate prior information about the model.

paragraphs: Shapley values assign contributions by considering variables in different orders and averaging their marginal contributions. Variable orderings also matter in causal inference, where they affect the explanatory graph constructed through the Pearl-Verma theorem. This paper connects the two procedures by examining the assumptions behind how they treat possible orderings.

From a maximum-entropy perspective, ordinary Shapley values express an absence of prior knowledge by treating all orderings equally. The causal approach described in the paper instead favors orderings that produce graphs with fewer edges, applying a preference for simpler explanations. This comparison makes the treatment of orderings an explicit modeling choice.

The authors find that directly applying this simplicity preference to Shapley values does not yield fully satisfactory explanations. They propose entropy-maximizing variations that incorporate prior information about the model into the weighting of orderings. The contribution is a framework for adapting contribution-based explanations to available knowledge, while clarifying why equal weighting and graph simplicity encode different assumptions about what an explanation should reflect.
summary.tldr: The paper uses maximum entropy to incorporate prior model information into Shapley explanations by reconsidering the weighting of variable orderings.

title: Incorporating Information into Shapley Values: Reweighting via a Maximum Entropy Approach

abstract: Multimodal fusion is crucial in joint decision-making systems for rendering holistic judgments. Since multimodal data changes in open environments, dynamic fusion has emerged and achieved remarkable progress in numerous applications. However, most existing dynamic multimodal fusion methods lack theoretical guarantees and easily fall into suboptimal problems, yielding unreliability and instability. To address this issue, we propose a Predictive Dynamic Fusion (PDF) framework for multimodal learning. We proceed to reveal the multimodal fusion from a generalization perspective and theoretically derive the predictable Collaborative Belief (Co-Belief) with Mono- and Holo-Confidence, which provably reduces the upper bound of generalization error. Accordingly, we further propose a relative calibration strategy to calibrate the predicted Co-Belief for potential uncertainty. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks confirm our superiority. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yinan-Xia/PDF.

title: Predictive Dynamic Fusion

abstract: Ensuring privacy-preserving inference on cryptographically secure data is a well-known computational challenge. To alleviate the bottleneck of costly cryptographic computations in non-linear activations, recent methods have suggested linearizing a targeted portion of these activations in neural networks. This technique results in significantly reduced runtimes with often negligible impacts on accuracy. In this paper, we demonstrate that such computational benefits may lead to increased fairness costs. Specifically, we find that reducing the number of ReLU activations disproportionately decreases the accuracy for minority groups compared to majority groups. To explain these observations, we provide a mathematical interpretation under restricted assumptions about the nature of the decision boundary, while also showing the prevalence of this problem across widely used datasets and architectures. Finally, we show how a simple procedure altering the finetuning step for linearized models can serve as an effective mitigation strategy.

The practical implication is that evaluating this computational shortcut requires attention to group-level accuracy, and that the fine-tuning stage offers a way to address the observed imbalance.
summary.tldr: Linearizing neural networks for faster private inference can disproportionately harm minority-group accuracy, with modified fine-tuning providing a mitigation.

title: Disparate Impact on Group Accuracy of Linearization for Private Inference

abstract: As AI model size grows, neural scaling laws have become a crucial tool to predict the improvements of large models when increasing capacity and the size of original (human or natural) training data. Yet, the widespread use of popular models means that the ecosystem of online data and text will co-evolve to progressively contain increased amounts of synthesized data. In this paper we ask: How will the scaling laws change in the inevitable regime where synthetic data makes its way into the training corpus? Will future models, still improve, or be doomed to degenerate up to total (model) collapse? We develop a theoretical framework of model collapse through the lens of scaling laws. We discover a wide range of decay phenomena, analyzing loss of scaling, shifted scaling with number of generations, the ”un-learning" of skills, and grokking when mixing human and synthesized data. Our theory is validated by large-scale experiments with a transformer on an arithmetic task and text generation using the large language model Llama2.

paragraphs: Scaling laws describe how model performance changes as training data and model capacity grow. This paper asks how those relationships change when training collections increasingly contain material generated by other models. Its central concern is whether the patterns used to predict progress from human or natural data still apply when synthetic data enters the process.

The authors develop a theoretical framework that describes model collapse through changes in scaling behavior. They analyze several outcomes: improvements can stop following their previous scaling pattern, scaling can shift across successive model generations, and previously acquired skills can be lost. They also study grokking when human and synthesized data are mixed, showing that their framework covers more than a single pattern of deterioration.

The theory is supported by large-scale experiments involving a transformer on arithmetic and Llama2 for text generation. The findings frame collapse as a range of changes in learning behavior, rather than establishing that every use of synthetic data inevitably produces complete failure.
summary.tldr: The paper explains model collapse through changes in scaling laws, revealing several ways synthetic training data can alter learning and skill retention.

title: A Tale of Tails: Model Collapse as a Change of Scaling Laws

abstract: Generation of graphs is a major challenge for real-world tasks that require understanding the complex nature of their non-Euclidean structures. Although diffusion models have achieved notable success in graph generation recently, they are ill-suited for modeling the topological properties of graphs since learning to denoise the noisy samples does not explicitly learn the graph structures to be generated. To tackle this limitation, we propose a generative framework that models the topology of graphs by explicitly learning the final graph structures of the diffusion process. Specifically, we design the generative process as a mixture of endpoint-conditioned diffusion processes which is driven toward the predicted graph that results in rapid convergence. We further introduce a simple parameterization of the mixture process and develop an objective for learning the final graph structure, which enables maximum likelihood training. Through extensive experimental validation on general graph and 2D/3D molecule generation tasks, we show that our method outperforms previous generative models, generating graphs with correct topology with both continuous (e.g. 3D coordinates) and discrete (e.g. atom types) features. Our code is available at https://github.com/harryjo97/GruM.

paragraphs: Generating a graph requires getting its pattern of connections right, alongside any attributes attached to its components. The paper argues that learning to remove noise does not explicitly teach a diffusion model the final graph structure it should produce. Its proposed framework makes that final structure a direct learning target.

The generative process mixes diffusion processes conditioned on their endpoints. A predicted final graph guides the evolving sample, which the authors report leads to rapid convergence. They also introduce a simple parameterization and an objective for learning the endpoint structure that enables maximum likelihood training. This connects the model's training target to the topology sought at the end of generation.

Experiments cover general graphs and both two-dimensional and three-dimensional molecular generation. The authors report improvements over previous generative models, including graphs with correct topology and combinations of discrete attributes, such as atom types, and continuous attributes, such as spatial coordinates. These findings support explicitly predicting the destination graph as a useful way to coordinate structural and attribute generation.
summary.tldr: Predicting final graph structures guides a diffusion mixture toward better graph and molecule generation in the reported experiments.

title: Graph Generation with Diffusion Mixture

abstract: In many reinforcement learning (RL) applications, we want policies that reach desired states and then keep the controlled system within an acceptable region around the desired states over an indefinite period of time. This latter objective is called stability and is especially important when the state space is unbounded, such that the states can be arbitrarily far from each other and the agent can drift far away from the desired states. For example, in stochastic queuing networks, where queues of waiting jobs can grow without bound, the desired state is all-zero queue lengths. Here, a stable policy ensures queue lengths are finite while an optimal policy minimizes queue lengths. Since an optimal policy is also stable, one would expect that RL algorithms would implicitly give us stable policies. However, in this work, we find that deep RL algorithms that directly minimize the distance to the desired state during online training often result in unstable policies, i.e., policies that drift far away from the desired state. We attribute this instability to poor credit-assignment for destabilizing actions. We then introduce an approach based on two ideas: 1) a Lyapunov-based cost-shaping technique and 2) state transformations to the unbounded state space. We conduct an empirical study on various queueing networks and traffic signal control problems and find that our approach performs competitively against strong baselines with knowledge of the transition dynamics. Our code is available here: https://github.com/Badger-RL/STOP

paragraphs: A controller often needs to reach a desired state and keep the system nearby indefinitely. This stability requirement becomes especially important when states can grow without bound. In a queueing network, for example, a stable policy keeps queues finite, while an optimal policy additionally minimizes their lengths.

The paper finds that deep reinforcement-learning methods trained online to minimize distance from the desired state often produce unstable policies. Although an optimal policy would be stable, the learning process does not reliably reach that behavior. The authors attribute the problem to poor credit assignment: training does not adequately connect destabilizing actions with their consequences.

Their approach combines Lyapunov-based cost shaping with transformations of the unbounded state space. These changes address the learning signal and the state representation together. Experiments on queueing networks and traffic-signal control find competitive performance against strong baselines that know the transition dynamics. The results support addressing stability explicitly in the learning setup when directly optimizing proximity to the desired state yields policies that drift away.
summary.tldr: Lyapunov-based cost shaping and state transformations help online reinforcement learning address unstable behavior in systems with unbounded states.

title: Learning to Stabilize Online Reinforcement Learning in Unbounded State Spaces

abstract: We present a new algorithm based on posterior sampling for learning in Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDP) in the infinite-horizon undiscounted setting. The algorithm achieves near-optimal regret bounds while being advantageous empirically compared to the existing algorithms. Our main theoretical result is a Bayesian regret bound for each cost component of $\tilde{O} (DS\sqrt{AT})$ for any communicating CMDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions, and diameter $D$. This regret bound matches the lower bound in order of time horizon $T$ and is the best-known regret bound for communicating CMDPs achieved by a computationally tractable algorithm. Empirical results show that our posterior sampling algorithm outperforms the existing algorithms for constrained reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning studies decisions that must account for several costs or requirements over time. This paper considers an infinite-horizon, undiscounted setting, where learning is evaluated through continuing performance rather than a finite episode or discounted future. It introduces a learning algorithm based on posterior sampling.

The main result bounds Bayesian regret separately for each cost component in a communicating constrained Markov decision process. With S states, A actions, diameter D, and time horizon T, the bound is approximately DS times the square root of AT, suppressing logarithmic factors. Its dependence on T matches the lower bound, which is the precise sense in which its time scaling is near-optimal.

The authors describe this as the best-known regret bound for communicating problems achieved by a computationally tractable algorithm. They also report empirical improvements over existing constrained reinforcement learning algorithms. Together, these results connect an efficient exploration strategy with strong theoretical time dependence and favorable observed performance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Posterior sampling achieves near-optimal time-dependent Bayesian regret for communicating constrained reinforcement learning problems.

title: Efficient Exploration in Average-Reward Constrained Reinforcement Learning: Achieving Near-Optimal Regret With Posterior Sampling

abstract: We aim to develop a fundamental understanding of modality collapse, a recently observed empirical phenomenon wherein models trained for multimodal fusion tend to rely only on a subset of the modalities, ignoring the rest. We show that modality collapse happens when noisy features from one modality are entangled, via a shared set of neurons in the fusion head, with predictive features from another, effectively masking out positive contributions from the predictive features of the former modality and leading to its collapse. We further prove that cross-modal knowledge distillation implicitly disentangles such representations by freeing up rank bottlenecks in the student encoder, denoising the fusion-head outputs without negatively impacting the predictive features from either modality. Based on the above findings, we propose an algorithm that prevents modality collapse through explicit basis reallocation, with applications in dealing with missing modalities. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal benchmarks validate our theoretical claims. Project page: https://abhrac.github.io/mmcollapse/.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can receive several kinds of input yet learn to depend on only some of them. This paper examines how that collapse can arise inside the component that combines modalities. Its explanation centers on noisy features from one modality sharing neurons with useful features from another, obscuring the useful information in the first modality.

The authors also analyze why cross-modal knowledge distillation can help. They prove that it implicitly separates these tangled representations by relieving rank bottlenecks in the student encoder. In their analysis, this reduces noise in the fusion outputs without harming predictive features from either modality. The issue is therefore tied to how representational capacity is allocated across inputs.

Building on that account, the paper proposes explicitly reallocating representation bases to prevent collapse. The method also has applications when some modalities are missing. Experiments across multiple multimodal benchmarks support the theoretical claims. Together, the analysis and algorithm connect a model's apparent neglect of an input to a concrete interaction between noise, shared neurons, and restricted representation capacity.
summary.tldr: The paper explains modality collapse through entangled noisy and predictive features and proposes reallocating representation capacity to prevent it.

title: A Closer Look at Multimodal Representation Collapse

abstract: Foundation models have emerged as a promising approach in time series forecasting (TSF). Existing approaches either repurpose large language models (LLMs) or build large-scale time series datasets to develop TSF foundation models for universal forecasting. However, these methods face challenges due to the severe cross-domain gap or in-domain heterogeneity. This paper explores a new road to building a TSF foundation model from rich, high-quality natural images. Our key insight is that a visual masked autoencoder, pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset, can naturally be a numeric series forecaster. By reformulating TSF as an image reconstruction task, we bridge the gap between image pre-training and TSF downstream tasks. Surprisingly, without further adaptation in the time series domain, the proposed VisionTS could achieve better zero-shot forecast performance than existing TSF foundation models. With fine-tuning for one epoch, VisionTS could further improve the forecasting and achieve state-of-the-art performance in most cases. Extensive experiments reveal intrinsic similarities between images and real-world time series, suggesting that visual models may offer a "free lunch" for TSF and highlight the potential for future cross-modality research. Our code is available in the https://github.com/Keytoyze/VisionTS.

The central idea is that a visual masked autoencoder trained on ImageNet can be used to forecast numerical sequences.

VisionTS reformulates forecasting as image reconstruction, connecting the downstream time series task to the visual model's existing training objective. The authors report that, without further adaptation to time series, VisionTS can outperform existing time series foundation models in zero-shot forecasting. This makes the form of the task itself a key part of transferring knowledge across modalities.

They also motivate further study of how models trained in one modality can benefit tasks in another.
summary.tldr: VisionTS converts forecasting into image reconstruction, enabling an ImageNet-pretrained visual model to perform zero-shot time series prediction.

title: VisionTS: Visual Masked Autoencoders Are Free-Lunch Zero-Shot Time Series Forecasters

abstract: We present Gradient Boosting Reinforcement Learning (GBRL), a framework that adapts the strengths of Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) to reinforcement learning (RL) tasks. While neural networks (NNs) have become the de facto choice for RL, they face significant challenges with structured and categorical features and tend to generalize poorly to out-of-distribution samples. These are challenges for which GBTs have traditionally excelled in supervised learning. However, GBT’s application in RL has been limited. The design of traditional GBT libraries is optimized for static datasets with fixed labels, making them incompatible with RL’s dynamic nature, where both state distributions and reward signals evolve during training. GBRL overcomes this limitation by continuously interleaving tree construction with environment interaction. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that GBRL outperforms NNs in domains with structured observations and categorical features, while maintaining competitive performance on standard continuous control benchmarks. Like its supervised learning counterpart, GBRL demonstrates superior robustness to out-of-distribution samples and better handles irregular state-action relationships.

paragraphs: Gradient Boosting Reinforcement Learning brings boosted trees into a setting usually dominated by neural networks. The motivation is that structured observations, categorical features, and irregular relationships can be difficult for neural networks, while boosted trees have strengths on these kinds of data in supervised learning. Applying those strengths to reinforcement learning requires changing how training proceeds.

Traditional gradient-boosting libraries assume a static dataset with fixed labels. Reinforcement learning instead changes the data encountered and the learning signals as interaction continues. GBRL handles this mismatch by repeatedly interleaving tree construction with environment interaction. The framework therefore adapts tree learning to an evolving learning process rather than treating the experience as one fixed supervised dataset.

Experiments show GBRL outperforming neural networks in domains with structured observations and categorical features, while remaining competitive on standard continuous-control benchmarks. The authors also report stronger robustness to out-of-distribution samples and better handling of irregular state-action relationships. These findings support boosted trees as a useful reinforcement-learning model family, particularly where the observation structure suits their strengths.
summary.tldr: GBRL adapts boosted trees to ongoing environment interaction, improving results on structured and categorical reinforcement-learning tasks.

title: Gradient Boosting Reinforcement Learning

abstract: How a single fertilized cell gives rise to a complex array of specialized cell types in development is a central question in biology. The cells replicate to generate cell lineages and acquire differentiated characteristics through poorly understood molecular processes. A key approach to studying developmental processes is to infer the tree graph of cell lineage histories, which provides an analytical framework for dissecting individual cells’ molecular decisions during replication and differentiation (i.e., acquisition of specialized traits). Although genetically engineered lineage-tracing methods have advanced the field, they are either infeasible or ethically constrained in many organisms. By contrast, modern single-cell technologies can measure high-content molecular profiles (e.g., transcriptomes) in a wide range of biological systems. Here, we introduce CellTreeQM, a novel deep learning method based on transformer architectures that learns an embedding space with geometric properties optimized for tree-graph inference. By formulating the lineage reconstruction problem as tree-metric learning, we systematically explore weakly supervised training settings at different levels of information and present the Cell Lineage Reconstruction Benchmark to facilitate comprehensive evaluation. This benchmark includes (1) synthetic data modeled via Brownian motion with independent noise and spurious signals; (2) lineage-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. Experimental results show that CellTreeQM recovers lineage structures with minimal supervision and limited data, offering a scalable framework for uncovering cell lineage relationships. To our knowledge, this is the first method to cast cell lineage inference explicitly as a metric learning task, paving the way for future computational models aimed at uncovering the molecular dynamics of cell lineage. Code and benchmarks are available at: https://kuang-da.github.io/CellTreeQM-page

This paper instead studies reconstruction from measured cell characteristics, including molecular profiles available through single-cell technologies, using limited information about the true lineage.

CellTreeQM uses a transformer to learn an embedding whose geometry is suited to tree reconstruction. The key formulation is tree-metric learning: the representation is trained so that distances support inference of lineage relationships. The authors systematically examine weakly supervised settings with different amounts of information, making the supervision requirement part of the study.

They also introduce a benchmark containing synthetic data generated through Brownian motion with independent noise and spurious signals, together with lineage-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. summary.tldr: CellTreeQM learns representations suited to lineage-tree reconstruction and recovers cell relationships with minimal supervision and limited data in experiments.

title: Reconstructing Cell Lineage Trees from Phenotypic Features with Metric Learning

abstract: Model calibration seeks to ensure that models produce confidence scores that accurately reflect the true likelihood of their predictions being correct. However, existing calibration approaches are fundamentally tied to datasets of one-hot labels implicitly assuming full certainty in all the annotations. Such datasets are effective for classification but provides insufficient knowledge of uncertainty for model calibration, necessitating the curation of datasets with numerically rich ground-truth confidence values. However, due to the scarcity of uncertain visual examples, such samples are not easily available as real datasets. In this paper, we introduce calibration-aware data augmentation to create synthetic datasets of diverse samples and their ground-truth uncertainty. Specifically, we present Calibration-aware Semantic Mixing (CSM), a novel framework that generates training samples with mixed class characteristics and annotates them with distinct confidence scores via diffusion models. Based on this framework, we propose calibrated reannotation to tackle the misalignment between the annotated confidence score and the mixing ratio during the diffusion reverse process. Besides, we explore the loss functions that better fit the new data representation paradigm. Experimental results demonstrate that CSM achieves superior calibration compared to the state-of-the-art calibration approaches. Our code is available here.

paragraphs: A calibrated classifier should express confidence that matches how often its predictions are correct. This paper argues that ordinary one-hot labels provide inadequate supervision for that goal: they identify a class with full certainty but offer little information about degrees of ambiguity. Obtaining real images with useful numerical uncertainty annotations is also difficult because suitable uncertain examples are scarce.

Calibration-aware Semantic Mixing, or CSM, addresses this data problem using diffusion models. It generates images that combine characteristics of different classes and assigns them distinct confidence values. The aim is to train with examples that explicitly represent uncertainty, so calibration can draw on richer information than a single categorical label provides.

The method also addresses a mismatch between the intended mixing ratio and the confidence annotation during diffusion generation through calibrated reannotation. The authors investigate loss functions suited to this richer label format. Experiments report better calibration than the state-of-the-art approaches compared, supporting synthetic uncertainty supervision as a useful ingredient in calibration.
summary.tldr: CSM improves model calibration by generating images with mixed class characteristics and explicit uncertainty annotations.

title: Beyond One-Hot Labels: Semantic Mixing for Model Calibration

abstract: Multimodal learning faces challenges in effectively fusing information from diverse modalities, especially when modality quality varies across samples. Dynamic fusion strategies, such as attention mechanism in Transformers, aim to address such challenge by adaptively emphasizing modalities based on the characteristics of input data. However, through amounts of carefully designed experiments, we surprisingly observed that the dynamic adaptability of widely-used self-attention models diminishes. Model tends to prefer one modality regardless of data characteristics. This bias triggers a self-reinforcing cycle that progressively overemphasizes the favored modality, widening the distribution gap in attention keys across modalities and deactivating attention mechanism’s dynamic properties. To revive adaptability, we propose a simple yet effective method Rolling Query (RollingQ), which balances attention allocation by rotating the query to break the self-reinforcing cycle and mitigate the key distribution gap. Extensive experiments on various multimodal scenarios validate the effectiveness of RollingQ and the restoration of cooperation dynamics is pivotal for enhancing the broader capabilities of widely deployed multimodal Transformers. The source code is available at https://github.com/GeWu-Lab/RollingQ_ICML2025.

Through controlled experiments, this paper finds that widely used self-attention models can lose that adaptability and favor one modality regardless of the current input.

The authors identify a self-reinforcing process: preference for one modality increases its dominance, while attention-key distributions across modalities move further apart. Experiments across multiple multimodal scenarios validate the method’s effectiveness and support the importance of restoring cooperation among modalities. The contribution combines a diagnosis of how adaptive fusion can deteriorate with a targeted intervention in the attention mechanism. Its practical significance is that having attention available does not by itself ensure input-sensitive fusion; the learned dynamics must also preserve that flexibility.
