title: RollingQ: Reviving the Cooperation Dynamics in Multimodal Transformer

abstract: Reward models are widely used as proxies for human preferences when aligning or evaluating LLMs. However, reward models are black boxes, and it is often unclear what, exactly, they are actually rewarding. In this paper we develop Rewrite-based Attribute Treatment Estimator (RATE) as an effective method for measuring the sensitivity of a reward model to high-level attributes of responses, such as sentiment, helpfulness, or complexity. Importantly, RATE measures the causal effect of an attribute on the reward. RATE uses LLMs to rewrite responses to produce imperfect counterfactuals examples that can be used to measure causal effects. A key challenge is that these rewrites are imperfect in a manner that can induce substantial bias in the estimated sensitivity of the reward model to the attribute. The core idea of RATE is to adjust for this imperfect-rewrite effect by rewriting twice. We establish the validity of the RATE procedure and show empirically that it is an effective estimator.

paragraphs: Reward models assign scores intended to reflect human preferences, but a score does not reveal which response attributes caused it. RATE addresses this by estimating how attributes such as sentiment, helpfulness, or complexity affect the reward. Its target is a causal effect: what changing an attribute does to the score, rather than how that attribute merely correlates with it.

The method uses language models to rewrite responses into counterfactual examples. A difficulty is that a rewrite may change more than the intended attribute, creating substantial bias in the estimated effect. RATE’s central idea is to rewrite twice and use that construction to adjust for the influence of imperfect rewriting.

The paper establishes the validity of the procedure and provides empirical evidence that it estimates effects effectively. This matters because counterfactual text edits are useful for probing reward models only when unintended changes are accounted for. RATE turns the imperfection of generated rewrites into an explicit estimation problem, providing a way to examine what a reward model actually favors.
summary.tldr: RATE estimates the causal effect of response attributes on reward scores by using a second rewrite to adjust for imperfect counterfactual edits.

title: RATE: Causal Explainability of Reward Models with Imperfect Counterfactuals

abstract: Zero-shot imitation learning algorithms hold the promise of reproducing unseen behavior from as little as a single demonstration at test time. Existing practical approaches view the expert demonstration as a sequence of goals, enabling imitation with a high-level goal selector, and a low-level goal-conditioned policy. However, this framework can suffer from myopic behavior: the agent’s immediate actions towards achieving individual goals may undermine long-term objectives. We introduce a novel method that mitigates this issue by directly optimizing the occupancy matching objective that is intrinsic to imitation learning. We propose to lift a goal-conditioned value function to a distance between occupancies, which are in turn approximated via a learned world model. The resulting method can learn from offline, suboptimal data, and is capable of non-myopic, zero-shot imitation, as we demonstrate in complex, continuous benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/zilot.

paragraphs: Zero-shot imitation aims to reproduce a previously unseen behavior from a demonstration provided at test time. Existing practical methods often break that demonstration into goals and use a goal-conditioned policy to pursue them. This can produce short-sighted behavior: an action that helps reach an immediate goal may make the overall demonstrated behavior harder to reproduce.

The proposed method instead directly optimizes occupancy matching, comparing behavior through the occupancies central to the imitation objective. It turns a goal-conditioned value function into a distance between occupancies and uses a learned world model to approximate them. This provides a way to evaluate behavior beyond a sequence of separately pursued immediate goals.

The method can learn from offline data that is itself suboptimal, and the authors demonstrate non-myopic zero-shot imitation on complex continuous benchmarks. The stated results show that learning useful imitation capabilities does not require all the offline behavior to be expert-quality. More broadly, the approach connects goal-conditioned values to a longer-horizon matching objective that addresses the short-sightedness of goal-by-goal imitation.
summary.tldr: An occupancy-matching method learns from suboptimal offline data and demonstrates zero-shot imitation that accounts for longer-term objectives.

title: Zero-Shot Offline Imitation Learning via Optimal Transport

abstract: Multimodal person re-identification (Re-ID) aims to match pedestrian images across different modalities. However, most existing methods focus on limited cross-modal settings and fail to support arbitrary query-retrieval combinations, hindering practical deployment. We propose FlexiReID, a flexible framework that supports seven retrieval modes across four modalities: RGB, infrared, sketches, and text. FlexiReID introduces an adaptive mixture-of-experts (MoE) mechanism to dynamically integrate diverse modality features and a cross-modal query fusion module to enhance multimodal feature extraction. To facilitate comprehensive evaluation, we construct CIRS-PEDES, a unified dataset extending four popular Re-ID datasets to include all four modalities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlexiReID achieves state-of-the-art performance and offers strong generalization in complex scenarios.

A cross-modal query fusion module further improves extraction of information from multimodal queries. Together, these components give the framework a way to account for diverse input types when constructing the representations used for matching, within the retrieval modes it supports.

The authors also introduce CIRS-PEDES, a unified dataset that extends four established person re-identification datasets to include all four modalities. This provides a shared setting for evaluating the broader retrieval capability. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization in complex scenarios. The contribution combines a more flexible matching framework with evaluation data designed to cover its multimodal scope.
summary.tldr: FlexiReID uses adaptive experts and query fusion to support seven person-retrieval modes across four modalities.

title: FlexiReID: Adaptive Mixture of Expert for Multi-Modal Person Re-Identification

abstract: Confidence calibration is critical for the safe deployment of machine learning models in the real world. However, such issue in vision-language models like CLIP, particularly after fine-tuning, has not been fully addressed. In this work, we demonstrate that existing prompt tuning methods usually lead to a trade-off of calibration between base and new classes: the cross-entropy loss used in standard fine-tuning (e.g., CoOp) causes overconfidence in new classes by increasing textual label divergence, whereas regularization-based tuning (e.g., KgCoOp) maintains the confidence level but results in underconfidence in base classes due to the improved accuracy. Inspired by the observations, we introduce Dynamic Outlier Regularization (DOR) to ensure the confidence calibration on both base and new classes after fine-tuning. In particular, we propose to minimize the feature deviation of novel textual labels (instead of base classes) sampled from a large vocabulary. In effect, DOR prevents the increase in textual divergence for new labels while easing restrictions on base classes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DOR can enhance the calibration performance of current fine-tuning methods on base and new classes.

paragraphs: A calibrated model’s confidence should match how often its predictions are correct. This paper finds that prompt tuning in vision-language models can create a trade-off between calibration on base classes and new classes. Standard cross-entropy tuning can make new-class predictions overconfident by increasing divergence among textual label representations.

Regularization-based tuning produces a different problem: confidence stays similar while base-class accuracy improves, leaving the model underconfident on those classes. The authors introduce Dynamic Outlier Regularization to address both behaviors. DOR minimizes feature changes for novel textual labels sampled from a large vocabulary, directing regularization toward labels outside the base classes.

This choice aims to prevent increased textual divergence for new labels while relaxing constraints on base-class representations. Experiments show that DOR can improve calibration for both groups when applied to existing fine-tuning methods. The contribution links a confidence problem to changes in textual representations and proposes a targeted regularizer, rather than treating all labels as needing the same restrictions during adaptation.
summary.tldr: DOR regularizes novel textual labels to improve confidence calibration for both base and new classes after prompt tuning.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Miscalibration in Prompt Tuning for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Latent diffusion models excel at generating high-quality images but lose the benefits of end-to-end modeling. They discard information during image encoding, require a separately trained decoder, and model an auxiliary distribution to the raw data. In this paper, we propose Latent Forcing, a simple modification to existing architectures that achieves the efficiency of latent diffusion while operating on raw natural images. Our approach orders the denoising trajectory by jointly processing latents and pixels with separately tuned noise schedules. This allows the latents to act as a scratchpad for intermediate computation before high-frequency pixel features are generated. We find that the order of conditioning signals is critical, and we analyze this to explain differences between REPA distillation in the tokenizer and the diffusion model, as well as conditional and unconditional generation. Applied to pixel-space diffusion on ImageNet, Latent Forcing achieves a new state of the art for diffusion transformer-based pixel generation at our compute scale. Code and checkpoints at https://github.com/AlanBaade/LatentForcing

paragraphs: Latent diffusion generates images through an intermediate representation, gaining efficiency but introducing an encoding step that discards information and a separately trained decoder. Latent Forcing aims to retain latent diffusion’s efficiency while modeling raw natural images. It does so by changing how latent and pixel information participate in the denoising trajectory.

The method jointly processes latents and pixels with separately tuned noise schedules. This ordering lets the latent representation serve as a scratchpad for intermediate computation before high-frequency pixel features are generated. The contribution is a modification to existing architectures that uses latents within the generation process while keeping raw images as the modeling target.

The authors find that the ordering of conditioning signals is critical. They use this analysis to explain differences involving REPA distillation in the tokenizer versus the diffusion model, and conditional versus unconditional generation. On ImageNet, Latent Forcing establishes a new state of the art for diffusion-Transformer pixel generation at the authors’ compute scale. That qualification defines the scope of the reported comparison.
summary.tldr: Latent Forcing coordinates latent and pixel denoising so latent computation can support efficient generation directly in pixel space.

title: Latent Forcing: Reordering the Diffusion Trajectory for Pixel-Space Image Generation

abstract: Bridging the sim2real gap between computationally inexpensive models and complex physical systems remains a central challenge in machine learning applications to engineering problems, particularly in multi-scale settings where reduced-order models typically capture only dominant dynamics. In this work, we present Cheap2Rich, a multi-scale data assimilation framework that reconstructs high-fidelity state spaces from sparse sensor histories by combining a fast low-fidelity prior with learned, interpretable discrepancy corrections. We demonstrate the performance on rotating detonation engines (RDEs), a challenging class of systems that couple detonation-front propagation with injector-driven unsteadiness, mixing, and stiff chemistry across disparate scales. Our approach successfully reconstructs high-fidelity RDE states from sparse measurements while isolating physically meaningful discrepancy dynamics associated with injector-driven effects. The results highlight a general multi-fidelity framework for data assimilation and system identification in complex multi-scale systems, enabling rapid design exploration and real-time monitoring and control while providing interpretable discrepancy dynamics.

paragraphs: Fast physical models often capture a system’s dominant behavior while leaving out interactions across smaller or faster scales. Cheap2Rich addresses the resulting gap between inexpensive simulation and complex physical systems. Its task is to reconstruct detailed system states from sparse sensor histories while retaining the computational advantages of a simpler model.

The framework combines a fast, low-fidelity prior with learned corrections for the discrepancy between that prior and higher-fidelity behavior. These corrections are designed to remain interpretable. The demonstration uses rotating detonation engines, where propagating detonation fronts interact with injector-driven fluctuations, mixing, and stiff chemistry across very different scales.

The reported results show successful reconstruction of high-fidelity engine states from sparse measurements. They also isolate physically meaningful discrepancy dynamics associated with injector effects, making the correction itself informative about the system. The paper presents this combination as a general approach to data assimilation and system identification, with potential value for rapid design exploration and real-time monitoring and control. Its central contribution is linking detailed reconstruction to an interpretable account of what the cheaper model misses.
summary.tldr: Cheap2Rich combines fast physical models with interpretable learned corrections to reconstruct detailed rotating detonation engine states from sparse measurements.

title: Cheap2Rich: A Multi-Fidelity Framework for Data Assimilation and System Identification of Multiscale Physics - Rotating Detonation Engines

abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is a fundamental challenge in organic chemistry, defined by its enormous search space. Existing methods typically formulate it as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with a fixed choice of transition model (i.e., a single-step retrosynthesis model), and focus on improving how to search through better policies and value functions. However, how the transition space itself is navigated remains largely unexplored. This limitation is particularly urgent given our observation of pronounced skill disparity among single-step prediction models: different models exhibit substantially different performance across molecule states. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RetrOrchestrator, an LLM-powered agent that explicitly accounts for model skill disparity by reframing retrosynthesis planning as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). By regarding each single-step prediction model as a tool, we further propose a scaffold-aware reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize navigation policy within the transition space. As a result, RetrOrchestrator jointly searches which molecule to expand and which single-step model to apply for the molecule at the current step. Empirically, RetrOrchestrator significantly outperforms static baselines on the Retro*-190 benchmark, achieving a state-of-the-art 94.21% success rate (vs. 9.47% off-the-shelf LLM and 82.63% non-LLM state-dependent router), with 92.49% of solved routes invoking two or more SSRs—evidence that the policy is not collapsing to a single specialist or a static router. The same gain persists on a larger out-of-distribution set (PDB-600), with RetrOrchestrator Pareto-optimal in both wall-clock time and model-query count. Code: https://github.com/ScottLiao920/verl-retro-agent.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis plans how to make a target molecule by working backward through possible precursor molecules. Existing planners often fix the model that proposes each backward step and concentrate on improving search. RetrOrchestrator starts from the observation that single-step models have different strengths across molecule states, making model selection part of the planning problem.

The system treats single-step predictors as tools for an LLM-powered agent and formulates planning as a partially observable decision process. A scaffold-aware reinforcement-learning algorithm trains the agent to choose both which molecule to expand and which predictor to apply. This lets the available transition choices change as the route develops.

summary.tldr: RetrOrchestrator improves retrosynthesis planning by jointly choosing the next molecule to expand and the single-step model best suited to that step.

title: RetrOrchestrator: A Multi-Step Retrosynthesis Agent Dynamically Orchestrating Single-Step Transition Models

abstract: Incomplete multi-view clustering (IMVC) aims to uncover shared clustering structures from heterogeneous views with partial observations. Recently, existing generative IMVC methods have made significant progress in this field; however, they still remain limited in two aspects. On the one hand, they rely on weak cross-view signals, resulting in unstable latent recovery when facing missing data. On the other hand, they overlook stable cross-view neighborhood structures, leading to weak structural constraint. To address these limitations, we propose neighborhood-conditioned diffusion for incomplete multi-view clustering (IMVC-NCD), which achieves robust latent completion. Our method learns compact view-specific latent representations and constructs a unified conditioning vector by aggregating stable local neighborhood structures from available views while encoding missingness states, providing reliable guidance for diffusion-based denoising. With neighborhood-level conditioning, IMVC-NCD produces semantically aligned and view-consistent latent representations that are well suited for clustering, even under high missing-view ratios. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our method compared with state-of-the-art IMVC approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/zgh1115/IMVC-NCD.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples using several kinds of information, even when some views are missing. Recovering missing representations is difficult when the available views offer weak guidance. This paper argues that stable local neighborhoods across observed views provide additional structure that existing generative approaches do not adequately exploit.

IMVC-NCD first learns compact representations specific to each view. It then aggregates neighborhood information from the available views into a shared conditioning vector, alongside information indicating which views are absent. A diffusion denoising process uses this conditioning to complete the latent representations. The guidance therefore includes relationships among nearby examples as well as the pattern of missing observations.

The resulting representations are designed to align meaning across views and remain consistent enough for clustering, including when many views are missing. Experiments on four benchmark datasets report effectiveness and robustness against state-of-the-art incomplete multi-view clustering approaches. The contribution links missing-data recovery to neighborhood structure, giving the denoising process a more stable basis for completion.
summary.tldr: IMVC-NCD guides diffusion-based completion with cross-view neighborhood structure and missingness information to improve clustering with incomplete observations.

title: Incomplete Multi-View Clustering via Neighborhood-Conditioned Diffusion

abstract: Effective data selection is essential for pretraining large language models (LLMs), improving efficiency and generalization to downstream tasks. However, existing approaches often rely on external pretrained models, making it difficult to separate the benefits of data selection from those introduced by external models. In addition, many methods estimate data importance from a fixed model state or short-horizon update, making it hard to capture how data preference changes as the model evolves during pretraining. In this paper, we introduce BLISS (BileveL Influence Scoring method for data Selection), a lightweight data selection method that operates entirely from scratch, without external pretrained oracle models, while modeling dynamic data preference. BLISS uses a small proxy model as a surrogate for the LLM and trains a score model to estimate sample importance through multi-step proxy updates induced by score-weighted training data. We formulate data selection as a bilevel optimization problem: the upper-level objective optimizes the score model to assign sample weights, so minimizing the lower-level weighted training loss improves validation performance. Once optimized, the score model predicts influence scores, enabling efficient selection of high-quality samples for LLM pretraining. We validate BLISS by pretraining 410M/1B/2.8B Pythia and LLaMA-0.5B models on selected C4 subsets. Under the 1B setting, BLISS achieves a $1.7\times$ speedup in reaching the same performance as the state-of-the-art method, while delivering superior performance across multiple downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Choosing pretraining data is difficult because a sample's usefulness can change as a language model learns. Existing selection methods may judge samples from a fixed model state or a short update, and some rely on external pretrained models. BLISS addresses both issues by learning data selection from scratch while tracking its effects across multiple training steps.

The trained scorer then assigns influence scores for selecting pretraining samples.

The authors evaluate selected C4 subsets with Pythia models of 410 million, 1 billion, and 2.8 billion parameters, plus a 0.5-billion-parameter LLaMA model. In the 1-billion-parameter setting, BLISS reaches the comparison method's performance 1.7 times faster and improves results across multiple downstream tasks. This supports learning data preferences through training dynamics without an external pretrained oracle.
summary.tldr: BLISS learns pretraining-data scores from scratch by measuring how weighted samples affect a small model over multiple updates.

title: BLISS: A Lightweight Bilevel Influence Scoring Method for Data Selection in Language Model Pretraining

abstract: Higher-order ODE solvers have become a standard tool for accelerating diffusion probabilistic model (DPM) sampling, motivating the widespread view that first-order methods are inherently slower and that increasing discretization order is the primary path to faster generation. This paper challenges this belief and revisits acceleration from a complementary angle: beyond solver order, the placement of DPM evaluations along the reverse-time dynamics can substantially affect sampling accuracy in the low-neural function evaluation (NFE) regime. We propose a novel training-free, first-order sampler named Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), whose leading discretization error has the opposite sign to that of DDIM. Algorithmically, the method approximates the forward-value evaluation via a cheap one-step lookahead predictor. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that the resulting sampler provably approximates the ideal forward-value trajectory while retaining first-order convergence. Empirically, across standard image generation benchmarks, the proposed sampler consistently improves sample quality under the same NFE budget and can be competitive with, and sometimes outperform, state-of-the-art higher-order samplers. Overall, the results suggest that the placement of DPM evaluations provides an additional and largely independent design angle for accelerating diffusion sampling. Our code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DPMSolver.

paragraphs: Diffusion sampling repeatedly evaluates a neural model while following a reverse-time trajectory. Higher-order numerical solvers are commonly used to reduce the number of evaluations needed for good samples. This paper asks whether another choice—the locations along the trajectory where the model is evaluated—can improve generation even when the solver remains first order.

The proposed F-DPMSolver requires no training and approximates a forward-value evaluation with a cheap one-step lookahead predictor. Its leading discretization error has the opposite sign to DDIM’s. The theoretical analysis shows that the implemented sampler approximates the ideal forward-value trajectory while retaining first-order convergence; its advantage does not come from changing its convergence order.

On standard image-generation benchmarks, the method consistently improves sample quality at the same neural evaluation budget. It is competitive with higher-order samplers and sometimes performs better. These empirical results are especially relevant when few model evaluations are available: formal solver order alone does not determine sample quality in that regime, and evaluation placement offers an additional design choice.
summary.tldr: A training-free first-order diffusion sampler improves low-budget generation by changing where model evaluations occur along the sampling trajectory.

title: Are First-Order Diffusion Samplers Really Slower? A Fast Forward-Value Approach

abstract: With the evolution of generative models, deepfakes have achieved near-perfect semantic realism, leaving forensic traces only in subtle structural anomalies. However, existing single-view paradigms often fail to generalize, as dominant semantic features overwhelm subtle artifact cues within entangled representations. This imbalance leads to overconfident yet brittle predictions—a phenomenon we term the Semantic Masking Effect. To address this challenge, we propose a reliable framework called Divide-and-Conquer Multi-View Evidential Learning (DiCoME) for Deepfake Detection. In the "Divide” phase, we employ Geometric View Purification to decompose the entangled representation space through principled geometric projection. This process suppresses semantic interference within artifact-sensitive representations, forming the foundation for decorrelated yet complementary semantic and artifact views. In the "Conquer” phase, we leverage Uncertainty-Aware Evidential Learning to synthesize these distinct views. By explicitly modeling the "epistemic conflict” between semantic and artifact cues, this mechanism provides calibrated uncertainty estimates instead of forcing rigid deterministic decisions. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing approaches in generalization performance, while providing reliable uncertainty estimation for trustworthy deepfake detection. Code is available at https://github.com/kxl0825/DiCoME.git.

paragraphs: A convincing deepfake can look semantically plausible while retaining subtle structural artifacts. The paper argues that representations mixing these signals can let strong semantic features obscure weaker forensic evidence. It calls this the Semantic Masking Effect and links it to predictions that are confident but brittle.

DiCoME first separates the representation through geometric projection. This purification step suppresses semantic interference in the artifact-sensitive view, producing semantic and artifact views that are less correlated while remaining complementary. The goal is to preserve evidence that could otherwise be overwhelmed by the image’s convincing overall content.

The framework then combines the views through uncertainty-aware evidential learning. It explicitly models disagreement between semantic and artifact cues, allowing that conflict to inform uncertainty estimates instead of forcing a rigid decision. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report better generalization than existing approaches together with reliable uncertainty estimation. The contribution therefore concerns both detection performance and how confidence is formed when different kinds of visual evidence point in different directions.
summary.tldr: DiCoME separates semantic and artifact evidence, then models their disagreement to improve deepfake detection and uncertainty estimates.

title: Divide and Conquer: Reliable Multi-View Evidential Learning for Deepfake Detection

abstract: Recovering scene-consistent 4D crowd motion from monocular video in large-scale scenes remains challenging due to severe depth ambiguity and complex scene geometry. Existing monocular crowd reconstruction methods typically rely on single-plane assumptions, leading to unreliable metric scale and spatial drift under complex terrain. We propose Crowd4D, the first scene-aware 4D crowd reconstruction framework that jointly optimizes the crowd and scene from a monocular RGB video in large-scale scenes. Crowd4D explicitly incorporates scene geometry and ensures consistency across image and scene spaces via a multi-stage optimization strategy. A key bottleneck of this task lies in accurate human–scene alignment, particularly in scale and position. However, human and scene reconstructions are typically decoupled. To address this, we introduce the Human–Scene Interaction Proxy (HSIP) as an intermediate representation, derived from Scene Interaction Point Clouds and a Scene Interaction Surface (SIPC&SIS), which encode explicit scene-aware geometric priors and redefine the optimization space for large-scale monocular 4D crowd reconstruction. To further improve temporal stability under occlusions, we introduce Crowd Structural Coherence Regularization (CSCR), which leverages HSIP-based spatial priors to impose soft temporal consistency on pairwise relative displacements and directions within local crowd neighborhoods. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Crowd4D consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods and enables robust monocular 4D crowd reconstruction in complex, large-scale real-world scenes. Project page is available at https://cic.tju.edu.cn/faculty/likun/projects/Crowd4D.

paragraphs: Recovering a crowd’s three-dimensional motion over time from one video requires resolving ambiguous depth, scale, and position. Assuming that everyone moves on a single plane becomes unreliable on complex terrain. Crowd4D addresses this by jointly optimizing the crowd and its surrounding scene from monocular RGB video.

A multi-stage optimization process enforces consistency between what appears in the image and the reconstructed scene. Its central intermediate representation, the Human–Scene Interaction Proxy, is derived from interaction point clouds and a scene interaction surface. These structures encode geometric information about the scene and help align reconstructed people with it, especially in scale and position.

The framework also uses Crowd Structural Coherence Regularization to improve temporal stability when people are occluded. It applies soft consistency constraints to relative displacements and directions among nearby people, using spatial priors from the interaction proxy. Experiments report consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in complex, large-scale scenes. The approach brings scene geometry and local crowd relationships directly into reconstruction rather than treating human motion as an isolated estimation problem.
summary.tldr: Crowd4D jointly reconstructs crowds and scene geometry from a single video, improving alignment and motion stability in complex environments.

title: Crowd4D: Scene-Aware Monocular 4D Crowd Reconstruction

abstract: While linear-complexity attention mechanisms offer a promising alternative to Softmax attention for overcoming the quadratic bottleneck, training such models from scratch remains prohibitively expensive. Inheriting weights from pretrained Transformers provides an appealing shortcut, yet the fundamental representational gap between Softmax and linear attention prevents effective weight transfer. In this work, we address this conversion challenge from two perspectives: architectural alignment and representational alignment. We identify Test-Time Training (TTT) as a linear-complexity architecture whose two-layer dynamic formulation is structurally aligned with Softmax attention, enabling direct inheritance of pretrained attention weights. To further align representational properties, including key shift-invariance and locality, we introduce key instance normalization and a lightweight locality enhancement module. We validate our approach by linearizing Stable Diffusion 3.5 and introduce SD3.5-T$^5$ (Transformer To Test Time Training). With only 1 hour of fine-tuning on 4$\times$H20 GPUs, SD3.5-T$^5$ achieves comparable text-to-image quality to the fine-tuned Softmax model, while accelerating inference by 1.32$\times$ and 1.47$\times$ at 1K and 2K resolutions. Code is available at this URL: https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/Transformer-to-TTT.

paragraphs: Linear-complexity attention offers a route around the quadratic cost of Softmax attention, but training a replacement model from scratch is expensive. Reusing pretrained weights is attractive, yet differences in representation can make direct conversion ineffective. This paper tackles conversion by aligning both the architecture and its representational behavior.

The authors identify a two-layer dynamic Test-Time Training formulation whose structure permits direct inheritance of pretrained attention weights. They then add key instance normalization and a lightweight locality module to address shift-invariance and locality properties. The approach therefore combines a compatible computational structure with targeted corrections to how the converted model represents information.

They apply the method to Stable Diffusion 3.5, producing SD3.5-T⁵. After one hour of fine-tuning on four H20 GPUs, it achieves text-to-image quality comparable to the fine-tuned Softmax model. Reported inference accelerations are 1.32 times at 1K resolution and 1.47 times at 2K. This demonstrates a practical conversion route for the tested generator, using a short fine-tuning run to retain quality while reducing inference cost.
summary.tldr: A weight-compatible Test-Time Training architecture converts Stable Diffusion 3.5 to linear complexity with comparable quality and faster reported inference.

title: Linearizing Vision Transformer with Test-Time Training

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in reasoning and generation tasks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism introduces new security risks, making them particularly vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing approaches often rely on static CoT templates to elicit harmful outputs, but such fixed designs suffer from limited diversity, adaptability, and effectiveness. To overcome these limitations, we propose an adaptive evolutionary CoT jailbreak framework, called AE-CoT. Specifically, the method first rewrites harmful goals into mild prompts with teacher role-play and decomposes them into semantically coherent reasoning fragments to construct a pool of CoT jailbreak candidates. Then, within a structured representation space, we perform multi-generation evolutionary search, where candidate diversity is expanded through fragment-level crossover and a mutation strategy with an adaptive mutation-rate control mechanism. An independent scoring model provides graded harmfulness evaluations, and high-scoring candidates are further enhanced with a harmful CoT template to induce more destructive generations. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed AE-CoT, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art jailbreak methods.

paragraphs: This paper examines explicit reasoning as a security risk for large reasoning models. Existing chain-of-thought jailbreak methods often use fixed templates, which limits the variety of attacks they can express and their ability to adapt. The authors propose AE-CoT as a framework for exploring a more diverse set of reasoning-based attacks.

At a high level, the framework represents candidate attacks as combinations of coherent reasoning fragments. It evolves these candidates over multiple generations, using recombination and adaptively controlled mutation to broaden the search. A separate scoring model supplies graded evaluations of harmfulness, guiding which candidates receive further refinement. This makes the attack process responsive to evaluation signals rather than dependent on one static pattern.

Experiments across multiple models and datasets show AE-CoT consistently outperforming state-of-the-art jailbreak methods. The security implication is that evaluating a model against fixed reasoning templates can leave an important adaptive threat insufficiently explored. The findings identify the reasoning process itself as part of the attack surface and demonstrate the effectiveness of evolutionary search in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: AE-CoT uses adaptive evolutionary search over reasoning-based attacks and outperforms existing jailbreak methods across the evaluated models and datasets.

title: Reasoning as an Attack Surface: Adaptive Evolutionary CoT Jailbreaks for LLMs

abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) typically requires thousands of benchmark items, making the process expensive, slow, and increasingly impractical at scale. Existing evaluation protocols rely on average accuracy over fixed item sets, treating all items as equally informative despite substantial variation in difficulty and discrimination. We introduce ATLAS, an adaptive testing framework based on Item Response Theory (IRT) that estimates model ability using Fisher information–guided item selection. ATLAS reduces the number of required items by up to 90% while maintaining measurement precision. For instance, it matches whole-bank ability estimates using only 41 items (0.157 MAE) on HellaSwag (5,600 items). We further reconstruct accuracy from ATLAS’s ability estimates and find that reconstructed accuracies closely match raw accuracies across all five benchmarks, indicating that ability preserves the global performance structure. At the same time, provides finer discrimination within accuracy-equivalent models: among more than 3,000 evaluated models, 23–31% shift by more than 10 rank positions, and models with identical accuracies receive meaningfully different ability estimates. Code and calibrated item banks available at https://github.com/Peiyu-Georgia-Li/ATLAS.

paragraphs: ATLAS evaluates language models by choosing questions adaptively rather than administering an entire fixed benchmark. Its starting point is that questions differ in difficulty and in how effectively they distinguish models. An average accuracy score treats every answer equally, potentially spending evaluation effort on questions that add little information about a particular model.

The framework uses Item Response Theory to estimate model ability. It selects questions using Fisher information, a measure of how informative an observation is for estimating that ability. The reported results show reductions of up to 90% in required items while retaining measurement precision. On HellaSwag, 41 questions approximate ability estimates from a 5,600-item bank with a mean absolute error of 0.157.

Across five benchmarks, accuracies reconstructed from ability estimates closely track raw accuracy, suggesting that the shorter evaluations retain broad performance patterns. They also distinguish models that accuracy places together: among more than 3,000 models, 23–31% move over ten ranking positions. These changes reflect a different measurement of performance, incorporating which questions models answer successfully.
summary.tldr: ATLAS adaptively selects informative benchmark questions to estimate LLM ability with fewer evaluations and distinguish models with similar accuracy.

title: Adaptive Testing for LLM Evaluation: A Psychometric Alternative to Static Benchmarks

abstract: Symbolic Regression aims to discover interpretable mathematical expressions from data. Equation Learner (EQL) is a gradient-based method with strong fitting capability and expressive potential, yet it often activates redundant operators as model complexity grows, leading to over-complex expressions and unstable equation recovery. We analyze a gradient residual issue induced by operators that do not vanish at zero, which can prevent the ideal sparse expression from acting as a stable attractor during training and bias training toward unnecessarily complex structures, making exact recovery highly unreliable in practice. To address this, we propose EQL-Z, a structurally controllable symbolic regression framework. EQL-Z enforces zero-point constraints via zero-point consistent operator transformations to eliminate residual gradients on silent paths, and performs a small-to-large structure search that grows depth/width from a compact seed under a complexity-penalized validation score. After selecting a compact structure, we apply BFGS fine-tuning to refine coefficients. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that EQL-Z substantially improves exact equation recovery and in-/out-of-distribution generalization over vanilla EQL, achieving performance close to leading symbolic regression baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/Caaaa-a/EQL-Z.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression seeks readable mathematical formulas that explain data. Equation Learner models can fit complex relationships, but increasing their size can activate unnecessary operators and make exact formula recovery unstable. This paper identifies a source of that problem: operators whose output is nonzero at zero can leave residual gradients on paths intended to remain inactive.

EQL-Z changes the operators to satisfy zero-point consistency, removing those residual gradients on silent paths. It also searches for structure gradually, expanding depth and width from a compact starting model. A validation score that penalizes complexity guides selection, after which BFGS fine-tuning refines the coefficients of the chosen expression.

These steps address both why redundant structure becomes active and how much structure the model is allowed to retain. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report substantial improvements over vanilla EQL in exact equation recovery and generalization within and beyond the training distribution. Performance approaches leading symbolic regression baselines. The findings support combining training stability with explicit structural control when the goal is recovering a concise equation.
summary.tldr: EQL-Z combines zero-point-consistent operators and gradual structure search to recover simpler equations more reliably.

title: Stabilizing Equation Learning via Zero-Point Constraints

abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong performance across multi-modal tasks but remain vulnerable to universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs). Existing UAP methods mainly operate on the visual modality, overlooking structured textual semantics and cross-modal interactions, which limits their ability to disrupt alignment and generalize across tasks and model architectures. To address these limits, we propose Multi-modal Attention Distraction Adversarial Attack (MADA-Attack) framework. We begin by conducting several insight experiments and discover that modality attention distributes differently over layers and early phase of optimization is decisive. Building on these observations, we introduce Semantic Token Manipulation (STM) to steer text-guided attention, and Fused Embedding Training (FET) to jointly optimize textual and visual embedding losses for coordinated misalignment. We further incorporate an Adaptive Data Augmentation (ADA) strategy that dynamically balances attack strength, transferability, and training efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MADA-Attack consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance and strong transferability while remaining computationally lightweight, with an average ASR of 82.60% and 73.42% in zero-shot classification and image captioning tasks. For the visual question answering (VQA) and I-T Retrieval task, our method exceeds the SOTA baseline by 10%. Our code is available at this GitHub Repository.

title: MADA-Attack: Transferable Multi-modal Attention Distraction Adversarial Attack against Vision Language Models

abstract: Scientific reasoning inherently demands integrating sophisticated toolkits to navigate domain-specific knowledge. Yet, current benchmarks largely overlook agents’ ability to orchestrate tools for such rigorous workflows. To bridge this gap, we introduce SciAgentGym, a scalable interactive environment featuring 1,780 domain-specific tools across four natural science disciplines, supported by a robust execution infrastructure. Complementing this, we present SciAgentBench, a tiered evaluation suite designed to stress-test agentic capabilities from elementary actions to long-horizon workflows. Our evaluation identifies a critical bottleneck: state-of-the-art models still struggle with complex scientific tool-use, and their performance degrades substantially as interaction horizons extend. To address this, we propose SciForge, a data synthesis method that models the tool action space as a dependency graph to generate logic-aware training trajectories. By fine-tuning on these trajectories, our SciAgent-8B outperforms the significantly larger Qwen3-VL-235B-Instruct while exhibiting positive cross-domain transfer of scientific tool-use capabilities. These results underscore the promising potential of next-generation autonomous scientific agents.

SciAgentGym provides an interactive execution environment with 1,780 domain-specific tools across four natural science disciplines. Its companion evaluation suite, SciAgentBench, ranges from elementary actions to long workflows, allowing evaluation at different levels of coordination difficulty.

summary.tldr: SciAgentGym exposes difficulties in long scientific tool workflows, while dependency-aware synthetic training improves an 8B agent's performance.

title: SciAgentGym: Benchmarking Multi-Step Scientific Tool-Use in LLM Agents

abstract: Message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) often suffer from an information bottleneck when capturing long-range dependencies, leading to the oversquashing (OSQ) phenomenon. Alongside spatial connectivity enrichment (e.g., rewiring), recent studies have shown that spectral filtering can yield strong long-range learning outcomes, as spectral operators enable global information mixing that alleviates OSQ. These approaches achieve this either by stabilizing the Jacobian energies in deep propagation or by guaranteeing OSQ mitigation under strong theoretical assumptions. We examine the practical attainability of these guarantees and show that the associated Jacobian sensitivity lower bound is generally difficult to achieve in practice. We then propose S$^3$GNN, which mitigates OSQ without such restrictive assumptions by lightweightly reintroducing omitted components with substantially lower computational complexity, while standard stability constraints on feature transformations remain effective under our new dynamics. Extensive experiments across diverse domains (e.g., long-range benchmarks, KGQA, and mesh-based fluid dynamics) demonstrate that S$^3$GNN achieves up to an order-of-magnitude error reduction with up to 50% fewer parameters. Our code can be found in https://github.com/EEthanShi/S3-GNN.git.

These approaches achieve this either by stabilizing the Jacobian energies in deep propagation or by guaranteeing OSQ mitigation under strong theoretical assumptions. We examine the practical attainability of these guarantees and show that the associated Jacobian sensitivity lower bound is generally difficult to achieve in practice. paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle to transmit information between distant nodes because many signals become compressed through limited message-passing channels. This is known as oversquashing. Spectral methods can help by mixing information globally, but some existing theoretical guarantees rely on strong assumptions about how influence propagates through the network.

The paper examines whether those guarantees are practically attainable and finds that the associated lower bound on Jacobian sensitivity is generally difficult to achieve. S³GNN then combines global mixing and local message passing while lightly restoring components omitted by earlier approaches. The proposed dynamics mitigate oversquashing without those restrictive assumptions and retain the effectiveness of standard stability constraints on feature transformations.

Experiments cover long-range graph benchmarks, knowledge-graph question answering, and mesh-based fluid dynamics. The authors report error reductions of up to an order of magnitude with up to 50% fewer parameters. These are maximum reported gains across the evaluated settings, supporting the approach’s potential to improve distant information exchange while using a smaller model.
summary.tldr: S³GNN improves long-range graph learning through efficient global mixing and local message passing without the restrictive assumptions of earlier guarantees.

title: S$^3$GNN: Efficient Global Mixing and Local Message Passing for Long-Range Graph Learning

abstract: Monocular 3D human pose estimation is fundamentally challenged by severe occlusion and inherent depth ambiguity. To address this, we propose Glimpse, a framework that learns robust 3D poses by explicitly modeling anatomical geometry from a single image. We recast the problem as geometry learning of multi-scale structural priors, realized through two synergistic components. First, structured sampling captures the body’s geometric continuity through dual-level feature extraction, acquiring both local joint appearance and continuous features along skeletal limbs via deformable sampling. By propagating limb-level geometric cues to their connected joints, this design bridges information gaps caused by occlusion. Second, geometric correction ensures global 3D consistency by lifting coherent 2D features into a canonical 3D reference space, where a shared 3D anchor guides a distance-aware fusion mechanism. Extensive experiments conducted on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP demonstrate that Glimpse achieves state-of-the-art performance, with superior robustness under severe occlusion and complex articulation.

paragraphs: Estimating a person’s three-dimensional pose from one image becomes difficult when joints are hidden and depth is ambiguous. Glimpse addresses these problems by explicitly learning anatomical geometry at multiple scales. Its central idea is to combine evidence around individual joints with continuous information along the limbs connecting them.

The first component uses structured, deformable sampling to collect both kinds of features. Limb information is then passed to connected joints, helping bridge gaps created by occlusion. The second component promotes consistency across the full body: it lifts coherent two-dimensional features into a canonical three-dimensional reference space, where a shared anchor guides fusion according to distance.

The two components connect local visual evidence with a common geometric reference. Experiments on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP report state-of-the-art performance, including stronger robustness when occlusion is severe or body articulation is complex. These findings support using continuous limb geometry and global spatial correction together to improve pose estimates when individual joints provide incomplete evidence.
summary.tldr: Glimpse combines joint and limb features with a shared three-dimensional reference to improve single-image pose estimation under occlusion and complex articulation.

title: Glimpse: Geometry Learning of Multi-scale Structural Priors for 3D Pose Estimation

abstract: Personalized federated LoRA fine tuning has become a key approach to addressing data heterogeneity in distributed fine tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing methods typically assume homogeneous personalization needs across clients, relying on dual LoRA or personalized calibration schemes. However, they fail to account for the heterogeneity of local personalization requirements and the conflicting optimization objectives in dual LoRA, limiting scalability and performance. To address this, we propose Het-CPFLoRA, a customizable heterogeneous federated LoRA fine tuning algorithm inspired by the decoupling properties of LoRA parameters. We employ a single adapter fine tuning scheme to mitigate conflicts between personalized and generalized optimization, decouple LoRA into generalized and personalized subspaces for local customization, and use SVD compression to integrate cross client generalized knowledge. During inference, we introduce an OOD oriented dynamic mechanism to adjust the weighting between personalized and generalized decoupling knowledge, improving performance on user data. Extensive experiments on two public benchmark datasets show that Het-CPFLoRA outperforms state of the art methods in both personalization and generalization across heterogeneous scenarios. The code will be released as an open-source project.

paragraphs: Federated language-model fine-tuning must balance knowledge shared across clients with adaptation to each client’s data. The paper argues that existing personalized LoRA approaches overlook differences in how much personalization individual clients need. Dual-adapter approaches can also introduce conflicting optimization objectives. Het-CPFLoRA addresses both issues through a customizable single-adapter design.

The algorithm separates LoRA parameters into generalized and personalized subspaces, allowing local customization while retaining a channel for shared knowledge. It uses singular value decomposition compression to integrate generalized information across clients. At inference time, a mechanism oriented toward out-of-distribution inputs dynamically adjusts the balance between personalized and generalized knowledge, making their relative contribution responsive to incoming user data.

Experiments on two public benchmark datasets show better personalization and generalization than the compared state-of-the-art methods across heterogeneous scenarios. The results support handling client differences within the adaptation structure and during inference. The contribution combines local flexibility, cross-client knowledge integration, and input-dependent weighting within one federated fine-tuning approach.
summary.tldr: Het-CPFLoRA customizes federated LoRA adaptation by separating shared and personal knowledge and adjusting their balance during inference.

title: Heterogeneous Customizable Personalized Federated Fine-Tuning Approach for Large Language Models

abstract: Designing high-performance neural networks for new tasks requires balancing optimization quality with search efficiency. Current methods fail to achieve this balance: neural architectural search is computationally expensive, while model retrieval often yields suboptimal static checkpoints. To resolve this dilemma, we model the performance gains induced by fine-grained architectural modifications as edit-effect evidence and build evidence graphs from prior tasks. By constructing a retrieval-augmented model refinement framework, our proposed M-DESIGN dynamically weaves historical evidence to discover near-optimal modification paths. M-DESIGN features an adaptive retrieval mechanism that quickly calibrates the evolving transferability of edit-effect evidence from different sources. To handle out-of-distribution shifts, we introduce predictive task planners that extrapolate gains from multi-hop evidence, thereby reducing reliance on an exhaustive repository. Based on our model knowledge base of 67,760 graph neural networks across 22 datasets, extensive experiments demonstrate that M-DESIGN consistently outperforms baselines, achieving the search-space best performance in 26 out of 33 cases under a strict budget.

paragraphs: M-DESIGN tackles the cost of designing a neural network for a new task. Searching many architectures is expensive, while retrieving an existing model can leave useful improvements unexplored. The paper instead treats previous architectural edits and their measured performance effects as reusable evidence about how to improve a model.

The framework organizes this evidence into graphs and retrieves it while constructing sequences of fine-grained modifications. Its adaptive retrieval mechanism reassesses how well evidence from different source tasks transfers as refinement proceeds. For tasks outside the familiar distribution, predictive planners connect evidence across multiple steps to estimate potential gains. This reduces dependence on a repository already containing every useful design.

The evaluation uses a knowledge base containing 67,760 graph neural networks across 22 datasets. Under a strict search budget, M-DESIGN consistently beats the tested baselines and reaches the best performance available within the search space in 26 of 33 cases. The result supports reusing knowledge about architectural changes, beyond simply reusing completed models.
summary.tldr: M-DESIGN reuses evidence about architectural edits to guide efficient network refinement, reaching search-space best performance in 26 of 33 cases.

title: Beyond Model Base Retrieval: Weaving Knowledge to Master Fine-grained Neural Network Design

abstract: This work proposes a framework LGKDE that learns kernel density estimation for graphs. The key challenge in graph density estimation lies in effectively capturing both structural patterns and semantic variations while maintaining theoretical guarantees. Combining graph kernels and kernel density estimation (KDE) is a standard approach to graph density estimation, but has unsatisfactory performance due to the handcrafted and fixed features of kernels. Our method LGKDE leverages graph neural networks to represent each graph as a discrete distribution and utilizes maximum mean discrepancy to learn the graph metric for multi-scale KDE, where all parameters are learned by maximizing the density of graphs relative to the density of their well-designed perturbed counterparts. The perturbations are conducted on both node features and graph spectra, which helps better characterize the boundary of normal density regions. Theoretically, we establish consistency and convergence guarantees for LGKDE, including bounds on the mean integrated squared error, robustness, and generalization. We validate LGKDE by demonstrating its effectiveness in recovering the underlying density of synthetic graph distributions and applying it to graph anomaly detection across diverse benchmark datasets. Extensive empirical evaluation shows that LGKDE demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on most benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Estimating graph density means characterizing which graphs are typical while accounting for both their structure and their semantic features. Conventional combinations of graph kernels and kernel density estimation use fixed, handcrafted features that can limit performance. LGKDE instead learns how graphs should be represented and compared for density estimation.

A graph neural network represents each graph as a discrete distribution. Maximum mean discrepancy supplies the basis for learning a graph metric used in density estimation at multiple scales. Training favors higher density for original graphs relative to deliberately perturbed counterparts. Perturbations affect node features and graph spectra, helping define the boundary around regions of normal data.

summary.tldr: LGKDE learns graph representations and similarity measures for density estimation, combining theoretical guarantees with strong graph anomaly detection results.

title: Learnable Kernel Density Estimation for Graphs and Its Application to Graph-Level Anomaly Detection

abstract: Expressivity has been a major focus in the design of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), yet a significant gap persists between theoretical universal expressivity and practical performance. While many expressive GNNs are efficient and achieve strong results, they often focus on specific graph properties and lack theoretical expressivity for general graph tasks. Conversely, theoretically universal-expressive models often suffer from high computational costs or poor generalization, limiting their real-world applicability. To bridge this gap, we introduce Equivariant Noise GNNs (ENGNNs), a framework that utilizes random noise features to enhance the expressivity of GNNs. Crucially, unlike prior methods that naively use noise, we enforce equivariance to nodewise noise transformations, such as orthogonal transformations. We prove that this property reduces the model’s theoretical sample complexity, thereby improving generalization. Our framework simultaneously reaches theoretical universal expressivity, maintains the linear scalability of standard Message-Passing Neural Networks in practice, and achieves performance comparable to computationally expensive, high-expressivity models. Extensive experiments confirm strong performance across node, link, subgraph, and graph-level prediction tasks, demonstrating that the equivariant use of noise provides a powerful and practical pathway for building expressive GNNs. Our code is available at https://github.com/MuLabPKU/EquivNoiseGNN.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks face a tension between theoretical expressivity and practical performance. Some efficient models capture particular graph properties well but lack general expressivity guarantees. Models with universal expressivity can instead be expensive or generalize poorly. This paper introduces Equivariant Noise GNNs to bring these capabilities together within a practical framework.

ENGNNs add random noise features while enforcing a structured response to transformations of that noise, including nodewise orthogonal transformations. This equivariance makes the treatment of randomness part of the architecture’s design. The authors prove that the property reduces theoretical sample complexity, providing a reason that noise can improve expressivity without imposing the same generalization burden as less structured uses.

The framework achieves theoretical universal expressivity and retains the practical linear scalability of standard message-passing networks. Experiments cover prediction at the node, link, subgraph, and whole-graph levels, with performance comparable to more computationally expensive expressive models. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical generalization result with a broadly evaluated design for using randomness efficiently in graph learning.
summary.tldr: ENGNNs use noise equivariantly to combine universal graph expressivity, reduced theoretical sample complexity, and practical message-passing scalability.

title: Expressive Graph Neural Networks via Equivariant Use of Noise

abstract: Recurring Pattern Bugs (RPBs) are defined as bugs where a single root cause appears repeatedly across multiple code segments. These bugs remain a persistent security threat even after individual instances are patched. Various static analyzers exist for finding specific bug patterns but require significant engineering effort and fail to generalize well beyond their predefined template, preventing them from detecting RPBs. To tackle RPBs, we introduce BugStone, a hybrid framework combining LLVM-based program analysis with Large Language Models to automate RPB detection. BugStone leverages a single patched instance to synthesize abstract error patterns and retrieves semantically similar bugs throughout the codebase. To evaluate BugStone, we create a ground truth dataset by analyzing over 1.9K security bugs reports, on which BugStone achieves 92.2% precision and 79.1% pairwise accuracy. We further validated BugStone through a large-scale real-world deployment. In the Linux kernel, BugStone identified over 22K potential issues; a manual audit of 400 samples confirmed 246 valid bugs, including invalid pointer dereferences, resource leaks, type errors, performance issues, and others. To evaluate the generalizability of BugStone, we further applied it to the top 100 Python projects, discovering multiple critical command injection vulnerabilities.

This paper calls these recurring pattern bugs and introduces BugStone to search for them from a single patched example. The approach targets a weakness of predefined static-analysis templates: adapting them to new patterns requires substantial engineering.

Applying the method to the top 100 Python projects also finds multiple critical command-injection vulnerabilities, providing evidence of applicability beyond the kernel deployment.
summary.tldr: BugStone combines program analysis and language models to turn one patched bug into a search for recurring instances across codebases.

title: One Bug, Hundreds Behind: LLMs for Large-Scale Bug Discovery

abstract: Recent progress has expanded the use of large language models (LLMs) in drug discovery, including synthesis planning. However, objective evaluation of retrosynthesis performance remains limited. Existing benchmarks and metrics typically rely on published synthetic procedures and Top-K accuracy based on single ground-truth, which does not capture the open-ended nature of real-world synthesis planning. We propose a new benchmarking framework for single-step retrosynthesis that evaluates both general-purpose and chemistry-specialized LLMs using ChemCensor, a novel metric for chemical plausibility. By emphasizing plausibility over exact match, this approach better aligns with human synthesis planning practices. We also introduce CREED, a novel dataset comprising millions of ChemCensor-validated reaction records for LLM training, and use it to train a model that improves over the LLM baselines under this benchmark.

paragraphs: Single-step retrosynthesis asks for a possible preceding reaction that could produce a target molecule. Existing benchmarks commonly compare predictions with one published answer using Top-K accuracy. The paper argues that this misses the open-ended nature of synthesis planning, where a chemically plausible proposal may differ from the recorded procedure.

The proposed benchmark evaluates general-purpose and chemistry-specialized language models with ChemCensor, a metric focused on chemical plausibility. This changes what counts as a useful prediction by emphasizing whether a proposed reaction is plausible rather than whether it exactly reproduces a single reference. The aim is to better reflect how people assess possible synthesis plans.

The authors also introduce CREED, a training dataset containing millions of reaction records validated with ChemCensor. A model trained on this resource improves over the language-model baselines under the proposed benchmark. The work therefore links a revised evaluation criterion to a corresponding training resource, with the reported improvement specifically measured through this plausibility-oriented framework.
summary.tldr: ChemCensor evaluates retrosynthesis by chemical plausibility, while the CREED dataset supports training a model that improves under this new benchmark.

title: When Single Answer Is Not Enough: Rethinking Single-Step Retrosynthesis Benchmarks for LLMs

abstract: Block-wise decoding effectively improves the inference speed and quality in diffusion language models (DLMs) by combining inter-block sequential denoising and intra-block parallel unmasking. However, existing block-wise decoding methods typically partition blocks in a rigid and fixed manner, which inevitably fragments complete semantic or syntactic constituents, leading to suboptimal performance. Inspired by the entropy reduction hypothesis (ERH), we recognize that constituent boundaries offer greater opportunities for uncertainty reduction, which motivates us to employ entropy analysis for identifying constituent boundaries. Therefore, we propose Swordsman, an entropy-driven adaptive block-wise decoding framework for DLMs. Swordsman adaptively partitions blocks by identifying entropy shifts between adjacent tokens to better align with semantic or syntactic constituent boundaries. In addition, Swordsman dynamically adjusts unmasking thresholds conditioned on the real-time unmasking status within a block, further improving both efficiency and stability. As a training-free framework, supported by KV Cache, Swordsman demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across extensive evaluations. Our code is now available.

paragraphs: Block-wise decoding lets diffusion language models process blocks sequentially while revealing tokens within each block in parallel. Fixed block boundaries can split meaningful semantic or syntactic units, making the partition poorly matched to the text. Swordsman adapts those boundaries using changes in the model’s uncertainty between adjacent tokens.

The approach draws on the entropy reduction hypothesis, which motivates looking for constituent boundaries through opportunities for uncertainty reduction. Swordsman uses entropy shifts to identify boundaries that better follow the structure of the emerging sequence. It also changes unmasking thresholds according to the current state of each block, so decisions about revealing tokens can respond as generation proceeds.

These two adaptations address where blocks are placed and how tokens are resolved inside them. The framework requires no additional training and supports KV caching. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across extensive evaluations, with improvements in efficiency and stability. The findings support using uncertainty as a practical signal for organizing diffusion decoding, while the proposed boundaries are intended to align better with constituents rather than guarantee perfect linguistic segmentation.
summary.tldr: Swordsman uses entropy shifts and adaptive unmasking thresholds to improve diffusion language model decoding without additional training.

title: Swordsman: Entropy-Driven Adaptive Block Partition for Efficient Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown strong decision-making capabilities in autonomous driving. However, existing VLAs often struggle with achieving efficient inference and generalizing to novel autonomous vehicle configurations and driving scenarios. In this paper, we propose Reasoning-VLA, a general and efficient action-generation VLA framework. The proposed model employs a set of learnable action queries, implicitly guided by predefined spatial representations to enhance spatial awareness. These learnable queries interact with reasoning-enhanced vision–language features to generate continuous action trajectories in parallel. To promote robust generalization, we consolidate eight publicly available autonomous driving datasets into a standardized, Chain-of-Thought reasoning–based, and easy-to-use data format for model training. Leveraging both supervised learning and reinforcement learning fine-tuning, extensive empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Reasoning-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, strong generalization capability, and the excellent inference speed with parallel decode.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models can make driving decisions, but efficient inference and transfer to unfamiliar vehicle configurations or scenarios remain challenges. Reasoning-VLA addresses both through an action-generation framework that combines spatial guidance, reasoning-enhanced visual and language features, and parallel trajectory generation. Its design connects how actions are represented with how quickly they can be produced.

The model uses learnable action queries that are implicitly guided by predefined spatial representations. Those queries interact with reasoning-enhanced features to generate continuous action trajectories in parallel. For training, the authors also standardize eight public driving datasets into a shared format incorporating chain-of-thought reasoning, providing a consolidated source of driving experience.

Training combines supervised learning with reinforcement learning fine-tuning. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, strong generalization, and fast inference using parallel decoding. These empirical findings support the combination of spatially informed action queries and standardized reasoning-based data. The contribution addresses driving quality and inference efficiency together, rather than treating the representation of future actions as independent of runtime performance.
summary.tldr: Reasoning-VLA uses spatially guided action queries and parallel decoding to improve autonomous-driving performance, generalization, and inference speed.

title: Reasoning-VLA: An Efficient and Spatial-Guided General Vision-Language-Action Reasoning Model for Autonomous Driving

abstract: Graph class-incremental learning (GCIL) has emerged to address the challenge of learning from dynamically evolving graphs, which continuously learns new classes over a sequence of tasks while retaining performance on previously seen classes. However, existing GCIL methods assume a closed-set test distribution drawn only from seen tasks. This fundamentally contradicts real-world open-ended scenarios where future unknown classes inevitably emerge. Empirically, we observe that existing GCIL methods falter in such open-set settings due to severe representation drift and generalized overconfidence. To bridge this gap, we investigate the Open-Set GCIL problem and propose SAFER (Subspace-Aware FEature Reshaping), a novel framework that endows GCIL with intrinsic open-set capabilities under a replay-free constraint. Specifically, SAFER performs subspace-aware feature reshaping with drift-free fingerprints, unifying task routing and open-set rejection into a single energy-based metric. Furthermore, we introduce a geometric space-consistency regularization that explicitly improves intra-class compactness and suppresses cross-task representation drift. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that SAFER outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by margins of up to 5.2% in accuracy and 31.3% in open-set AUROC, all while maintaining near-zero forgetting under strict no-replay constraints.
