Empirically, we observe that existing GCIL methods falter in such open-set settings due to severe representation drift and generalized overconfidence. To bridge this gap, we investigate the Open-Set GCIL problem and propose SAFER (Subspace-Aware FEature Reshaping), a novel framework that endows GCIL with intrinsic open-set capabilities under a replay-free constraint. Specifically, SAFER performs subspace-aware feature reshaping with drift-free fingerprints, unifying task routing and open-set rejection into a single energy-based metric. Furthermore, we introduce a geometric space-consistency regularization that explicitly improves intra-class compactness and suppresses cross-task representation drift. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that SAFER outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by margins of up to 5.2% in accuracy and 31.3% in open-set AUROC, all while maintaining near-zero forgetting under strict no-replay constraints.

paragraphs: Graph class-incremental learning adds new classes over successive tasks while trying to retain older knowledge. Existing methods commonly assume that test examples belong to classes already encountered. This paper studies the more open-ended case in which unknown classes also appear, finding that existing approaches suffer from shifting representations and excessive confidence in these settings.

SAFER addresses the problem without replaying past data. It reshapes features using subspace information and drift-free fingerprints, then uses one energy-based metric for both task routing and rejection of unknown classes. A geometric consistency regularizer also makes same-class representations more compact and suppresses representation changes across tasks. These components connect retaining old knowledge with recognizing unfamiliar inputs.

On four benchmarks, SAFER improves over state-of-the-art baselines by margins reaching 5.2% in accuracy and 31.3% in open-set AUROC. It also maintains near-zero forgetting under strict no-replay constraints. The reported maxima describe observed improvements, while the broader finding is that open-set recognition and incremental retention can be addressed within a shared representation framework.
summary.tldr: SAFER reshapes graph representations to recognize unknown classes and retain previous knowledge without replaying past data.

title: Subspace-Aware Feature Reshaping for Open-Set Graph Class-Incremental Learning

abstract: Multi-objective optimization (MOO) has emerged as a powerful approach to solving complex optimization problems involving multiple objectives. In many practical scenarios, function evaluations are unavailable or prohibitively expensive, necessitating optimization solely based on a fixed offline dataset. In this setting, known as offline MOO, the goal is to find out the Pareto set without access to the true objective functions. This setting suffers from the out-of-distribution (OOD) issue, where the surrogate model is not accurate for unseen designs. Due to the OOD issue, surrogate errors may cause the optimizer to select solutions that do not lie on the true Pareto front and are biased toward its extremes. To address this, this paper proposes Diversity-driven Offline Multi-Objective Optimization (DOMOO), which aims to find out a diverse and high-quality set of solutions. First, DOMOO incorporates an accumulative risk control module that estimates the potential risk of candidate solutions and alleviates the OOD issue between the training data and the generated solutions. In addition, a nested Pareto set learning (PSL) strategy is proposed to jointly learn preference and PSL parameters, then optimize them, enabling adaptation to diverse Pareto front geometries. To further enhance solution quality, we design a diversity-driven selection strategy that extracts a representative and well-distributed set of final solutions. To achieve this diversity-driven selection strategy, we propose $\text{IGD}_\text{offline}$, a tailored indicator for the offline setting that considers both diversity and convergence, and avoids the bias of hypervolume indicator. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that DOMOO achieves the best average rank across tasks in both convergence and diversity among the compared methods.

summary.tldr: DOMOO combines risk control, adaptive Pareto-set learning, and diversity-aware selection to improve offline multi-objective optimization.

title: Diversity-Driven Offline Multi-Objective Optimization via Nested Pareto Set Learning

abstract: The accelerated development, deployment and adoption of artificial intelligence systems has been fuelled by the increasing presence of big tech in the AI field. This trend has been accompanied by growing ethical concerns and intensified societal and environmental impacts. This position paper argues that irresponsible AI development is strongly driven by big tech’s influence and involvement in the field. First, we examine the growing and disproportionate influence of big tech in AI research and argue that its drive for scaling and general-purpose systems is fundamentally at odds with the responsible, ethical, and sustainable development of AI. Second, we review key current environmental and societal negative impacts of AI and trace their connections to big tech’s influence. Third, we discuss the underlying economic forces driving big tech’s actions. Finally, as a call to action, we invite AI researchers to counter big tech’s influence in irresponsible AI development through strategies that build on the responsibility of implicated actors and collective action.

This framing directs attention to the incentives and influence shaping technical agendas, making responsibility a question about the actors and structures driving development as well as the systems produced.
summary.tldr: The authors connect big tech’s research influence and economic incentives to AI harms and call for collective action by researchers.

abstract: We present a new method for automatically creating useful temporal abstractions in reinforcement learning. We argue that states that allow the agent to transition to a different region of the state space are useful subgoals, and propose a method for identifying them using the concept of relative novelty. When such a state is identified, a temporally-extended activity (e.g., an option) is generated that takes the agent efficiently to this state. We illustrate the utility of the method in a number of tasks.

paragraphs: The paper proposes automatically constructing extended activities for a reinforcement learning agent. It focuses on identifying useful destinations for those activities: states that allow movement into another region of the state space. The authors argue that such transition states make useful subgoals because reaching them gives the agent access to a different part of its environment.

The proposed method uses relative novelty to identify these states. Once it identifies a suitable state, it creates a temporally extended activity, such as an option, that efficiently takes the agent there. The process therefore links subgoal discovery to action construction: finding a promising transition point leads directly to learning a way to reach it.

The authors illustrate the method's utility across several tasks. The stated contribution is a mechanism for choosing subgoals and turning them into useful temporal abstractions. Its significance lies in organizing behavior around access to different state-space regions. The abstract reports demonstrations of usefulness, while presenting the value of these transition states as the motivating argument for the design.
summary.tldr: Relative novelty identifies states connecting different regions, which become subgoals for automatically generated extended actions.

title: Using relative novelty to identify useful temporal abstractions in reinforcement learning

abstract: We present new, general-purpose kernels for protein structure analysis, and describe how to apply them to structural motif discovery and function classification. Experiments show that our new methods are faster than conventional techniques, are capable of finding structural motifs, and are very effective in function classification. In addition to strong cross-validation results, we found possible new oxidoreductases and cytochrome P450 reductases and a possible new structural motif in cytochrome P450 reductases.

paragraphs: The paper introduces general-purpose kernels for analyzing protein structure. It develops applications to two related questions: identifying structural motifs and classifying protein function. Motif discovery concerns recurring structural patterns, while function classification uses structural information to help assign functional categories. The proposed kernels provide a common basis for addressing both tasks.

Experiments show that the methods run faster than conventional techniques, can find structural motifs, and are effective at classifying function. The abstract also reports strong cross-validation results. These findings support the methods as computational tools for extracting useful information from protein structures, combining practical speed with evidence of classification and motif-discovery capability.

The analysis identifies possible new oxidoreductases and cytochrome P450 reductases, together with a possible new structural motif in cytochrome P450 reductases. These are presented as candidate discoveries, so the biological interpretation remains tentative. Their significance is that the same methods used for classification also generate specific possibilities for further investigation of protein function and structure.
summary.tldr: New protein-structure kernels improve computational analysis and identify possible functional assignments and a possible structural motif.

title: New kernels for protein structural motif discovery and function classification

abstract: Many collective labeling tasks require inference on graphical models where the clique potentials depend only on the number of nodes that get a particular label. We design efficient inference algorithms for various families of such potentials. Our algorithms are exact for arbitrary cardinality-based clique potentials on binary labels and for max-like and majority-like clique potentials on multiple labels. Moving towards more complex potentials, we show that inference becomes NPhard even on cliques with homogeneous Potts potentials. We present a 13 15 -approximation algorithm with runtime sub-quadratic in the clique size. In contrast, the best known previous guarantee for graphs with Potts potentials is only 0.5. We perform empirical comparisons on real and synthetic data, and show that our proposed methods are an order of magnitude faster than the well-known Tree-based re-parameterization (TRW) and graph-cut algorithms.

paragraphs: In some collective labeling problems, a group’s score depends on how many members receive a particular label. The paper exploits this count-based structure to design efficient inference algorithms for graphical models. The central question is which forms of group scoring permit exact solutions and which require approximation.

The authors give exact algorithms for arbitrary cardinality-based clique potentials with binary labels. For multiple labels, exactness is established for max-like and majority-like potentials. The distinction matters because efficient exact inference is tied to the particular family of potentials. The paper also proves that inference becomes NP-hard even for cliques with homogeneous Potts potentials.

For the harder setting, the authors provide a 13/15 approximation guarantee with runtime growing less than quadratically in clique size. They contrast this with a previously known guarantee of 0.5 for graphs with Potts potentials. Experiments on real and synthetic data show their methods running an order of magnitude faster than tree-based reparameterization and graph-cut algorithms. The contribution combines exact methods, a hardness boundary, and a stronger approximation result.
summary.tldr: Count-based clique structure enables efficient exact inference for several potential families and a strong approximation for a harder Potts setting.

title: Efficient inference with cardinality-based clique potentials

abstract: The inhomogeneous Poisson process is a point process that has varying intensity across its domain (usually time or space). For nonparametric Bayesian modeling, the Gaussian process is a useful way to place a prior distribution on this intensity. The combination of an Poisson process and GP is known as a Gaussian Cox process, or doubly-stochastic Poisson process. Likelihood-based inference in these models requires an intractable integral over an infinite-dimensional random function. In this paper we present the first approach to Gaussian Cox processes in which it is possible to perform inference without introducing approximations or finite-dimensional proxy distributions. We call our method the Sigmoidal Gaussian Cox Process, which uses a generative model for Poisson data to enable tractable inference via Markov chain Monte Carlo. We compare our methods to competing methods on synthetic data and also apply it to several real-world data sets.

paragraphs: An inhomogeneous Poisson process models events whose intensity varies across time or space. Placing a Gaussian-process prior on that intensity yields a Gaussian Cox process, allowing Bayesian modeling of an unknown intensity function. The difficulty is computational: likelihood-based inference involves an intractable integral over an infinite-dimensional random function.

The paper introduces the Sigmoidal Gaussian Cox Process. Its generative formulation for Poisson data enables tractable inference through Markov chain Monte Carlo. The authors present it as the first approach to Gaussian Cox processes that supports inference without introducing approximations or replacing the function distribution with a finite-dimensional proxy.

This distinction concerns the model and inference construction: it avoids the approximations described in the abstract while still using a sampling-based inference method. The authors compare the approach with competing methods on synthetic data and apply it to several real-world datasets. The contribution makes this flexible class of event-intensity models computationally accessible through a generative construction designed around the inference obstacle.
summary.tldr: The Sigmoidal Gaussian Cox Process enables tractable MCMC inference without the model approximations or finite-dimensional proxies described in the abstract.

title: Tractable nonparametric Bayesian inference in Poisson processes with Gaussian process intensities

abstract: We consider the problem of selecting a subset of $m$ most informative features where $m$ is the number of required features. This feature selection problem is essentially a combinatorial optimization problem, and is usually solved by an approximation. Conventional feature selection methods address the computational challenge in two steps: (a) ranking all the features by certain scores that are usually computed independently from the number of specified features $m$, and (b) selecting the top $m$ ranked features. One major shortcoming of these approaches is that if a feature $f$ is chosen when the number of specified features is $m$, it will always be chosen when the number of specified features is larger than $m$. We refer to this property as the ``{\em monotonic}'' property of feature selection. In this work, we argue that it is important to develop efficient algorithms for non-monotonic feature selection. To this end, we develop an algorithm for non-monotonic feature selection that approximates the related combinatorial optimization problem by a Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) problem. We also present a strategy that derives a discrete solution from the approximate solution of MKL, and show the performance guarantee for the derived discrete solution when compared to the global optimal solution for the related combinatorial optimization problem. An empirical study with a number of benchmark data sets indicates the promising performance of the proposed framework compared with several state-of-the-art approaches for feature selection.

paragraphs: The supplied title names a prototype vector machine, but the supplied abstract describes non-monotonic feature selection. The explanation here follows that abstract. It addresses choosing a requested number of informative features without requiring every larger selection to retain all features chosen for a smaller one.

Conventional ranking-based selection produces that retention property because it uses one feature ordering for different subset sizes. The described method instead approximates a combinatorial selection problem through Multiple Kernel Learning. A further procedure converts the approximate solution into a discrete feature subset, connecting the tractable optimization formulation back to the requested selection task.

Benchmark experiments also indicate promising performance against several state-of-the-art feature-selection methods. The supported contribution is therefore a framework for revising feature choices as the requested subset size changes, backed by a theoretical guarantee and empirical comparisons; the supplied abstract does not describe a prototype-vector construction.
summary.tldr: Despite the title, the supplied abstract presents a Multiple Kernel Learning approach to non-monotonic feature selection.

title: Prototype vector machine for large scale semi-supervised learning

abstract: A system for musical accompaniment is presented in which a computer-driven orchestra follows and learns from a soloist in a concerto-like setting. The system is decomposed into three modules: the first computes a real-time score match using a hidden Markov model; the second generates the output audio by phase-vocoding a preexisting audio recording; the third provides a link between these two, by predicting future timing evolution using a Kalman filter-like model. Several examples are presented showing the system in action in diverse musical settings. Connections with machine learning are highlighted, showing current weaknesses and new possible directions.

Several examples are presented showing the system in action in diverse musical settings. Connections with machine learning are highlighted, showing current weaknesses and new possible directions.

paragraphs: The paper presents a musical accompaniment system in which a computer-driven orchestra follows and learns from a soloist. The setting resembles a concerto, with the accompaniment responding to an ongoing performance. The system separates this task into three modules that handle score matching, sound generation, and prediction of future timing.

A hidden Markov model determines the real-time match between the performance and the score. A second module generates accompaniment audio by applying phase vocoding to an existing recording. Between them, a Kalman filter-like model predicts how timing will evolve, connecting the estimate of the soloist’s current progress to the audio that should follow.

This architecture matters because following a performer requires both tracking the present and anticipating what comes next. The paper presents examples in diverse musical settings to show the system operating. It also discusses connections to machine learning, identifies current weaknesses, and points toward possible new directions. The contribution is an integrated accompaniment system illustrated through performance examples.
summary.tldr: A computer accompaniment system combines real-time score tracking, recorded-audio transformation, and timing prediction to follow a soloist.

title: Music Plus One and Machine Learning

abstract: Boosting is a popular way to derive powerful learners from simpler hypothesis classes. Following previous work (Mason et al., 1999; Friedman, 2000) on general boosting frameworks, we analyze gradient-based descent algorithms for boosting with respect to any convex objective and introduce a new measure of weak learner performance into this setting which generalizes existing work. We present the first weak to strong learning guarantees for the existing gradient boosting work for smooth convex objectives, and also demonstrate that this work fails for non-smooth objectives. To address this issue, we present new algorithms which extend this boosting approach to arbitrary convex loss functions and give corresponding weak to strong convergence results. In addition, we demonstrate experimental results that support our analysis and demonstrate the need for the new algorithms we present.

paragraphs: Boosting builds stronger predictors from simpler hypothesis classes. This paper studies that process as gradient-based optimization of a convex objective. It introduces a measure of weak-learner performance that generalizes previous work, providing a basis for analyzing when repeated use of weak learners leads to stronger learning.

For smooth convex objectives, the authors establish weak-to-strong learning guarantees for existing gradient boosting work. They also show that the same approach fails for non-smooth objectives. This distinction identifies a substantive boundary: a guarantee for smooth losses does not by itself justify applying the existing method to every convex loss.

The paper addresses that boundary with new algorithms designed for arbitrary convex loss functions and supplies corresponding weak-to-strong convergence results. Experiments support the analysis and demonstrate the need for the proposed algorithms. The contribution therefore includes both a stronger understanding of an existing boosting approach and an extension that handles a broader class of objectives. The new methods respond directly to the failure identified in the non-smooth setting.
summary.tldr: The paper proves guarantees for smooth-objective gradient boosting and develops new algorithms with convergence results for arbitrary convex losses.

title: Generalized Boosting Algorithms for Convex Optimization

abstract: Managing risk in dynamic decision problems is of cardinal importance in many fields such as finance and process control. The most common approach to defining risk is through various variance related criteria such as the Sharpe Ratio or the standard deviation adjusted reward. It is known that optimizing many of the variance related risk criteria is NP-hard. In this paper we devise a framework for local policy gradient style algorithms for reinforcement learning for variance related criteria. Our starting point is a new formula for the variance of the cost-to-go in episodic tasks. Using this formula we develop policy gradient algorithms for criteria that involve both the expected cost and the variance of the cost. We prove the convergence of these algorithms to local minima and demonstrate their applicability in a portfolio planning problem.

paragraphs: Dynamic decision-making often needs to account for variability as well as average outcomes. Variance-related risk criteria make that concern explicit, but optimizing many such criteria is NP-hard. This paper develops a framework for local policy-gradient reinforcement learning methods that incorporate both expected cost and its variance.

The starting point is a new expression for the variance of cost-to-go in episodic tasks. Cost-to-go describes the remaining accumulated cost, so its variance captures uncertainty in that accumulated outcome. The authors use this formula to derive policy-gradient algorithms for objectives involving both the mean and variability of cost, connecting a risk-sensitive objective to a policy update procedure.

The paper proves that the algorithms converge to local minima and demonstrates their applicability in portfolio planning. The local nature of the guarantee is central: the result establishes convergence to locally optimal solutions within a difficult optimization setting. The contribution provides a formally supported way to learn policies for variance-related objectives while addressing risk directly in the learning criterion.
summary.tldr: A new episodic cost-variance formula supports risk-sensitive policy-gradient algorithms with proven convergence to local minima.

title: Policy Gradients with Variance Related Risk Criteria

abstract: Approximate dynamic programming is a popular method for solving large Markov decision processes. This paper describes a new class of approximate dynamic programming (ADP) methods—distributionally robust ADP—that address the curse of dimensionality by minimizing a pessimistic bound on the policy loss. This approach turns ADP into an optimization problem, for which we derive new mathematical program formulations and analyze itsp properties. DRADP improves on the theoretical guarantees of existing ADP methods—it guarantees convergence and L_1 norm-based error bounds. The empirical evaluation of DRADP shows that the theoretical guarantees translate well into good performance on benchmark problems.

The empirical evaluation of DRADP shows that the theoretical guarantees translate well into good performance on benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Large Markov decision processes can be difficult to solve because the space of possible situations grows too large to handle directly. Approximate dynamic programming addresses this through approximation. This paper proposes a class of methods that chooses approximations by minimizing a pessimistic bound on policy loss, tying the optimization target to decision quality.

The approach, called distributionally robust approximate dynamic programming, turns this task into an explicit optimization problem. The authors develop mathematical programming formulations and analyze their properties. Working with a pessimistic bound means optimizing a conservative assessment of how much performance a policy may lose, giving the approximation procedure a directly relevant objective.

The theoretical results provide convergence guarantees and error bounds measured using an L1 norm, improving on the guarantees of existing approximate dynamic programming methods discussed by the authors. Benchmark experiments also show good performance. Together, these findings suggest that the conservative optimization formulation can offer useful practical behavior alongside stronger mathematical guarantees.
summary.tldr: Distributionally robust approximate dynamic programming minimizes a pessimistic policy-loss bound and provides convergence guarantees with good benchmark performance.

title: Approximate Dynamic Programming By Minimizing Distributionally Robust Bounds

abstract: In this paper we propose a unified framework for structured prediction with hidden variables which includes hidden conditional random fields and latent structural support vector machines as special cases. We describe an approximation for this general structured prediction formulation using duality, which is based on a local entropy approximation. We then derive an efficient message passing algorithm that is guaranteed to converge, and demonstrate its effectiveness in the tasks of image segmentation as well as 3D indoor scene understanding from single images, showing that our approach is superior to latent structural support vector machines and hidden conditional random fields.
originalAbstract: In this paper we propose a unified framework for structured prediction with hidden variables which includes hidden conditional random fields and latent structural support vector machines as special cases. We describe an approximation for this general structured prediction formulation using duality, which is based on a local entropy approximation. We then derive an efficient message passing algorithm that is guaranteed to converge, and demonstrate its effectiveness in the tasks of image segmentation as well as 3D indoor scene understanding from single images, showing that our approach is superior to latent structural support vector machines and hidden conditional random fields.

paragraphs: Structured prediction with hidden variables must account for both relationships among outputs and information that is not directly observed. The paper presents a common framework for this setting. Hidden conditional random fields and latent structural support vector machines both appear as special cases, connecting two established approaches within one formulation.

To make the general formulation computationally manageable, the authors construct an approximation using duality and a local approximation to entropy. They then derive an efficient message passing algorithm with a convergence guarantee. The guarantee concerns the derived algorithm; the method still uses an approximation to the general structured prediction formulation.

The authors demonstrate the approach on image segmentation and on understanding three-dimensional indoor scenes from single images. In these tasks, they report better performance than hidden conditional random fields and latent structural support vector machines. The results support the usefulness of the unified formulation and its inference procedure for these visual prediction problems, while the convergence result gives a separate theoretical property of the algorithm.
summary.tldr: A unified framework for structured prediction with hidden variables yields a convergent message passing algorithm and improved results on two visual tasks.

title: Efficient Structured Prediction with Latent Variables for General Graphical Models
